33.s: India's basic unemployment problem is mainly:
33.x: India's problem is structural, with seasonal, disguised and underemployment, unlike the demand-deficient unemployment Keynes stressed for developed economies.

33.s: Which situation best illustrates structural unemployment?
o: A firm laying off workers during a recession
A worker changing jobs after voluntarily quitting
A farm worker remaining idle during the agricultural off-season
A labour-intensive economy shifting towards capital-intensive production
33.x: A shift from labour-intensive to capital-intensive production changes the demand for labour and creates a long-term structural mismatch.
33.tq: Match the example to long-term structural change rather than a temporary interruption.
xs: A **labour-intensive economy shifting towards capital-intensive production** illustrates **structural** unemployment — so option **(4)** is correct.
Recession layoffs = **cyclical**; voluntary job change = **frictional**; idle in the off-season = **seasonal**.
xa: Structural unemployment is **long-run** and needs **reskilling**.
**Technological** unemployment is a sub-type of structural.
**Indian unemployment is basically structural** — labour demand < supply.

33.s: Which combination best explains the structural nature of unemployment in India?
o: Only seasonal rainfall variations and tourism cycles
High labour mobility, labour-intensive production and low population growth
Rapid population growth, labour immobility and a shift towards capital-intensive production
Short job-search periods and temporary workplace transfers

33.tq: Select the option containing the structural causes rather than temporary causes.
xs: India's unemployment is basically **structural** due to **rapid population growth**, **labour immobility** and a **shift to capital-intensive production** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Labour **demand < supply** in the **long run**; option 2 lists the opposites.
xa: Also high **seasonal** + **disguised** unemployment and underemployment.
It differs from the **Keynesian** demand-deficient unemployment of developed countries.
**Jobless growth**: growth driven by **IT, finance**.

33.s: Which one of the following is NOT a structural cause of unemployment in India identified in the context of the secondary sector?

Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing generating abundant jobs
Slow infrastructure and delays in official paperwork
Neglected structural transformation of the secondary sector

xs: **Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing** creating jobs is NOT a cause — it would cut unemployment — so option **(2)** is correct.

xa: Also: **stringent labour laws** and an **import-oriented** rather than export-led economy.

Indian unemployment is basically **structural**.

33.s: Disguised unemployment generally means
o: large number of people remain unemployed
marginal productivity of labour is zero
33.x: Disguised unemployment occurs when more people are employed in a task than necessary. If some workers are removed, the total output does not decrease. This implies their marginal productivity is zero. It is common in agriculture and informal sectors, where surplus labour is used but does not contribute to additional productivity. Indian Economy: Growth and Development PMF IAS IE – 130 Imagine a family runs a small farm requiring 5 workers to cultivate the land efficiently. However, 8 family members are working on the farm. The extra 3 members do not add to the farm's output. If 3 leave the farm to take up another job, the total farm output remains unchanged, illustrating that their marginal productivity is zero.

33.s: Disguised unemployment generally means :
o: large number of people remain unemployed
marginal productivity of labour is zero

33.s: Disguised unemployment means :
o: Unemployment resulting from change in technology
Marginal productivity of labour is zero
People in large numbers remaining unemployed
33.x: The term ‘disguised unemployment’ commonly refers to a situation of employment with surplus manpower, in which some workers have zero marginal productivity (change in output resulting due to employing an additional unit of input) so that there removal will not affect the volume of total output. Also known as hidden unemployment, this refers to a situation where labour that is employed in a job is not actually utilized for the production of goods and services. In other words, it refers to employment of more persons in a job which lesser number of persons can accomplish.

Labour intensive industries include restaurants, hotels, agriculture, mining, as well as healthcare and caregiving.

34.s: Under the Usual Principal Status (UPS) approach, a person is treated as employed if he or she worked for at least how many days in the 365-day reference period?

34.s: Which of the following method is not used by N.S.S.O. for the measurement of unemployment in India ?
34.x: In National Sample Survey (NSS) on employment and unemployment in India, persons are classified into various activity categories on the basis of activities pursued by them during certain specified reference periods. Three reference periods are used in NSS surveys, viz. (i) one year, (ii) one week, and (iii) each day of the reference week. Based on these three periods, three different measures of activity status are arrived at. The activity status determined on the basis of the reference period of one year is known as the usual principal status or usual activity status (US) of a person, that determined on the basis of a reference period of one week is known as the current weekly status (CWS) of the person and the activity status determined on the basis of the engagement on each day during the reference week is known as the current daily status (CDS) of the person.

o: Percentage of employed persons in labour force
Percentage of employed persons in working age
Percentage of employed persons in total population

34.x: The Worker Population Ratio (WPR) is defined as the percentage of employed persons in the total population. It's a key indicator of a country's employment situation and the proportion of its workforce contributing to the economy. The WPR is calculated by dividing the number of employed persons by the total population and multiplying by 100. The WPR helps analyze the employment landscape and assess the proportion of the population actively engaged in producing goods and services. A higher WPR suggests a greater engagement of the population in productive activities, while a lower WPR may indicate a higher degree of unemployment or underemployment. The WPR is often used in conjunction with other labour market indicators, such as the Unemployment Rate (UR) and the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR), to provide a comprehensive understanding of the employment situation.

36.s: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed in :
36.x: The Indian Parliament passed the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) on 23 August, 2005. The Act was notified on 7 September, 2005 and came into force on 2 February, 2006 in 200 backward districts. On 2 October, 2009 an amendment was made in the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005, to change the nomenclature of the Act from NREGA to Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA). MGNREGA was implemented in 200 districts in the first phase with effect from February, 2006 and extended subsequently, to additional 113 and 17 districts (total 330 districts) w.e.f. April 1, 2007 and May 15, 2007, respectively. The remaining districts were included under the Act w.e.f. April 1, 2008. The Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) or VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 was enacted by the Parliament in December, 2025 to replace MGNREGA. The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 represents a comprehensive statutory overhaul of MGNREGA, aligning rural employment with the long-term vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, while strengthening accountability, infrastructure outcomes and income security. The Act modernizes the rural wage scheme by increasing guaranteed employment to 125 days per household and linking work with durable rural infrastructure.

Consider the following statements :
1. The Self-Help Group (SHG) programme was originally initiated by the State Bank of India by providing microcredit to the financially deprived.
2. In an SHG, all members of a group take responsibility for a loan that an individual member takes.
3. The Regional Rural Banks and Scheduled Commercial Banks support SHGs.
How many of the above statements are correct?
37.x: The Self-Help Group (SHG) programme was originally initiated in India by the NABARD. Based on the observations of various research studies and an action research project carried out by NABARD, the model of Self Help Group- Bank Linkage Programme (SHG-BLP) has evolved as a cost-effective mechanism for providing financial services to the unreached and underserved poor households. What started as a pilot to link around 500 SHGs of poor to the formal financial institutions during the year 1992-93 has now become the largest microfinance programme in the world, in terms of the client base and outreach. In an SHG, naturally all members become equally responsible for the loan amount sanctioned. If a member fails to repay the loan, all other remaining members should take the responsibility of repayment. Since the decisions are taken collectively, all members will take up the responsibility of recovering the loans. The Regional Rural Banks and Scheduled Commercial Banks are key financing institutions to support SHGs. Hence, statement 1 is incorrect, while other two statements are correct.

38.s: When was the ‘PM Kisan Maan-dhan Yojana’ launched for the purpose of pension to small and marginal farmers?
38.x: On September 12, 2019, the Prime Minister of India launched the ‘PM Kisan Maan-dhan Yojana’ at Ranchi, Jharkhand. The scheme is meant for old age protection and social security of small and marginal farmers. Under this scheme, the farmers would receive a minimum assured pension of Rs. 3000/- per month after attaining the age of 60 years and if the farmer dies, the spouse of the farmer shall be entitled to receive 50% of the pension as family pension. The eligible farmer is required to contribute to a Pension Fund between Rs. 55 to Rs. 200 per month (depending on the entry age) till the retirement age of 60 years. The Central Government will also contribute the equal amount to the Pension Fund. A farmer of age between 18 to 40 years, who owns cultivable lands up to 2 hectare is eligible for this scheme.

38.s: Who among the following can join the National Pension System (NPS)?

All State Government employees joining the services
All Central Government employees including those
38.x: The National Pension System (NPS) is a voluntary defined contributory pension system in India. Any citizen of India (whether resident or non-resident) and overseas citizen of India (OCI) between the age of 18-70 years can join NPS. NPS is applicable to all Central Government employees (except Armed Forces) joining the services on or after 1st January, 2004 and to all State Government employees joining the services after the date of notification by the respective State Governments. It was opened up for all citizens of India in 2009 and for OCI card holders in October, 2019. It is administered and regulated by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA). Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

38.s: In Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan Scheme, each subscriber shall receive the minimum assured pension of ......... per month after attaining the age of 60 years.

The unorganized sector workers, with monthly income of less than Rs. 15000 and who belong to the entry age group of 18-40 years, are eligible for this scheme.

38.s:
With reference to the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM) Yojana, consider the following statements:
1. The entry age group for enrolment in the scheme is 21 to 40 years.

3. Each subscriber under the scheme shall receive a minimum pension of Rs. 3,000 per month after attaining the age of 60 years.
4. Family pension is applicable to the spouse and unmarried daughters.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
38.x: Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM) is a voluntary and contributory Pension Scheme for Unorganized Workers at the entry age of 18 to 40 years with a maximum monthly income of Rs. 15000 or less. The applicants between the age group of 18 to 40 years will have to make monthly contributions ranging between Rs. 55 to Rs. 200 per month (as per their entry age) till they attain the age of 60. The Central Government will deposit equal matching share in the pension account of the worker every month. Each subscriber under this scheme shall receive a minimum assured pension of Rs.3000 per month after attaining the age of 60 years and if the beneficiary dies, the spouse of the beneficiary shall be entitled to receive 50% of the pension as family pension. Family pension is applicable only to spouse. Hence, only statements 2 and 3 are correct while statements 1 and 4 are incorrect.

39.s: According to the World Food Summit, 1996, food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to which of the following?
o: Food of their choice irrespective of dietary needs
Adequate food supplied exclusively by the government
Sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active and healthy life
Food grains available only during periods of shortage
39.x: The World Food Summit definition emphasizes physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active and healthy life.
39.tq: Use the precise official definition and reject the look-alike phrase ‘food of their choice’.
xs: Per the **World Food Summit 1996** (FAO), food security means access to **sufficient, safe and nutritious food** for an **active and healthy life**, option **(3)**.
⚠ It does **not** mean food "**of their choice**" — a trap set in **APPSC G2 2017**; nor does it require supply only by government.
xa: The definition says **all people, at all times**, with **physical and economic access**.
Four dimensions: **availability, access (affordability), utilisation/absorption, stability**.
India achieved **national** food security (buffer stocks) without fully assuring **household** food security — hence **PDS** and **NFSA**.

39.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognized dimension of food security?
39.x: Availability, accessibility, affordability or access, utilisation/absorption and stability are associated with food security. Accountability is not a dimension.
39.tq: Find the odd term among the established dimensions.
xs: **Accountability** is **not** a dimension of food security, option **(2)** (UPPSC 2025 trap).
**Stability**, **accessibility** and **availability** are recognised dimensions, along with **affordability** and **absorption/utilisation**.
xa: **Availability** = production + imports + previous stocks.
**Absorption/utilisation** = the body's ability to use the food.
Price and quantity of exports are also **not** dimensions.

39.s: According to Amartya Sen's entitlement approach, famines primarily arise from:

Excessive buffer stocks maintained by the government
A collapse of people's command over food through income, exchange and transfers
39.x: Sen argued that famine results from a collapse of people's entitlements or command over food, not merely from a decline in overall food availability.

xs: For **Sen**, famines arise from a **collapse of people's command over food through income, exchange and transfers** (entitlements), option **(4)**.
He rejected the view that a **fall in food availability/supply** alone causes famine.
xa: Book: **Poverty and Famines**, **1981**.
⚠ Sen = **entitlement**, not availability.

39.s: Which of the following best distinguishes national food security from household food security?
o: National food security concerns only imports, whereas household food security concerns only domestic production.
National food security concerns aggregate availability, whereas household food security concerns actual access and affordability for each household.
National food security applies to urban areas, whereas household food security applies only to rural areas.
National food security is based on nutrition, whereas household food security is based only on buffer stocks.
39.x: National food security refers to adequate aggregate production and stocks. Household food security requires that each household can actually obtain and afford food.
39.tq: Split the comparison into aggregate availability versus household-level access.
xs: **National** food security = **aggregate production/availability + buffer stock**; **household** = each household can **access and afford** food — option **(2)**.
Neither is defined by urban/rural or by imports alone.
xa: India achieved national food security without fully assuring household — hence **PDS** and **NFSA**.
**Affordability** = money enough for sufficient, safe, nutritious food.
**Accessibility** = food within reach of every person.

40.s: In which year was the ‘National Extension Service’ launched?
40.x: The National Extension Service (NES) programme was launched in 1953. 40.s: Who among the following was the architect of community development in India ?
40.x: The main architect of community development in India was S.K. Dey. He was the first Cooperative and Panchayati Raj Minister of India. Mr. Dey is remembered as the man who pioneered and steered community development in independent India. He was instrumental in starting the Community Development Programme by the Government of India in the year 1952. Jawahar Lal Nehru was the Prime Minister at that time.

Consider the following pairs: Programme/Projects Ministry
1. Drought-Prone Area Programme Ministry of Agriculture
2. Desert Development Programme Ministry of Environment and Forests
3. National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas Ministry of Rural Development Which of the pairs given above is/are correct?
40.x: Pair 1 is incorrect: This programme was initiated during the Fourth Five-Year Plan with the objectives of providing employment to the people in drought-prone areas and creating productive assets. The National Committee on the Development of Backwards Areas reviewed the performance of this programme. Pair 2 is incorrect: The Desert Development Programme (DDP) by the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, aims to minimise the adverse effects of drought and control desertification by rejuvenating the natural resource base of identified desert areas. 40.s: The second phase of the Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) is to be implemented during which time period?
40.x: On 27th September, 2019, the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS) under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, launched the 10 Year Rural Sanitation Strategy (2019-2029), with focus on sustaining the sanitation behaviour change that has been achieved under the Swachh Bharat Mission Grameen (SBM-G).

40.s: Jal Jeevan Mission Scheme was declared in the Union Budget of which Financial Year?
40.x: Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), a Central Government initiative under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, aims to ensure access of piped water to every household in India. The mission’s goal was to provide all households in rural India safe and adequate water through individual household tap connections by 2024. This mission was launched by the PM Narendra Modi on 15 August, 2019 from the ramparts of Red Fort. The ‘Har Ghar Nal Se Jal’ programme was announced by the Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in her Budget 2019-20 Speech. This programme forms a crucial part of the Jal Jeevan Mission. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer. Union Budget 2025- 26 has extended the Jal Jeevan Mission till 2028 with the aim of benefitting the remaining (about 20%) rural households. Rural households with tap water connection at the launch of JJM (i.e., as on 15 August, 2019) were around 3.24 crore only (16.72% of total rural households). As on 29 May, 2026, under JJM (since its inception) around 12.62 crore additional rural households have been provided with tap water connections. Thus, as on 29 May, 2026, out of about 19.36 crore rural households in the country, about 15.86 crore (81.91%) households are reported to have tap water supply in their homes.

40.s: Which programme was approved by the Union Cabinet in April, 2025 to develop border villages ?
40.x: In April 2025, the Union Cabinet approved the Vibrant Villages Programme-II (VVP-II) for the comprehensive development of border villages and for improving their living standards. This programme focuses on the socioeconomic development of villages located in blocks abutting international land borders, strengthening basic infrastructure and amenities, and expanding livelihood opportunities, with the objective of developing border villages.

40.s: A village in the plain area of India comes under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojna, if its population is more than :
40.x: Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojna (PMGSY) was started on 25 December, 2000. The objective of the PMGSY is to provide all-weather road connectivity, to the eligible unconnected habitations in the rural areas with a population of 500 persons and above in plain areas. In respect of hill States, the desert areas and the tribal areas, the objective would be to connect eligible unconnected habitations with a population of 250 persons and above. In this scheme the rural roads to be taken up will, by and large, be surface roads (black topped/cement concrete). However, depending upon the soil conditions, all-weather roads may also be gravel roads, but with all necessary cross-drainage structures.

40.s: Which initiative was launched to provide a tap water connection to every rural household by 2024?
40.x: The Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, has the specific target of providing Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTC) to every rural household in India by 2024, under the ' Har Ghar Jal ' vision. AMRUT focuses on urban infrastructure, while SBM focuses on sanitation.

40.s: Which of the following scheme is an attempt to make rural areas socially economically and physically sustainable regions?
40.x: Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (SPMRM) was launched in 2016 as an attempt to make the selected rural areas socially, economically and physically sustainable regions by providing economic, social, basic and digital amenities, thus leading to sustainable and balanced regional development in the country. The objective of this mission is to stimulate local economic development, enhance basic services, and create well planned Rurban clusters.

40.s: PURA (Providing Urban Amenities to Rural Areas) model was advocated by :
40.x: Providing Urban Amenities to Rural Areas (PURA) is a strategy for rural development in India. This concept was given by the former President Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. On the eve of India’s 54th Republic Day, in 2003, Dr. Kalam addressed the nation explaining them his vision of transformation of rural India through PURA model. PURA was envisaged as a self-sustainable and viable model of service delivery to be managed through an implementation framework between the different stakeholders involved, namely local people, pubic authorities and the private sector.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences appoints the prize-winner(s) according to the same principles as for the Nobel Prizes. 41.s: Which of the following is a cause of rural to urban migration in India?

While the desire for a better life and economic stability is a primary motivator, the decision to migrate is influenced by a complex interplay of economic, social, and environmental conditions (including unbalanced rural-urban development) in both rural and urban areas. 48.s:
In India, which of the followings can be considered as public investment in agriculture?
1. Fixing Minimum Support Price for agricultural produce of all crops.
2. Computerization of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies.
3. Social Capital development.
4. Free electricity supply to farmers.
5. Waiver of agricultural loans by the banking system.
6. Setting up of cold storage facilities by the governments.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
48.x: Public investment means investment in creation of physical infrastructure, such as, setting up cold storage facilities, construction of canals and rural roads, computerization of primary credit societies, social capital formation with education and training, research and development etc. Hence, statement (2), (3) and (6) are correct. Investment is a term associated with the capital part of the budget. Subsidy is a revenue part and it is not included in public investment. Thus, subsidies and loan waivers are not investment. Free electricity supply to farmers and waiver of agricultural loans by the banking system are parts of the government's subsidy policy. Public investment in agriculture constitutes investment made by government to create capital or social assets to improve agricultural productivity. Fixing MSP gives farmers the remunerative price without creating any durable infrastructure. Hence, statement (1), (4) and (5) are incorrect.

48.s: Why does the Government of India promote the use of 'Neem-coated Urea' in agriculture?
o: Release of Neem oil in the soil increases nitrogen fixation by the soil microorganisms.
Neem coating slows down the rate of distribution of urea in the soil
Nitrous oxide, which is a greenhouse gas, is not at all released into the atmosphere by crop fields.
It is a combination of a weedicide and a fertilizer for particular crops.
48.x: Urea is a white crystalline substance; it is highly water-soluble and contains 46% nitrogen. It is used extensively as a chemical fertiliser and for industrial purposes. In May 2015, the Centre made it mandatory to coat all indigenously manufactured and imported urea with neem oil. Neem coating was intended to curb the illegal diversion of highly subsidised urea for nonagricultural uses, including plywood, dyes, cattle feed, and synthetic milk makers. Neem has proven Nitrification-inhibitory properties and thus slows the release of nitrogen from urea, making nitrogen available over a longer period with minimal loss, thereby increasing nitrogen use efficiency. It reduces the likelihood of diversion of agricultural-grade urea to non-agricultural uses

48.s: Which one of the following agriculture practices is eco-friendly?
48.x: Organic farming is an eco-friendly agricultural practice that uses fertilizers of organic origin such as compost manure, green manure, and bone meal and places emphasis on techniques such as crop rotation and companion planting. It is defined as production of crops without the use of synthetic chemical fertilizers and pesticides. Compared with conventional agriculture, organic farming reduces soil erosion, decreases nitrate leaching into groundwater and surface water and recycles animal wastes back into farm.

51.x: The Blue Box is Amber-type support with production limits; the Green Box causes minimal distortion and the Amber Box is distorting support subject to limits.
n: Green Box support causes minimal or no trade distortion. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
Amber Box support distorts trade or production. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
Amber Box support is subject to limits. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
Blue Box support is Amber-type support with production-limiting conditions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
Blue Box support combines Amber Box support with production limitation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
xa: ⚠ **MSP** is Amber Box; de minimis **10%** for developing countries, **5%** for developed.
India joined the **WTO** in **1995**; import competition rose afterwards.
**Bt cotton (2002)** is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation.

51.s:
Assertion (A): Production-linked subsidies are examples of Amber Box support.
Reason (R): Amber Box support is trade- or production-distorting and is subject to limits.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
51.x: Both are true: production-linked subsidies are Amber Box because the Amber Box covers support that distorts trade or production and is subject to limits. R explains A.
51.tq: Ask whether the definition explains the example.
n: Production-linked subsidies are examples of Amber Box support. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 16-17]
xs: Both A and R are true, and **R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Amber Box** support **distorts trade or production** and is **subject to limits**.
**Production-linked subsidies** distort production, so they fall in the Amber Box — R explains A.
xa: **Price support** and **MSP** are also Amber Box.
Green Box = **decoupled income support**, environmental programmes — allowed.
Liberalisation after 1991 saw a **decline in government investment in agriculture** (APPSC 2023 key).

51.s: The National Food Security Mission was renamed as which of the following in Financial Year 2024-25?
o: National Food Security and Nutrition Mission

51.s: Which of the following funding ratios is associated with the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture, including its special-region pattern?

90:10 generally and 60:40 for the Himalayan States

**NMSA** also dates from **2014-15** (operational launch).

51.s: The National Mission on Edible Oils–Oilseeds, announced on 3 October 2024, has an outlay of:

NMEO-Oil Palm focuses on **NE** and **A&N**.

AP aims at **30%** agri growth in five years with **17 growth engines**.

51.s: Under the Per Drop More Crop component of NMSA, the micro-irrigation subsidy can be up to:

51.s: According to the Union Budget 2026–27 figure cited for agriculture, the allocation was approximately:

**PM-AASHA** (**2018**) aims at remunerative prices.

51.s: Which one of the following was an effect of liberalisation after 1991 on Indian agriculture?
o: Replacement of agricultural subsidies by foreign aid
Increase in government investment in agriculture in every period
A ban on all private participation in agriculture
Decline in government investment in agriculture

xs: Post-**1991** liberalisation brought a **decline in government investment in agriculture** — option **(4)** (APPSC **2023** key).
Option (2) says the opposite; liberalisation encouraged, not banned, private participation (e.g. **contract farming** in NAP **2000**).
xa: GDP share of agriculture fell from **29.02% (1991)** to **17.9% (2014)**, with rising rural indebtedness.
**WTO entry 1995**: import competition rose; subsidies as a share of farm income declined.
Input costs rose over **300%** since the early 2000s.

51.s: Which genetically modified crop was approved for commercial cultivation in India in 2002?

xs: **Bt cotton**, approved in **2002**, is India's only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation — option **(2)**.
No Bt rice, soybean or wheat is approved for commercial cultivation.
xa: It is listed among the post-**1991** liberalisation-era changes in farming.
Input costs rose over **300%** since the early 2000s.
**WTO entry 1995** brought rising import competition.

51.s: Sustainable agriculture seeks to combine environmental health, economic profitability and:

**NMSA** components: Rainfed Area Development, **Soil Health Management**, **Per Drop More Crop**, Agroforestry.

51.s: Sustainable agriculture is best understood as the use of land in a manner that:

Maximises present output regardless of future soil quality
Maintains land quality while meeting present needs without compromising future generations
Uses land only for export-oriented crops

xs: Sustainable agriculture uses land so its **quality remains intact**, meeting present needs **without compromising future generations** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2019** key).
Maximising present output regardless of soil quality (option 2) is the opposite of sustainability.
xa: Its ultimate goal covers **all three pillars**: environmental health, economic profitability, social and economic equity (APPSC **2018** key).
**NMSA** is the **NAPCC** mission for sustainable, climate-resilient farming.

51.s: Ultimate goal of sustainable agriculture is
o: Enhancement of health and safety of human population
51.x: Sustainable agriculture ultimately seeks to conserve natural resources, protect the environment, and enhance human health and safety simultaneously making ' All of these ' the most complete answer.

51.s: Which is not included in 'National Agricultural Development Yojna'?
51.x: National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) has been made operational from the year 2014-15 which aims at making agriculture more productive, sustainable, remunerative and climate resilient by promoting location specific integrated/composite farming systems; soil and moisture conservation measures; comprehensive soil health management; efficient water management practices and mainstreaming rainfed technologies. Programs under the NMSA include Soil Health Management (SHM), Rainfed Area Development (RAD), Sub-Mission on AgroForestry (SMAF), National Bamboo Mission (NBM) and the Climate Change and Sustainable Agriculture : Monitoring, Modeling and Networking (CCSAMMN) component. RAD and SHM includes activities under Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) and the Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme. On Farm Water Management (OFWM) was implemented as one of the component of NMSA during 2014-15 with the objective of enhancing water use efficiency by promoting technologicial interventions like drip and sprinkler technologies, efficient water application and distribution system, secondary storage etc. Thereafter, these activities have been subsumed under the 'Per Drop More Crop (PDMC)' component of Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PM- KSY) during 2015-16. Hence, PM-KSY is not associated with NMSA.

Abolition of producer organisations and cluster-based activities

Because CCRCs automatically cancel crop insurance

52.s: Which one of the following sequences correctly represents the debt cycle faced by distressed farmers?
o: Borrowing → high input cost → asset sale → crop failure → fresh borrowing
High input cost → borrowing → crop failure or low price → inability to repay → fresh borrowing → asset sale → debt trap
Crop failure → institutional credit → higher income → asset purchase → debt repayment
Low input cost → borrowing → assured procurement → inability to repay → debt trap
52.x: The stated cycle begins with high input costs, leads to borrowing, crop failure or low prices, non-repayment, fresh borrowing and asset sales, ultimately producing a debt trap.
52.tq: Arrange the stages by cause and consequence, beginning with the initial financial pressure.
xs: The debt cycle: **high input cost → borrowing → crop failure or low price → inability to repay → fresh borrowing → asset sale → debt trap** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) puts borrowing before input cost; options (3) and (4) start with relief factors, not distress.
xa: Input costs rose **300%+** since the early 2000s.
ADSI **2015**: the biggest cause of farmer suicides = **bankruptcy or indebtedness**.
Root causes: debt = **immediate trigger**; roots = rain-fed risk, low prices, no social security.

52.s: National Agricultural Insurance Scheme replacing Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme was introduced in the year:
52.x: The Union Ministry of Agriculture launched the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) from the Rabi, 1999- 2000 season in place of Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme which was started on April 1, 1985. NAIS was launched as part of risk management in agriculture with the objective of providing financial support to the farmers in the event of failure of crops as a result of natural calamities, pests and diseases. NAIS was extended to Kharif crops as well by the Union Budget 2004-05. A new central sector scheme 'National Crop Insurance Programme' (NCIP) was formulated by grouping NAIS, Pilot Modified NAIS (started from Rabi 2010-11), Pilot Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (WBCIS-started from Kharif 2007) and Pilot Coconut Palm Insurance Scheme (CPIS- started in 2009-10). NCIP came into force from Rabi 2013-14 season and covers all districts. A new umbrella scheme 'Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojna' (PMFBY) was launched in India by the Ministry of Agriculture from Kharif 2016 season onwards. It incorporates the best features of all previous schemes and at the same time, all previous shortcomings/weaknesses have been removed. PMFBY replaced the NAIS and modified NAIS. Further, WBCIS has also been modified on par with PMFBY in 2016.

53.s: Legally stipulated maximum size beyond which no individual farmer can hold any land is :
53.x: Land ceiling is the legal maximum limit on the amount of land that an individual or family can own. Land held in excess of this limit, known as surplus land, is then taken by the government for redistribution to landless farmers and other marginalized groups. The main purpose of land ceiling legislation is to reduce land inequality, promote fairer distribution of land, and prevent wealthy individuals or groups from amassing excessive amounts of land. It is a key aspect of agrarian reform, intended to prevent the concentration of land in the hands of a few and to redistribute surplus land to landless farmers and the rural poor. By redistributing land, it aims to reduce economic and social disparities in rural areas.

53.s: The rent ceiling contemplated under tenancy reform was generally in the range of:
o: One-half to two-thirds of the produce
One-tenth to one-twentieth of the produce
One-third to one-half of the produce
One-fourth to one-sixth of the produce
53.x: Tenancy reform sought to regulate rent by limiting it to approximately one-fourth to one-sixth of the produce.

xs: Rent was capped at **one-fourth to one-sixth** (**1/4 to 1/6**) of produce — option **(4)**.

xa: ⚠ Rent cap **1/4 to 1/6**; Bhoodan appeal **1/6th** of land; bargadar share **75%**.

53.s: Land ceiling laws in India redistributed about what share of the cultivable area?
53.x: Despite two rounds of ceiling laws (1950s and early 1970s), less than 2% of cultivable area was redistributed.

AP phase II: **20 lakh acres** surplus estimated vs only **5 lakh acres** taken over.

53.s: Consolidation of holdings achieved comparatively greater success in which group of regions?
o: Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh
53.x: Consolidation succeeded in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, while it made little progress in southern and eastern States.

xs: **Consolidation** succeeded in **Punjab, Haryana and western UP** — option **(4)**.
It made **little progress in southern and eastern States**, ruling out options (1), (2) and (3).
xa: Consolidation is one of the land-reform types along with abolition, tenancy and ceilings.
**Operation Barga** (**West Bengal**) was the eastern success — in tenancy, not consolidation.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about Operation Barga:
1. It was carried out in West Bengal under the Left Front government.
2. Recorded bargadars got heritable rights.
3. Recorded bargadars were entitled to 25% of the produce.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Statement 1 is correct: Operation Barga was a West Bengal Left Front programme. Statement 2 is correct: recorded bargadars got heritable rights. Statement 3 is wrong: their share was 75% of the produce, not 25%. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses statement 2, and options with 3 include the wrong share.
53.tq: Barga = bargadar keeps three-fourths (75%).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Operation Barga** was a **West Bengal**, **Left Front** programme.
Statement 2 correct: recorded **bargadars** got **heritable rights**.
Statement 3 wrong: their share was **75%** of produce, not 25%.

53.s: Which of the following was an important reason for the limited redistribution achieved through land ceiling laws?
o: Absence of any ceiling legislation in the States
Exemptions for plantations, orchards and mechanised farms
Automatic transfer of all surplus land to corporations
53.x: Exemptions for plantations, orchards and mechanised farms reduced the amount of land available for redistribution.
53.tq: Identify the implementation factor that explains the limited outcome.
xs: **Exemptions** for **plantations, orchards** and **"mechanised" farms** limited redistribution — option **(2)**.
About **21 States** had ceiling laws, so ceiling legislation was not absent.
xa: Outcome: less than **2%** of cultivable area redistributed.
The pre-1972 **individual** unit encouraged **benami** transfers.

53.s: Under the AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, which pair is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Basic unit of ceiling – family of five
Each extra family member – one-fifth of the ceiling added
Lands of husband and wife – treated as separate units
53.x: The husband's and wife's lands are clubbed together, not treated as separate units.
xa: ⚠ **1961** Act = individual unit; **1973** Act = family of 5.

53.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Land consolidation is associated with land reform.
Tenancy reform concerns rent, tenure and ownership.
Land ceiling refers to the minimum legal holding permitted.
Abolition of intermediaries aims to remove middlemen.
53.x: Option C is incorrect: a land ceiling is the maximum land one may legally hold, not the minimum. Surplus above it is redistributed.
53.tq: Watch for 'minimum' replacing 'maximum'.
n: Land consolidation is associated with land reform. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
Tenancy reform concerns rent, tenure and ownership. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
Land ceiling means the maximum legal holding. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
Abolition of intermediaries means removing middlemen. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **land ceiling refers to the minimum legal holding** — so option **(3)** is the answer.
A **land ceiling** is the **maximum legal holding**; **surplus land** above it is redistributed.
Options 1, 2, 4 are correct: **consolidation** is a land reform; **tenancy reform** = **rent, tenure and ownership**; **abolition of intermediaries** removes **middlemen**.
xa: ⚠ **Multiple cropping** is **not** a land reform.
Ceiling outcome: less than **2%** of cultivable area redistributed.
**1972** national guidelines made the **family** the ceiling unit.

53.s:
Assertion (A): Land reforms contribute to reduction of inequality.
Reason (R): Land ceiling facilitates redistribution of surplus land.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
53.x: Both are true: land reforms reduce inequality because land ceilings free up surplus land to give to the landless. R explains A.

n: Land reforms reduce inequality. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
Land ceiling means the maximum legal holding. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
Surplus land is associated with redistribution. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #49 · pp 73-74]
xs: Both A and R are true, and **R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Land reforms **reduce inequality**, involve agrarian restructuring and promote agricultural growth.
The **land ceiling** frees **surplus land** for **redistribution** — R explains A.
xa: **Tenancy reform** covers regulation of rent, **security of tenure** and **ownership rights**.
Tenancy reform failed through "**voluntary surrenders**" and evictions.
**National Council for Land Reforms** (**2008**) is headed by the **Prime Minister**.

53.s: With reference to land reforms in independent India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: The ceiling laws were aimed at family holdings and not individual holdings.
The major aim of land reforms was providing agricultural land to all the landless.
It resulted in cultivation of cash crops as a predominant form of cultivation.
Land reforms permitted no exemptions to the ceiling limits.
53.x: Land reforms in post-independence India unfolded in two broad phases. The first phase, known as the institutional reforms phase, began soon after Independence and continued until the early 1960s. It focused on restructuring agrarian relations through the abolition of intermediaries such as zamindars and jagirdars; the implementation of tenancy reforms to provide security of tenure, reduce rents, and confer ownership rights on tenants; the imposition of ceilings on landholdings; and the promotion of cooperatives and community development programmes. The primary objective of these reforms was to achieve a more equitable distribution of land by transferring land from large landlords to poor and landless peasants. The second phase, which began in the mid-tolate 1960s, coincided with the Green Revolution and shifted the emphasis from institutional changes to technological reforms aimed at increasing agricultural productivity by adopting modern inputs and farming techniques.

14-digit alphanumeric ID generated from the geo-coordinates of a parcel's vertices

Banks provide loans to SHGs against a group guarantee, and the loan quantum can be several times the deposits placed by such SHGs with the banks. The concept underscores the principles of Thrift, Credit, and Self- Help. Members of SHG agree to save regularly and contribute to a common fund. The concept of joint liability plays a significant role in SHG loans. This means that all members of the group are collectively responsible for repaying the loan taken by an individual member. 56.tq: Select the option containing the characteristic structural problems of APMC markets.
xs: **Cartels of licensed traders and dependence on approved middlemen** is an APMC problem — option **(4)**.
APMC problems also include **market and licence fees**, **commission charges** and **too few mandis** — so options (1), (2), (3) state the opposite.
xa: **Intermediaries** raise consumer prices; onion hit **Rs 62/kg** in Delhi, blamed on hoarding and middlemen.
About **40%** of built storage lies idle → **distress sale**.
**Price spread** = consumer price minus farmer's price; measures middlemen's share.

56.s: Which of the following is NOT a reform required from States for participation in e-NAM?
o: A single licence valid across the State
Regulating all agricultural prices through the State Government
A single-point levy of market fee
56.x: The required reforms include a single State-wide licence, single-point market-fee levy and electronic trading. State-wide administrative price regulation is not the specified reform.
56.tq: Find the option that substitutes price regulation for the actual market reform.
xs: **Regulating all agricultural prices** is not a required reform — option **(2)**; it was the distractor in APPSC **2016**.
States must **allow e-trading/e-auction**, give a **single licence** valid across the State and a **single-point levy** of market fee.
xa: ⚠ The APPSC **2016** answer was **allow electronic trading**.
The **Model APLM Act, 2017** proposed the same: **unified licence**, **single-point fee**, **e-trading**.
e-NAM grant: up to **₹75 lakh per mandi**.

56.s: ‘AGMARK’ is related with :
56.x: AGMARK is a certification mark employed on agricultural products, assuring that they conform to a grade standard notified by Directorate of Marketing & Inspection (which also issues the certificate of 'AGMARK'), Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare under Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The AGMARK is legally enforced by the Agricultural produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937. While the certification scheme is essentially voluntary, Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restriction on Sales) Regulation 2011 have prescribed mandatory certification under AGMARK for certain products viz. Blended Edible Vegetable Oil, etc.

56.s: The Agricultural Produce and Livestock Markets in Andhra Pradesh are governed by which enactment?
o: Andhra Pradesh Agricultural Marketing and Warehousing Act, 1966
AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966
56.x: The governing law is the AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966.
56.tq: Use the exact official title to avoid a look-alike legislation trap.
xs: AP's markets are governed by the **AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966** (**Act 16 of 1966**) — option **(4)**.
The **Farmers' Trade and Commerce Act, 2020** was one of the farm laws **repealed in November 2021**; after repeal the **AP 1966 Act** remains the operative framework.
xa: Rules of **1969** under **Section 33** govern licences.
APMC Acts are **enacted by States** because agriculture market is a **State subject**.
District supervision is by the **DATMO**.

56.s: Agricultural markets are regulated by APMC Acts enacted by the States because agriculture markets are included in the:
56.x: Agricultural markets are a State subject; hence APMC laws are enacted by State legislatures.

xs: Agriculture market is a **State subject**, so APMC Acts are **enacted by States** — **State List**, option **(3)**.
⚠ The **2020 farm laws** used Concurrent List **Entry 33**, though agriculture is **State List Entry 14**.
xa: AP's law is the **AP (Agricultural Produce and Livestock) Markets Act, 1966**.
The farm laws were **repealed in November 2021**, leaving reform to States.
The **Model APMC Act, 2003** and **Model APLM Act, 2017** are models for States to adopt.

56.s: Which of the following is NOT a feature ensured by regulated agricultural markets?
o: Compulsory sale exclusively to unlicensed buyers
56.x: Regulated markets provide open auctions, standard weights, recorded prices and licensed buyers; they do not require sale to unlicensed buyers.
56.tq: Find the option that reverses the licensing principle of a regulated market.
xs: **Compulsory sale exclusively to unlicensed buyers** is not a feature — option **(1)** — regulated markets use **licensed buyers**.
Their features are **open auction**, **standard weights**, **recorded price** and **licensed buyers**.
xa: About **2,477** primary regulated markets + **4,843** sub-market yards.
Swaminathan's **National Commission on Farmers** suggested a regulated market within about **5 km** of farmers.
⚠ Problem side: **cartels of licensed traders** and **too few mandis**.

56.s: The proposal known as “One Nation, One Regulator” in agricultural quality certification primarily seeks to address which issue?
o: Replacement of all State mandis by private markets
Transfer of procurement from FCI to SFAC
Ending dual certification under BIS and AGMARK
56.x: The proposal seeks to end the dual certification arrangement involving BIS and AGMARK through a single regulatory framework.
56.tq: Identify the policy problem addressed by the reform proposal.
xs: **"One Nation, One Regulator"** seeks to **end dual certification** under **BIS and AGMARK** — option **(4)**.
It is a quality-certification debate; it does not touch mandis, grading laboratories or FCI procurement.
xa: AGMARK is certified by the **DMI**, Ministry of Agriculture.
AGMARK law: **Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937**.
⚠ e-NAM's motto is **"One Nation, One Market"** — do not confuse.

56.s: AGMARK, the quality certification mark for agricultural produce, is issued under which Act?
o: Agricultural Produce (Development and Warehousing) Corporations Act, 1956
56.x: AGMARK is issued under the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937. 'Grading and Marketing' is a common misprint used as a trap. The BIS Act governs BIS certification, and the 1956 Act set up the CWC.
56.tq: AGMARK: Grading and MARKING Act 1937.
xs: AGMARK is issued under the **Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937** — option **(2)**.
⚠ "Grading and **Marketing**" (option 1) is a misprint trap.
The **1956** Act set up the **CWC** (now under the **Warehousing Corporations Act 1962**).
xa: Certifying body: **DMI**, not the FCI.
**Central Agmark Laboratory**: **Nagpur**.
Dual certification (**BIS + AGMARK**) is the target of "One Nation, One Regulator" proposals.

56.s: The Central Agmark Laboratory and the Central Quality Control Laboratory for agricultural produce are located at:
56.x: Both the Central Agmark Laboratory (APPSC 2018 key) and the Central Quality Control Laboratory (APPSC 2025 key) are at Nagpur. New Delhi, Faridabad and Hyderabad are distractors.
56.tq: Agmark labs = Nagpur.
xs: Both the **Central Agmark Laboratory** (APPSC **2018** key) and the **Central Quality Control Laboratory** (APPSC **2025** key) are at **Nagpur** — option **(3)**.
**State grading laboratories** grade produce for packers under Agmark.
xa: AGMARK is certified by the **DMI**, Ministry of Agriculture.
AGMARK Act: **Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937**.

56.s: Which one of the following was a feature of the Model APMC Act, 2003?
o: Whole State treated as one market area
Livestock and services brought within contract farming regulation
Contract farming kept outside the APMC framework
56.x: The Model APMC Act, 2003 permitted direct sale of agricultural produce to contract-farming sponsors. The other features are associated with the 2017 or 2018 model acts.
56.tq: Identify the feature belonging to the correct model act rather than a neighbouring reform.
xs: The **Model APMC Act, 2003** allowed **direct sale to contract sponsors** — option **(4)**.
**Whole State as one market area** is from the **Model APLM Act, 2017**.
Contract farming **outside APMC** and coverage of **livestock and services** are from the **2018** Model Contract Farming Act.
xa: The 2003 Act also gave **private markets**, **special markets for perishables**, **farmer-consumer markets** and **common registration of intermediaries**.
⚠ **2003** = Model APMC; **2017** = Model APLM; **2018** = Model Contract Farming.

56.s: The Model APLM Act, 2017 proposed:
o: keeping contract farming outside the APMC purview
treating the entire State as one market area
transfer of land title to the contract sponsor
56.x: The Model APLM Act, 2017 proposed treating the whole State as one market area; keeping contract farming outside APMC belongs to the 2018 Contract Farming Act.
xa: 2017 Act also: **warehouses as market yards**, **single-point (capped) market fee**, **unified licence**, **e-trading**, livestock included.
⚠ **2003** = Model APMC; **2017** = Model APLM; **2018** = Model Contract Farming.

56.s: Under the Model Contract Farming Act, 2018, the sponsor must purchase:
o: Only a part of the pre-agreed quantity
At least half of the pre-agreed quantity
Only produce that meets export grades
56.x: The sponsor must buy the entire pre-agreed quantity and gets no right in the farmer's land.
xa: The farmer is treated as the **weaker party**; the Act covers **livestock and services**.
**FPOs** may contract for farmers; produce is **insurable**.
Registration: **RARC**; disputes via **CFFGs** at the lowest level.

56.s: The Model Contract Farming Act, 2018 treats which party as the weaker party?
56.x: The model Act recognises the farmer as the weaker party and keeps contract farming outside the APMC Act.
xa: Sponsor must buy the **entire pre-agreed quantity**.
**No permanent structure** on the farmer's land.
Online registration by the **Registering and Agreement Recording Committee (RARC)**.

56.s: Under the Model Contract Farming Act, 2018, online registration of agreements is done by the:
56.x: Registration is by the RARC; CFFGs work at village/panchayat level.
xa: Sponsor must buy the **entire pre-agreed quantity**; gets **no title** to land.
Farmer is the **weaker party**; livestock and services covered.
AP has **district-level monitoring committees (D-MC)** in **13** districts — for FPOs, not contract registration.

56.s: Under the Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce Act, 2020, trade in a 'trade area' outside APMC yards was:
o: Subject to the State market fee

Regulated APMC markets charge a **1%** market fee.

56.s:
Assertion (A): The Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act, 2020 removed stock limits on cereals, pulses, oilseeds, edible oils, onion and potato.
Reason (R): The Act provided the framework for contract farming with sponsors.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
56.x: A is correct (limits only in extraordinary situations), but contract farming was the subject of the Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement Act, not this Act.
xa: The **FPTC Act** allowed trade outside APMC yards.

Repealed in **November 2021** after a farmers' movement mainly from **Punjab and Haryana**.

56.s: The 2020 farm laws were repealed in:
56.x: The laws were repealed in November 2021; the AP Markets Act, 1966 remains the operative framework.
xa: Criticism: **APMC monopoly vs farmer choice** — the **2020** repeal left reform to States.
The three Acts dated from **Sept 2020**.
⚠ Concurrent **Entry 33** used; agriculture = State **Entry 14**.

56.s: Price spread in agricultural marketing is calculated as:
56.x: Price spread is the consumer price minus the price received by the farmer; it indicates marketing margins and the share of intermediaries.
56.tq: Use the formula direction carefully to avoid reversing the two prices.
xs: **Price spread** = **consumer price minus farmer's price** — option **(2)**.
It measures **marketing margins** and the **middlemen's share**; option (1) reverses the subtraction.
xa: Middlemen and brokers **raise consumer prices** and add **red tape**.

**Rythu Bazars** cut the spread by letting farmers sell **directly to consumers**.

56.s: The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF), launched in 2020, provides a medium- and long-term debt-financing facility of what amount for post-harvest infrastructure and community farming assets?
56.x: The AIF is a ₹1 lakh crore medium- and long-term debt-financing facility launched in 2020 for post-harvest infrastructure and community farming assets.

xs: The **AIF** is a **₹1 lakh crore** medium- and long-term debt-financing facility — option **(1)**.

56.s: In India, markets in agricultural products are regulated under the

Food Products Order, 1956 and Meat and Food Products Order, 1973
56.x: Option (b) is correct: Agriculture falls under the State List of the Constitution. Agriculture marketing in most states is regulated by the Agricultural Produce Market Committees established by state governments under the respective Agricultural Produce Market Committee Act. The APMCs provide infrastructure for the marketing of agricultural produce, regulate the sale of such produce, collect market fees from such sales, and regulate competition in agricultural marketing. Option (a) is incorrect: The Act empowers the central government to control the production, supply, distribution, storage, and trade of essential commodities. Option (c) is incorrect: The Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937 was the first legislation enacted by the Central Government to formulate standards and carry out grading and marking of agricultural and allied commodities. Option (d) is incorrect: Fruit Products Order -1955, promulgated under Section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act - 1955, aims at regulating sanitary and hygienic conditions in the manufacture of fruit and vegetable products. In 1973, the Government of India promulgated an Order (the Meat Food Products Order, 1973) under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, to enforce strict quality control over the production and processing of meat. The acts were repealed after the commencement of the FSS Act, 2006.

Which of the followings are the objectives of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) ?

2. To ensure meaningful real income levels to the farmers
3. To protect the interest of the consumers by providing essential agricultural commodities at reasonable rates through public distribution system
4. To ensure maximum price for the farmer
Select the correct answer from the codes given below :
57.x: The Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP) is mandated to recommend Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) to incentivize the cultivators to adopt modern technology, and raise productivity and overall grain production in line with the emerging demand patterns in the country. Assurance of a remunerative and stable price environment is considered very important for increasing agricultural production and productivity since the market place for agricultural produce tends to be inherently unstable, which often inflicts undue losses on the growers, even when they adopt the best available technology package and produce efficiently. Public procurement of foodgrains on the basis of MSPs also ensures the food stocks for public distribution to protect the interest of consumers by providing essential agricultural commodities at reasonable rate through public distribution system. Towards this end, MSP for major agricultural products are fixed by the government, each year, after taking into account the recommendations of the Commission.

57.s:
Which of the following factors/policies were affecting the price of rice in India in the recent past?
1. Minimum Support Price
2. Government's trading
3. Government's stockpiling
4. Consumer subsidies
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
57.x: Factor/policy 1 is correct: Impact: The MSP is the price at which the government purchases crops from farmers, regardless of the market price. For rice, a major staple crop, the MSP ensures that farmers receive a minimum income, incentivising rice production. • Effect on Price: Higher MSP leads to higher procurement prices, which can push up market prices as it sets a price floor. It prevents rice prices from falling below a certain level, stabilising farmer incomes but also influencing market supply and prices. Factor/policy 2 is correct: Impact: The government, through agencies like the Food Corporation of India (FCI), engages in large-scale trading of rice, including imports and exports. When there is a shortage, the government may import rice to stabilise the domestic supply. Conversely, if there is a surplus, it may allow exports. • Effect on Price: Government trading decisions affect supply levels in the domestic market. For instance, allowing rice exports in a year of strong production can reduce domestic supply, leading to price increases. Conversely, import decisions in a shortage year can help stabilise or reduce prices by boosting supply. 57.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Government of India provides Minimum Support Price for niger (Guizotia abyssinica) seeds.
2. Niger is cultivated as a Kharif crop.
3. Some tribal people in India use niger seed oil for cooking. Indian Agriculture PMF IAS Misc – 25
How many of the above statements are correct?
57.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Among the 14 kharif crops for which the Centre announces Minimum Support Prices (MSP) each year, niger or ramtil (Guizotia abyssinica) is included. Despite being a lesser-known oilseed, it is offered one of the highest MSPs, reflecting its relatively higher production costs and market considerations. The area under its cultivation has been steadily shrinking over the past three decades. In 1985-86, niger was cultivated on around 0.6 million hectares (ha), according to a 2013 report by the All India Coordinated Research Project on Sesame and Niger (AICRP). In 2020-21, the cultivated area shrank by 80 per cent to just over 0.1 million ha, the lowest among the 14 kharif crops with MSP. Statement 3 is correct: Some tribal people in India use niger seed oil for cooking, use the press cake after oil extraction as livestock feed, and also consume the seeds as a condiment. Niger seed oil has medicinal properties, which is the reason for its commercial demand by the cosmetics, perfumeries and other allied industries. The crop can grow even on denuded soils and requires minimal water, fertiliser, or pesticide use. However, its cultivation is often affected by amarbel, a twining parasitic plant scientifically known as Cuscuta chinensis, which can regularly damage niger plants.

2. Government's trading
3. Government's stockpiling
4. Consumer subsidies
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
57.x: All of the given factors/policies were affecting the price of rice in India in the recent past. Minimum support price impacts the price of rice in India as it is directed at providing insurance to agricultural producers against any sharp fall in farm prices. The government typically buys more than onethird of the country's rice output at a fixed price, which also has a direct impact on prices paid by traders. In the recent years, sale of wheat and rice is undertaken through Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) so as to check inflationary trend in prices of foodgrains. Prices of rice (and wheat) remained stable in recent past due to adequate supply and also due to maintenance of adequate buffer stock of rice (and wheat) by the FCI. The impact of consumer subsidies is to lower prices for the consumers, e.g. the National Food Security Act provided rice at Rs. 3 per kg to the poor families.

57.s: 'PM-AASHA' Scheme is related to the welfare of :
57.x: The Government of India is implementing the integrated Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM- AASHA) with the objective of ensuring remunerative prices to farmers, controlling price volatility, and making essential commodities available to consumers at affordable prices. It comprises components like the Price Support Scheme (PSS) for notified pulses, oilseeds and copra, the Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS) for oilseeds, and the Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) for perishable horticultural crops. The scheme also involves the Price Stabilization Fund (PSF). The Government maintains the buffer stocks of major pulses such as Tur, Urad, Chana, Moong and Masur under PSF to control hoarding and speculation. The PM-AASHA was launched in September, 2018 with an aim to provide price assurance for pulses, oilseeds and copra, ensuring financial stability for farmers, reduce post-harvest distress selling and promote crop diversification towards pulses and oilseeds. In September, 2024, cabinet approved the continuation of integrated scheme of PM-AASHA with Price Support Scheme (PSS), Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS) and Market intervention Scheme (MIS) as its components.

Consider the following statements in the context interventions being undertaken under Anaemia Mukt Bharat Strategy:
1. It provides prophylactic calcium supplementation for pre-school children, adolescents and pregnant women.
2. It runs a campaign for delayed cord clamping at the time of child-birth.

4. It addresses non-nutritional causes of anaemia in endemic pockets with special focus on malaria, hemoglobinopathies and fluorosis.

59.x: Statement 1 is incorrect: Anaemia is a condition in which the number of red blood cells or their oxygen-carrying capacity is insufficient to meet the body's physiological requirements, which vary by age, sex, altitude, smoking habits, and during pregnancy. In 2018, the Government of India launched the Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategy with the target to reduce anaemia in the vulnerable age groups, such as women, children and adolescents in a life cycle approach, providing preventive and curative mechanisms through a 6X6X6 strategy including six target beneficiaries, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms for all stakeholders to implement the strategy. Under the AMB strategy, the interventions to tackle anaemia in all States and UTs include prophylactic iron (not prophylactic calcium) and folic acid supplementation across all six target age groups. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: It includes intensified year-round Behaviour Change Communication (BCC) Campaign for: (a) improving compliance to Iron Folic Acid supplementation and deworming, (b) enhancing appropriate infant and young child feeding practices, (c) encouraging increase in intake of iron-rich food through diet diversity/quantity/frequency and/or fortified foods with focus on harnessing locally available resources, and (d) ensuring delayed cord clamping after delivery (by 3 minutes) in health facilities, Testing and treatment of anaemia, Indian Polity: Other Concepts PMF IAS IP – 141 using digital methods

60.x: The Scheme of Mega Food Park has been initiated for providing a mechanism to link agricultural production to the market by bringing together farmers, processors and retailers so as to ensure maximizing value addition, minimizing wastage, increasing farmers' income and creating employment opportunities particularly in rural sector. The Mega Food Park Scheme was based on 'Cluster' approach and envisages creation of state of art support infrastructure in a welldefined agri/horticultural zone for setting up of modern food processing units in the industrial plots provided in the park with well-established supply chain. 60.s: As per the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which of the following mark is made mandatory on all processed fruit products sold in our country?
60.x: The Food Products Order (FPO) mark is a mandatory certification mark for all processed fruit products sold in India, such as fruit jams, packaged fruit beverages, crushes and squashes, dehydrated fruit products, pickles, and fruit extracts. The FPO mark guarantees that the food products are manufactured in a hygienic and food-safe environment, ensuring that the product is fit for consumption. The Ministry of Food Processing Industries develops food safety hygiene standards and issues the FPO mark certification to processed food manufacturers. In India, the FPO certificate has been effective since the promulgation of Food Products Order 1955, but it became mandatory for manufacturers only after the enactment of the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006.

xa: ES 2025-26: medium- and high-tech manufacturing share is **46.3%**.
About **57 lakh** jobs were added in organised manufacturing (2015-16 to 2024-25).

61.s: Industry accounts for approximately what share of Gross Value Added in India?
61.x: Industry accounts for approximately 25.3 per cent of GVA. The 13–14 per cent figure relates to the public sector's contribution to GDP, while 17–18 per cent refers to manufacturing's real-term share.
61.tq: Separate similar percentages by linking each figure to its correct economic aggregate.
xs: Industry is about **25.3 per cent** of GVA — option **(4)** is correct.
**13-14%** is the public sector's share of GDP; **17-18%** is manufacturing's real share.
xa: Real industry GVA grows at about **7%**.
Industry GVA grew **7.0%** in H1 FY26.

61.s:
Consider the following about India's sectoral GDP structure after 1991:
1. Services gained the largest share.
2. Industry gained more share than services.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
61.x: After 1991 services gained the most share in GDP; industry's share did not rise significantly relative to services.
xa: Industry is about **25.3%** of GVA.
Manufacturing's **real** share stays at **17-18%**.

61.s: Why did manufacturing's share of nominal GVA decline despite its real-term share remaining broadly stable?
o: Because the private sector withdrew from manufacturing
Because construction was excluded from GVA
Because manufacturing output ceased to grow after 1991
61.x: The decline in manufacturing's nominal GVA share was attributed to relative price changes. In real terms, manufacturing's share remained broadly steady at 17–18 per cent.
61.tq: Distinguish nominal changes caused by prices from real changes in output.
xs: Manufacturing's **nominal** GVA share fell only because of **relative price** changes — option **(1)** is correct.
Its **real** share stayed steady at **17-18%**, so output did not stop growing.
xa: Manufacturing GVA grew **9.13%** in Q2 FY26.
Industry as a whole is about **25.3%** of GVA.

61.s: India was the world's second-largest crude steel producer in 2024, with production of
61.x: India produced 149.4 million tonnes of crude steel in 2024 and ranked second after China, which produced 1,005.1 million tonnes.
61.tq: Distinguish production from capacity and from the leading country's output.
xs: India produced **149.4 million tonnes** of crude steel in **2024**, 2nd largest — option **(4)** is correct.
**1,005.1 MT** is China's output; **200.33 MT** is India's capacity; **93** is the % of coal-based ironmaking.
xa: India depends on **imported coking coal**, its main imported input.
SAIL plants **Bhilai**, **Rourkela**, **Durgapur** date to the **Second Plan**.

61.s: The principal cause of capacity under-utilisation in Indian industry is
61.x: Deficient basic infrastructure is identified as the main cause of capacity under-utilisation, although weak demand also contributes.
61.tq: Select the primary cause while distinguishing it from a secondary contributing factor.
xs: The main cause of capacity under-utilisation is **deficient basic infrastructure** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2007).
**Weak demand** also adds: the Manufacturing PMI in **Jul 2026** was the lowest since **Aug 2021**.
xa: Other problems: **regional concentration**, **jobless growth**, **import dependence**, **low R&D**.
Infrastructure bottlenecks also drove the **1965-80** slowdown.
61.fixed: stem referred to 'the material'; APPSC 2007 wording

61.s: In FY 2023, which use-based groups of the IIP recorded the highest growth?
61.x: In FY 2023, the capital goods and infrastructure/construction goods indices grew the most (BPSC 2024). Primary goods had the highest weight in the 2011-12 series, but they were not the fastest-growing group. The other pairs did not lead.
61.tq: FY23 IIP leaders: capital goods + infra/construction goods.
xs: In **FY 2023**, the **capital goods** and **infrastructure/construction goods** indices grew most — option **(2)** is correct (BPSC 2024).
**Primary goods** had the highest **weight** (**34%**) in the 2011-12 series, but did not grow fastest.
xa: **Capital goods** had the lowest weight (**8.22%**) in that series.
In **Feb 2026**, non-core manufacturing and capital goods outpaced core sectors.

61.s: The Index of Services Production, with base year 2024-25, is best described as:
o: A supplementary index of agricultural production
A measure of wholesale price inflation in services
A replacement for the IIP covering only manufacturing
The services counterpart of the IIP
61.x: The Index of Services Production is the services counterpart of the IIP. Its first release was scheduled for 14 July 2026 with a 60-day lag.
61.tq: Discriminate between two similarly named production indices by their sectoral coverage.
xs: The **Index of Services Production** (base **2024-25**) is the **services counterpart of the IIP** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is not about agriculture, prices or manufacturing; services lie **outside** the IIP.
xa: Its first release came on **14 July 2026**, with a **60-day** lag.
The IIP itself was rebased to **2022-23** from **1 June 2026**.
IIP is compiled by the **NSO (MoSPI)**.

61.s: The MSMED Amendment Bill, 2026, as described in the current policy context, requires every CPSE to settle MSME invoices through
61.x: The 2026 amendment requires every CPSE to settle MSME invoices on the Trade Receivables Discounting System, or TReDS.
61.tq: Match the current legal requirement with the exact institutional platform.
xs: The **MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026** makes every CPSE settle MSME invoices on **TReDS** — option **(3)** is correct.
It was passed by the **Rajya Sabha** (**Aug 2026**).
**DPE schedules** set CEO pay and **BRPSE** advised on sick CPSEs — neither handles invoices.
xa: Budget **2026-27** proposes **REITs** to recycle CPSE real estate.
There are **250+ operating CPSEs**.

61.s: Which of the following is related with the field of electricity generation?
61.x: Among the given options, NHPC is related with the field of electricity generation. At present, NHPC Ltd. (erstwhile National Hydroelectric Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd.) is a Navratna CPSE. It has become the largest organization for hydropower development in India, with capabilities to undertake all the activities from conceptualization to commissioning in relation to setting up of hydro products. NHPC Ltd. has also diversified in the field of Solar & Wind power.

61.s: The Index of Industrial Production covers mining, manufacturing and:
61.x: IIP covers mining, manufacturing and electricity; agriculture, services and construction lie outside it.
xa: It is compiled monthly by the **NSO (MoSPI)**.
The base moved from **2011-12** to **2022-23** from **1 June 2026**.

61.s: The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is compiled monthly by the:
o: National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
61.x: The IIP is compiled monthly by the National Statistical Office under MoSPI. The NSO replaced the earlier Central Statistical Office in this role.
61.tq: Identify the present compiling agency while distinguishing it from the former agency.
xs: The IIP is compiled monthly by the **National Statistical Office** under **MoSPI** — option **(1)** is correct.
It was formerly done by the **CSO**.

xa: The new **Index of Services Production** (base **2024-25**) was first released on **14 July 2026**.

61.s: With effect from 1 June 2026, the base year of the IIP was shifted from:
61.x: The new IIP series shifted the base year from 2011-12 to 2022-23, effective 1 June 2026. Readings before June 2026 use the old base.
61.tq: Test the direction and effective date of a base-year revision.
xs: The IIP base moved from **2011-12 to 2022-23**, effective **1 June 2026** — option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ Any IIP reading from before June 2026 is on the old base.
xa: The new basket has **1,042 products** in **463** item groups (old: **407** items).
The **WPI** base was revised to **2022-23** at the same time.
This was the **10th** revision.

61.s:
Consider the following about Andhra Pradesh's industrial profile:
