61.s: In the 2011-12 series of the IIP, which use-based category had the highest and which had the lowest weight respectively?
61.x: Primary goods had the highest weight at about 34 per cent, while capital goods had the lowest weight at 8.22 per cent in the 2011-12 series.
61.tq: Pair the maximum and minimum values instead of considering either value in isolation.
xs: In the 2011-12 series, **primary goods** weighed most (**34%**) and **capital goods** least (**8.22%**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses them.
xa: In **FY 2023**, **capital goods** and **infrastructure/construction goods** indices grew most (BPSC 2024).
New-series weights: **manufacturing 76.1%**, mining **11.1%**, electricity and gas **10.9%**.

61.s: Which of the following has been added to the new IIP series?
o: Gas supply, water supply, sewerage and waste management
61.x: The new series adds gas, water, sewerage and waste management, minor and rare-earth minerals, and shows renewable electricity separately.
xa: New weights: manufacturing **76.1%**, mining **11.1%**, electricity and gas **10.9%**, water supply **2.02%**.
Weights rest on each sector's share of **GVA in 2022-23**.

61.s: In the new IIP series, sectoral weights are based on each sector's share of:
o: Gross Domestic Product at current prices in 2022-23
61.x: The weights in the new IIP series are derived from the sectoral shares of Gross Value Added in 2022-23.
61.tq: Distinguish the statistical basis of weights from other macroeconomic aggregates.
xs: New IIP weights are based on each sector's share of **Gross Value Added in 2022-23** — option **(3)** is correct.
GDP, employment and exports are not the weighting basis.
xa: Manufacturing **76.1%**, mining **11.1%**, electricity and gas **10.9%**, water supply **2.02%**.
The base year itself is **2022-23**, effective **1 June 2026**.

61.s: The revised series of the Index of Core Industries has base year:
61.x: The revised ICI (Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT) uses 2022-23 as base and adds iron ore at 4.905% weight.
xa: The revision came in **July 2026**, with effect from **April 2023**.

61.s: Under the revised 2022-23 series of the Index of Core Industries, which one of the following has the highest weight?
61.x: Electricity carries the highest weight in the revised series, at 30.93 per cent. Refinery products have the second-highest weight at 22.57 per cent.
61.tq: Compare the revised weights rather than relying on the older series.
xs: In the 2022-23 series **electricity** weighs most (**30.93%**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Refinery products** come second (**22.57**), then **steel** (**17.58**) and **crude oil** (**7.43**).
xa: In the old series, **refinery products** led (**28.04%**), electricity was second (**19.85%**).
**Fertilisers** remain the lowest (**2.73** new; **2.63** old).

61.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the number of industries and the combined IIP weight under the revised 2022-23 series of the Index of Core Industries?
61.x: The revised series contains nine core industries and their combined weight in the IIP is 32.88 per cent. Iron ore was added to the earlier list of eight industries.
61.tq: Split the option into two parts and verify both the count and the percentage.
xs: The revised ICI has **9 industries** with a combined IIP weight of **32.88 per cent** — option **(4)** is correct.
The old series had **8** industries weighing **40.27%**.
xa: **Iron ore** is the ninth, newest core industry (weight **4.905%**).
In **Jun 2026**, the new-series ICI grew **5%**, driven by iron ore (+**43.9%**).

61.s: Which industry had the lowest weight in the old Index of Eight Core Industries?
61.x: In the old eight-core series, fertilisers had the lowest weight (2.63%). They are still the lowest in the new 2022-23 series (2.73%).
61.tq: Identify the minimum value rather than the largest component.
xs: **Fertilisers** had the lowest weight in the old eight-core index (**2.63%**) — option **(2)** is correct.
**Cement** (**5.37**), **natural gas** (**6.88**) and **crude oil** (**8.98**) weighed more.
xa: Fertilisers are still lowest in the new series (**2.73%**).
⚠ **Transport is NOT a core industry** (APPSC-G2 2011).

61.s: What is the principal purpose of granting Maharatna status?
o: To provide greater autonomy and financial and managerial powers to large, high-performing CPSEs
To provide agricultural credit to public enterprises
To regulate foreign trade by CPSEs
To convert CPSEs into private companies
61.x: Maharatna status gives large, high-performing CPSEs more autonomy and financial and managerial powers, so they can expand and compete globally.
61.tq: Recall the purpose of Maharatna status.
n: The purpose of Maharatna status is to provide greater autonomy to large, high-performing CPSEs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
Maharatna status provides greater financial powers to large, high-performing CPSEs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
Maharatna status provides greater managerial powers to large, high-performing CPSEs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
xs: Maharatna status gives **greater autonomy** and **greater financial and managerial powers** to **large, high-performing CPSEs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was introduced to let selected **Navratna** CPSEs **compete globally** — not for agricultural credit, trade regulation or privatisation.
xa: Maharatna is administered by the **Department of Public Enterprises (DPE)**.
Criteria: 3-year average **turnover >₹25,000 cr**, **net worth >₹15,000 cr**, **net profit >₹5,000 cr**.
A Maharatna can invest up to **₹5,000 cr** in one project without Government approval.

61.s: The Maharatna status for CPSEs is administered by:
61.x: The DPE administers Maharatna, which helps selected Navratnas compete globally and uses net profit as a test.
n: Maharatna status was introduced in 2010. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) administers Maharatna status. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
Maharatna was introduced to enable selected Navratna CPSEs to compete globally. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
Net profit is a factor in the categorisation of Maharatna CPSEs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 93-94]
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes date the scheme to **2009**.
Maharatna requires being a **Navratna** already and listed with minimum public shareholding.
All tiers: no budgetary support/government guarantee and no default on government loans.

61.s: During the 1965-80 phase of deceleration, India's industrial growth was about:
61.x: Growth fell to about 4% in 1965-80, against about 7-8% in 1951-65 and in the 1980s.
xa: The 1965-80 slowdown came from **wars**, **droughts**, **infrastructure bottlenecks** and **licensing**.
**Dani Rodrik**'s **premature deindustrialisation**: manufacturing peaks at lower income than in early industrialisers.

61.s: India's first integrated public-sector steel plant was:
61.x: Rourkela in Odisha, with a capacity of one million tonnes, was the first integrated public-sector steel plant.
xa: ⚠ First PSU steel unit = **Bhadravati**; first integrated PSU steel plant = **Rourkela**.
**Durgapur** (West Bengal) = **UK**; **Bhilai** = **USSR**.

61.s: The textile industry, the largest employer after agriculture, provides direct employment to about:
61.x: It directly employs about 4.5 crore persons, with indirect employment above 10 crore.
xa: Cotton textiles have three segments: **mill**, **powerloom**, **handloom**.
**Powerlooms** make the bulk of cloth.

61.s: Which one of the following has traditionally been the top profit-making CPSE?
61.x: ONGC has traditionally been the top profit-making CPSE. The latest ranking may vary by Public Enterprises Survey year.
61.tq: Distinguish a traditional leading enterprise from other major CPSEs.
xs: **ONGC** (Oil and Natural Gas Corporation) is the traditional top profit-maker — option **(4)** is correct.
**IOC** and **BHEL** are **Maharatnas**, but ONGC is the noted top earner.

CPSEs' combined net profit is above **₹3.43 lakh crore**.

61.s: The Public Enterprises Survey covers CPSEs in which the Government of India holds more than:
61.x: The annual Survey covers CPSEs with over 50% GoI equity and excludes departmental undertakings, banks and insurers.
xa: It is prepared by the **DPE Survey Division** on the **Estimates Committee's** advice.

61.s: To be eligible for Maharatna status, a CPSE must already be a:
61.x: Maharatna eligibility requires existing Navratna status; a Maharatna may invest up to ₹5,000 crore in one project.
xa: Thresholds (3-year average): turnover >**₹25,000 cr**, net worth >**₹15,000 cr**, net profit >**₹5,000 cr**.

61.s:
Consider the following three-year average thresholds for Maharatna eligibility:
1. Net profit above ₹15,000 crore
2. Turnover above ₹25,000 crore
3. Net worth above ₹15,000 crore
Which of the above is/are correct?
61.x: Maharatna needs average turnover above ₹25,000 crore, net worth above ₹15,000 crore and net profit above ₹5,000 crore, not ₹15,000 crore.
xa: It must also be **listed** with minimum public shareholding and have **significant global presence**.
Investment autonomy: up to **₹5,000 cr** in one project.

61.s: The Navratna scheme for CPSEs was introduced in:
61.x: The Navratna scheme came in 1997; eligibility needs Miniratna-I and Schedule 'A' status and a score of 60+ on six parameters.
xa: The first Navratnas were **9** PSUs.

61.s: A Navratna CPSE can invest without Government approval up to:
o: ₹500 crore or equal to net worth

xa: All tiers: **no budgetary support**/government guarantee and no default on government loans.

xa: Miniratna-II needs profit in the last **3** years in a row and **positive net worth**.
Ratna status gives **financial and operational autonomy**.

61.s: HAL is related to manufacturing of :
61.x: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) is an Indian stateowned aerospace and defence company headquartered in Bangalore (Bengaluru). Further, a decision was taken by the Government to set up three more plants for the manufacture of heavy electrical equipment. The first one was at Tiruchirappalli (Tamil Nadu) for high pressure boilers, the second one at Hyderabad (Telangana) for steam turbo generators and high pressure pumps and compressors - both of these with collaboration from Czechoslovakia and the third plant at Haridwar (Uttarakhand) with erstwhile USSR collaboration for large steam turbo generating sets and motors and also hydro generating sets including turbines and generators. These three newly conceived projects were part of Heavy Electricals (India) Limited for which the work was initiated at Bhopal. All the initial preparatory work was carried out from Bhopal till November, 1964. Then, Government decided to create a separate corporation for setting-up and managing these three units. Thus Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited was born and formally incorporated on 13th November, 1964. Industries like oil and gas, automotive, and telecommunications are considered capital intensive due to their need for high fixed capital investments. As per the data of Annual Survey of Industries 2017-18, the ratio of invested capital to the number of workers employed in manufacturing sector was highest in Madhya Pradesh among the given States. As per the ASI 2023-24, Gujarat's share is the highest in respect of aggregates Gross Value of Plant and Machinery (19.96%), Fixed Capital (19.53%), Invested Capital (18.61%), Total Input (17.80%) and Total Output (17.22%).

62.s: Reservation of items for the small-scale sector began in 1967 with how many items?
62.x: SSI reservation began in 1967 with 47 items and peaked at about 873 items in 1984; the last 20 were dereserved in 2015.
xa: **Abid Hussain** recommended **abolishing reservation** + wide deregulation.
The **1991** Industrial Policy raised the SSI investment ceiling.

62.s: The MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026 makes settlement of MSME invoices through TReDS mandatory for:
62.x: The MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026 makes TReDS settlement mandatory for CPSEs.
xa: It also provides a **National Digital Platform** for registration and additional **State MSEFCs**.
The parent **MSMED Act** came into force on **2 October 2006**; Bill introduced **12 May 2005**.
Under **Chapter V**, buyers must pay within **45 days**, else compound interest at **3 times the RBI bank rate** (**Sec. 16**).

62.s: Udyam Abhilasha is best described as:
o: A KVIC subsidy programme for traditional artisans launched in 2008
A World Bank credit programme for CPSEs launched in 2020
A SIDBI entrepreneurship-awareness campaign launched in 2021 in aspirational districts
A GeM procurement platform launched in 2016
62.x: Udyam Abhilasha is a SIDBI entrepreneurship-awareness campaign of 2021 aimed at aspirational districts.
62.tq: Match the programme with its implementing institution, year and target area.
xs: **Udyam Abhilasha** is a **SIDBI entrepreneurship-awareness campaign** launched in **2021** in **aspirational districts** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **KVIC** scheme formed in **2008** is **PMEGP**, not Udyam Abhilasha.
**RAMP** is the **World Bank**-supported programme; Stand-Up India (not GeM) dates from **2016**.
xa: **SIDBI** was set up on **2 April 1990** under the **SIDBI Act, 1989**, HQ **Lucknow**.
SIDBI is the implementing agency of **PM SVANidhi**.
⚠ **Udyam Abhilasha** = SIDBI (2021); **PMEGP** = KVIC (2008).

62.s: The Andhra Pradesh MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 covers which period?
62.x: AP MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 covers 2024-29 and was issued through G.O.Ms.No.69 dated 26 October 2024. 2019 is the year of YSR Navodayam, and 2026 brought a revamped MSME Policy for women-led units, not a 2026-31 policy.
xs: AP **MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0** covers **2024-29** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was issued as **G.O.Ms.No.69** dated **26 Oct 2024**.
**2019** is the year of **YSR Navodayam**; **2026** brought a revamped policy for **women-led** MSMEs, not a 2026-31 plan.
xa: AP follows the same national MSME definition (**APSES 2024-25**).
AP MSME base: about **20.77 lakh** units, **48%** services.
In AP, **MSE-CDP** is implemented through **APIIC**.

62.s: Abid Hussain Committee was related to :
Which one of the following best explains the role of small industries in the Indian economy?
o: They mainly reduce agricultural employment without affecting regional development
They are labour-intensive, require relatively little capital and help disperse industries to rural and semi-urban areas
They depend exclusively on imported technology and raw materials
They are capital-intensive and promote industrial concentration in metropolitan areas
62.x: Small industries are labour-intensive, require little capital and help disperse industrial activity to rural and semi-urban areas.
62.tq: Identify the option combining the core employment, capital and dispersal functions.
xs: Small industries are **labour-intensive**, need **little capital** and **disperse** industry to **rural and semi-urban** areas — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) is the reverse: they **reduce** concentration and regional imbalance.
xa: They also spread ownership of wealth and **reduce concentration of economic power**.
They have been a priority since the **First Plan**.

62.s: Small-scale industries have been treated as a priority in India since which Plan?
62.x: Small-scale industries have been a policy priority since the First Five-Year Plan.
62.tq: Use direct plan-period recall for a policy-origin question.
xs: Small industries have been a priority since the **First Plan** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **Karve Committee (1955)** then planned village and small industries for the **Second Plan**.
xa: **IPR 1948** listed their handicaps: raw materials, finance, marketing, technology.
MSMEs are the second-largest employer after **agriculture**.

62.s: The Karve Committee on village and small industries recommended:
o: deregulation and competitiveness of small industry
avoiding technological unemployment and promoting decentralised development
62.x: The Karve Committee proposed avoiding technological unemployment, maximising employment in the Second Plan and decentralised development.
xa: It was a **Planning Commission** committee of **1955**.
⚠ One note prints Karve as "1995" — an OCR error.

62.s: The Karve Committee relating to village and small industries was constituted in—
62.x: The Planning Commission set up the Karve Committee in 1955 on village and small industries for the Second Plan. The year '1995' that is sometimes printed is a misprint.
62.tq: Distinguish the close historical dates using the committee’s subject and period.
xs: The **Karve Committee** was set up in **1955** — option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ "1995" in one note is an OCR error; **1992** is **P.R. Nayak** and **1997** is **Abid Hussain**.
xa: It was a **Planning Commission** body on village and small industries for the **Second Plan**.
Chronology: **Karve → Nayak → Abid Hussain → S.P. Gupta → U.K. Sinha**.

62.s: Which committee on the MSME sector was constituted in 2019?
62.x: The U.K. Sinha Committee dates to 2019; Karve was 1955, Abid Hussain 1997 and S.P. Gupta 2001.
xa: The **PM's Task Force on MSMEs** came in **2010**.

62.s: YSR Navodayam, launched in 2019, was primarily associated with:
o: A merger of two entrepreneurship schemes
A one-time restructuring of stressed MSME loans
62.x: YSR Navodayam was launched in 2019 for one-time restructuring of stressed MSME loans.
62.tq: Identify the specific intervention associated with a named state scheme.
xs: **YSR Navodayam** (**2019**) was a **one-time restructuring of stressed MSME loans** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The merger of two schemes describes **PMEGP** (PMRY + REGP, **2008**), not YSR Navodayam.
xa: AP's **MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0** covers **2024-29**.
The revamped **MSME Policy 2026** favours **women-led MSMEs**.
The MSME single window in AP is run by **DICs**.

62.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Karve Committee – Working-capital credit to SSIs
Abid Hussain Committee – Deregulation and competitiveness of small industry
P.R. Nayak Committee – Deregulation of small industry
U.K. Sinha Committee – Village and small industries in the Second Plan
62.x: Abid Hussain dealt with deregulation and competitiveness; Karve with village and small industries, Nayak with working-capital credit, and U.K. Sinha with MSME finance.
xa: Years: Karve **1955**, Nayak **1992**, Abid Hussain **1997**, U.K. Sinha **2019**.
**S.P. Gupta (2001)** dealt with SSI credit access.

62.s: The contribution of India's small scale sector to the gross turnover in the manufacturing sector since 1992 has been of the order of :
62.x: As per the question period, the contribution of small scale sector to the country's gross turnover in the manufacturing was about 40%. As per the Economic Survey 2025-26. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) form the backbone of India's industrial economy, accounting for approximately 35.4 percent of manufacturing, around 48.58 percent of exports, and 31.1 percent of GDP in the country

62.s:
Under the original MSMED definitions of 2006:
1. A small manufacturing enterprise could invest up to ₹5 crore in plant and machinery.
2. The corresponding limit for a small service enterprise was ₹2 crore.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
62.x: The 2006 limit for small manufacturing was ₹5 crore in plant and machinery, and for small services ₹2 crore.
xa: Micro manufacturing: up to **₹25 lakh**.
Medium services: up to **₹5 crore**.

62.s: Disputes relating to delayed payments to micro and small enterprises are referred to which body?
62.x: Disputes concerning delayed payments are referred to the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council.
62.tq: Identify the specialised statutory forum rather than a general commercial or financial institution.
xs: Delayed-payment disputes go to the **MSE Facilitation Council** — option **(2)** is correct.
**SFCs** are state-level term lenders, not dispute bodies.
xa: The **MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026** adds more State **MSEFCs**.
Samadhaan cases exceed **2.56 lakh**, worth **₹55,244 crore**.

62.s:
As per the latest Union-level figures, MSMEs account for:
1. About 45 per cent of exports
2. About 31 per cent of GDP
3. About 36 per cent of manufacturing output
Which of the above is/are correct?
62.x: MSMEs contribute about 31 per cent of GDP, 36 per cent of manufacturing output and 41 per cent (not 45 per cent) of exports.
xa: Stated by the Union MSME Minister in the **Rajya Sabha** (**4 Aug 2026**).
⚠ Memory aid: **31 – 36 – 41** = GDP – manufacturing – exports.

62.s: What proportion of Udyam registrations is accounted for by micro units?
62.x: Micro units account for 95.88 per cent of Udyam registrations.
62.tq: Use exact percentage recall for a composition question.
xs: **Micro units** are **95.88%** of Udyam registrations — option **(3)** is correct.
**Udyam Registration (2020)** is a free, paperless, **self-declaration** portal.
xa: **6.63 crore** MSMEs registered on Udyam (**1 July 2020 – 31 July 2025**).
These include **2.72 crore** informal micro enterprises.
**46.7 lakh+** are women-owned (Aug 2025).

62.s: Which one of the following statements regarding SIDBI is NOT correct?
o: It is an apex institution for MSME finance and development.
It partnered with SVC Co-operative Bank for MSME lending in July 2022.
62.x: SIDBI is headquartered in Lucknow, not Hyderabad. The other statements correctly describe its establishment, role and 2022 partnership.
62.tq: Find the incorrect location while retaining the institution’s other correctly stated attributes.
xs: SIDBI is **not** headquartered in Hyderabad — its HQ is **Lucknow**; option **(3)** is the answer.
It is the **apex institution** for MSME finance, set up on **2 April 1990**.
It partnered **SVC Co-operative Bank** in **July 2022** (APPSC-GS 2021).
xa: SIDBI implements **PM SVANidhi**.
SIDBI ran the **Udyam Abhilasha** campaign in **2021**.

62.s:
Consider the following about SIDBI:
1. It is the implementing agency for PM SVANidhi.
2. TReDS, which it supports, is an offline cash-payment system for MSME invoices.
3. It co-founded CGTMSE with the Ministry of MSME.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
62.x: SIDBI implements PM SVANidhi and co-founded CGTMSE with the Ministry of MSME; TReDS is an online invoice-discounting system.
xa: SIDBI's **Udyam Abhilasha** (**2021**) ran in aspirational districts.
SIDBI HQ: **Lucknow**.

62.s: KVIC succeeded which organisation?
o: All India Khadi and Village Industries Board
62.x: KVIC succeeded the All India Khadi and Village Industries Board, which was established in 1953.
62.tq: Distinguish a statutory successor from related institutions.
xs: **KVIC** succeeded the **All India Khadi and Village Industries Board** (**1953**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Ministry of Small-Scale Industries** was merged into the **Ministry of MSME** (**2007**), not succeeded by KVIC.
xa: KVIC became a **statutory body** in **1956** under the **KVIC Act**.
KVIC implements **PMEGP** (formed **2008** from **PMRY + REGP**).
⚠ Board **1953**, Commission **1956**.

62.s: The Ministry of MSME was formed in 2007 by merging the Ministry of Small-Scale Industries with the Ministry of:
62.x: The Ministry of MSME was formed in 2007 by merging the Ministry of Small-Scale Industries with the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.
62.tq: Use a ministry-merger question with a neighbouring ministry as the trap.
xs: The **Ministry of MSME** (**2007**) merged the Ministry of SSI with the Ministry of **Agro and Rural Industries** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The new ministry covers **khadi**, **village** and **coir** industries.
xa: **KVIC** (statutory, **1956**) handles khadi and village industries and implements **PMEGP**.
The **MSMED Act** came into force on **2 October 2006**.
**PM Vishwakarma** is a scheme of **MoMSME**.

62.s: The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) was set up as a statutory body in:
62.x: KVIC became a statutory body in 1956 under the KVIC Act. 1953 is when its predecessor, the All India Khadi and Village Industries Board, was set up; 1948 is the first Industrial Policy Resolution; 2007 is when the Ministry of MSME was formed.
62.tq: Board 1953 -> KVIC (statutory) 1956.
xs: **KVIC** became a **statutory body** in **1956** under the KVIC Act — so option **(3)** is correct.
**1953** is when its predecessor, the **All India Khadi and Village Industries Board**, was set up.
**1948** is the **IPR 1948**; **2007** is when the **Ministry of MSME** was formed.
xa: KVIC implements **PMEGP** (**2008**, PMRY + REGP).
**SIDBI**: Act **1989**, set up **2 April 1990**, HQ **Lucknow**.
**SFCs** were created under the **SFC Act, 1951**.

62.s: Under Chapter V of the MSMED Act, a buyer must pay an MSE supplier within:
62.x: Chapter V requires payment within 45 days, beyond which compound interest at three times the RBI bank rate is payable.
xa: This is **Sec. 16** of the MSMED Act.
Disputes go to the **MSE Facilitation Council**.
**MSME Samadhaan** (**2017**) takes cases under the **45-day** rule.

62.s: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 identified the handicaps of small industries as relating to:
o: Raw materials, finance, marketing and technology
62.x: IPR 1948 identified difficulties relating to raw materials, finance, marketing and technology.
xa: Today's problems still include a **credit gap**, **obsolete technology** and **weak marketing**.
Others: **delayed payments**, compliance burden, **skill deficit**.

62.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a major problem faced by MSMEs?
o: Excessive access to low-cost collateral-free credit
62.x: The identified problems include obsolete technology, weak marketing and exports, compliance burden, skill deficit and costly or inadequate credit; excessive access to cheap credit is not a problem listed here.
62.tq: Use the ‘not a problem’ format to separate a real constraint from its opposite.
xs: **Excessive access to low-cost collateral-free credit** is not a problem — option **(1)** is the answer.
The real issue is a **credit gap**: little collateral and **costly credit**.
**Weak marketing and exports**, **skill deficit** and **obsolete technology** are listed problems.
xa: Other problems: **delayed payments** and **compliance burden**.
**CGTMSE** gives **collateral-free credit guarantee** cover.

62.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
62.x: MSME Samadhaan was introduced in 2017 to address delayed payments. Udyam dates from 2020, RAMP is World Bank-backed, and PM Vishwakarma covers 18 trades.
62.tq: Check the scheme, objective and year together to catch cross-swapped features.
xs: **MSME Samadhaan — delayed payments — 2017** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**RAMP** is World Bank-backed; **PM Vishwakarma** covers **18** trades; **Udyam** dates to **2020**.
xa: Samadhaan takes cases under the MSMED Act's **45-day** rule.
It has over **2.56 lakh** cases worth **₹55,244 crore**.

62.s: SIDBI co-founded the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) in:
62.x: CGTMSE was co-founded by the Ministry of MSME and SIDBI in 2000 to provide credit guarantee support for collateral-free lending.
62.tq: Distinguish the year of SIDBI’s establishment from the later year of CGTMSE’s formation.
xs: **CGTMSE** was set up in **2000** by the **Ministry of MSME** and **SIDBI** — option **(3)** is correct.
**1990** is SIDBI's own founding year.
xa: It gives **collateral-free credit guarantee** cover to lenders.
Its corpus is shared **Government : SIDBI = 4:1**.

62.s: The corpus contribution ratio between the Government and SIDBI in CGTMSE is:
62.x: The corpus of CGTMSE is shared between the Government and SIDBI in the ratio of 4:1.
62.tq: Recall the exact institutional contribution ratio rather than the scheme’s broad objective.
xs: The CGTMSE corpus is shared **Government : SIDBI = 4:1** — option **(1)** is correct.
CGTMSE was set up in **2000**.
xa: Budget **2026-27** adds **CGTMSE** guarantees for **TReDS** discounting.
**MUDRA** ceiling: **₹20 lakh** (**Tarun Plus**).

62.s: TReDS platforms such as RXIL, M1xchange and Invoicemart, which discount MSME receivables, are regulated by:
62.x: TReDS platforms are RBI-regulated and discount MSME receivables owed by corporates, government and PSUs.
xa: TReDS has run since **2017**.
Budget **2026-27**: **all CPSE purchases from MSMEs** to settle on TReDS, plus a **GeM-TReDS** link.

62.s:
Consider the following about the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS):
1. It is an RBI platform for discounting receivables.
2. It was a Covid-era emergency credit scheme introduced in 2020.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
62.x: ECLGS was the Covid-era (2020) emergency credit-guarantee line for MSMEs; the receivables-discounting platform is TReDS.
xa: **ECLGS 5.0** (**May 2026**) gives a **100%** guarantee to units hit by the **West Asia crisis**.
**Udyam Registration** also began in **2020**.

62.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two loan limits stated for MSE lending in February 2026?
o: No collateral is required up to ₹25 lakh, while banks may lend only up to ₹20 lakh.
No collateral is required up to ₹20 lakh, while banks may extend the limit up to ₹25 lakh.
Both limits are fixed at ₹20 lakh.
Both limits are fixed at ₹25 lakh.
62.x: The stated position is a ₹20 lakh no-collateral threshold, with banks permitted to go up to ₹25 lakh.
62.tq: Separate two closely related numerical limits instead of treating them as identical.
xs: RBI (**Feb 2026**): **no collateral** for MSE loans up to **₹20 lakh**, and banks may go up to **₹25 lakh** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) swaps the two limits.
xa: **MUDRA** loans are also collateral-free up to **₹20 lakh**.
**CGTMSE** backs collateral-free lending with a **4:1** Government:SIDBI corpus.

62.s: With reference to TReDS, Budget 2026-27 announced which of the following?
o: TReDS platforms will be regulated by SEBI instead of the RBI
All CPSE purchases from MSMEs are to be settled on TReDS, with CGTMSE guarantees for TReDS discounting
TReDS will be merged with the MSME Samadhaan portal
Only private corporates will be allowed to use TReDS
62.x: Budget 2026-27 mandated settlement of all CPSE purchases from MSMEs on TReDS, CGTMSE guarantees for TReDS discounting, a GeM-TReDS link and receivables as asset-backed securities. TReDS platforms remain RBI-regulated, are not merged with Samadhaan (a delayed-payment portal), and serve government and PSU buyers as well as corporates.
62.tq: Budget 2026-27: CPSE-MSME bills via TReDS + CGTMSE cover + GeM link.
xs: Budget 2026-27 said **all CPSE purchases from MSMEs** are to be settled on **TReDS**, with **CGTMSE guarantees for TReDS discounting** — so option **(2)** is correct.
TReDS platforms are **RBI-regulated** (since **2017**), not SEBI-regulated.
**MSME Samadhaan** (2017) is a separate delayed-payment portal; TReDS also serves **government and PSU** buyers, not only private corporates.
xa: The Budget also proposed a **GeM-TReDS link** and treating receivables as **asset-backed securities**.
TReDS platforms include **RXIL**, **M1xchange** and **Invoicemart**.
**GeM:** **Rs 18.4 lakh crore** GMV with **11 lakh+** MSEs (Aug 2026).

62.s: Which one of the following is a feature of Udyam Registration?
o: It is operated only for enterprises receiving PMEGP subsidy.
It is restricted to large manufacturing companies.
It is a paid, paper-based registration requiring physical verification in every case.
It is a free, paperless, self-declaration portal linked with GeM, income tax, GST and TReDS.
62.x: Udyam Registration, introduced in 2020, is free, paperless and based on self-declaration; it is linked with GeM, income tax, GST and TReDS.
62.tq: Identify the exact administrative features of a digital registration system.
xs: **Udyam Registration** is a **free, paperless, self-declaration portal linked with GeM, income tax, GST and TReDS** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not paid or paper-based, is not restricted to large companies, and is not limited to **PMEGP** beneficiaries.
xa: Udyam Registration began in **2020**; **6.63 crore** MSMEs registered between **1 July 2020** and **31 July 2025**.
**Micro units** form **95.88%** of Udyam registrations.
Of the registrations, **2.72 crore** are informal micro enterprises; **46.7 lakh+** are women-owned (Aug 2025).

62.s: The RAMP programme for strengthening MSME institutions, market access and credit is supported by:
62.x: RAMP is a World Bank-supported programme to strengthen Centre-State MSME institutions, market access and credit.
xa: **ECLGS 5.0** (**May 2026**) gives a **100% guarantee** to units hit by the **West Asia crisis**.
**MSE-CDP** funds cluster common facilities and industrial parks; **SFURTI** regenerates traditional-industry clusters.
**CGTMSE** has given collateral-free credit guarantee cover since **2000**.

62.s: In the case of a non-individual enterprise under Stand-Up India, eligibility requires that at least what shareholding and control be with SC/ST persons or women?
62.x: A non-individual enterprise qualifies when at least 51 per cent of its shareholding and control is held by SC/ST persons or women.
62.tq: Use a percentage threshold to distinguish eligibility conditions.
xs: A non-individual enterprise qualifies under **Stand-Up India** if at least **51 per cent** shareholding and control is with **SC/ST** persons or **women** — so option **(3)** is correct.
51% is the majority-control threshold the scheme fixes; 26, 33 and 75 are not the notes' figure.
xa: Stand-Up India was launched in **April 2016**.
It supports **greenfield** enterprises only.
⚠ **PMEGP** gives women up to **35%** capital subsidy — a different scheme.

62.s: Stand-Up India, launched in April 2016, supports which kind of enterprise?
62.x: Stand-Up India supports only greenfield (new) enterprises promoted by SC/ST persons or women. It is not a rehabilitation scheme for sick units, does not fund expansion of existing units, and has nothing to do with disinvestment of PSEs.
62.tq: Stand-Up India = greenfield only; 51% SC/ST or women.
xs: **Stand-Up India** (**April 2016**) supports **greenfield enterprises only** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not for sick-unit rehabilitation, expansion of existing units or disinvestment of public enterprises.
xa: Non-individual enterprises qualify if **51%** shareholding and control are with **SC/ST** persons or **women**.
**YSR Navodayam** (**2019**) in AP restructured stressed MSME loans — the rehabilitation-type scheme.
**PMEGP** gives a margin-money subsidy for **new micro-enterprises**, run by **KVIC**.

62.s: PM Vishwakarma provides support to:
o: 12 trades, with credit up to ₹3 lakh at 7% interest
24 trades, with credit up to ₹5 lakh at 4% interest
18 trades, with credit up to ₹10 lakh at 5% interest
18 trades, with credit up to ₹3 lakh at 5% interest
62.x: PM Vishwakarma covers 18 trades and provides credit up to ₹3 lakh at 5 per cent interest.
xa: Other components: **ID card**, skilling with **Rs 500/day** stipend, toolkit incentive up to **Rs 15,000**, marketing support.
It is a scheme of the **Ministry of MSME**.
**PMMY (MUDRA)** tiers: **Shishu**, **Kishor**, **Tarun**, **Tarun Plus**.

62.s:
Assertion (A): PMEGP is a credit-linked margin-money subsidy scheme for new micro-enterprises.
Reason (R): PMEGP is implemented by NABARD.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
62.x: PMEGP is indeed a credit-linked margin-money subsidy scheme for new micro-enterprises, but it is implemented by KVIC, not NABARD.
xa: **KVIC** became a statutory body in **1956**, succeeding the **All India Khadi and Village Industries Board** (**1953**).
**Stand-Up India** (**April 2016**) funds **greenfield** units with **51%** SC/ST or women control.
**PM Vishwakarma** offers collateral-free credit up to **Rs 3 lakh at 5%** for **18** trades.

62.s: Under the Public Procurement Policy for MSEs Order, 2012, central ministries and CPSEs are required to procure what minimum share of their annual procurement from MSEs?
62.x: The mandatory procurement share from MSEs is 25 per cent; it was raised from 20 per cent in 2018.
62.tq: Test the current mandatory share against its earlier level.
xs: Central ministries and CPSEs must buy at least **25 per cent** of annual procurement from MSEs — so option **(3)** is correct.
**20 per cent** was the earlier mandate, raised to 25% in **2018**.
xa: Sub-targets: **4%** from **SC/ST-owned** MSEs and **3%** from **women-owned** MSEs.
**Achieved** in FY26 (to **1 Dec 2025**): **44.76%**, above the mandate.
**GeM:** **Rs 18.4 lakh crore** GMV; **11 lakh+** MSEs.

62.s: Under the Public Procurement Policy for MSEs, the sub-target for procurement from women-owned MSEs is:
62.x: The sub-targets are 3 per cent from women-owned MSEs and 4 per cent from SC/ST-owned MSEs.
xa: Overall mandate: **25%** of annual procurement (raised from **20%** in **2018**).
Order issued as the **Public Procurement Policy for MSEs Order, 2012**.
Actual MSE procurement reached **44.76%** in FY26.

62.s: A revamped MSME Policy introduced in Andhra Pradesh in 2026 particularly adds incentives for:
62.x: The revamped Andhra Pradesh MSME Policy 2026 adds incentives for women-led MSMEs.
62.tq: Test the beneficiary group of a recently introduced policy measure.
xs: AP's revamped **MSME Policy 2026** adds incentives for **women-led MSMEs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The policy is for MSMEs, not multinationals, state corporations or export-only PSEs.
xa: The earlier **AP MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0** covers **2024-29** (**G.O.Ms.No.69**, **26 Oct 2024**).
AP has about **20.77 lakh** MSMEs, mostly in **services**.
The **single window** for MSMEs in AP is run by **DICs**.

62.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Formation of the Ministry of MSME
B. Launch of PMEGP
C. Launch of Stand-Up India
D. Introduction of Udyam Registration
62.x: The Ministry of MSME was formed in 2007, PMEGP was formed in 2008, Stand-Up India was launched in 2016 and Udyam Registration was introduced in 2020.
62.tq: Anchor the sequence using the earliest and latest dates first.
xs: The order is **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ministry of MSME** (**2007**) → **PMEGP** (**2008**) → **Stand-Up India** (**April 2016**) → **Udyam Registration** (**2020**).
xa: **MSMED Act** in force from **2 October 2006**, before all four.
**Udyam Abhilasha** (SIDBI) and the **Self-Reliant India Fund** both date from **2021**.
**MSME Samadhaan** portal and **TReDS** both began in **2017**.

62.s:
Consider the following about the MSME base of Andhra Pradesh:
1. The State has about 20.77 lakh MSME units.
2. Most of these units are in the services sector.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?

The PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana is a fully online initiative, meaning all aspects of the scheme, from registration to subsidy disbursement, are handled digitally through the National Portal for Rooftop Solar. The process involves online registration, application submission, feasibility approval, vendor selection, installation, net meter application, and finally, subsidy disbursement. 71.s: Reduction of tariffs and quantitative restrictions under the 1991 reforms is termed:

n: De-licensing is associated with international trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Deregulation is associated with foreign investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Import liberalisation is associated with multinational corporation participation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Liberalisation promotes greater market orientation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xa: Average import tariff fell from **~125%** (late 1980s) to **~30%** (early 2000s).
Remaining **QRs removed April 2001**.
⚠ LERMS **1992** → unified rate **1993** → convertibility **1994** → WTO **1995**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): Liberalisation removes or reduces domestic controls.
Reason (R): Liberalisation focuses on removing state controls through industrial de-licensing, import deregulation and private-sector expansion.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true: liberalisation reduces domestic controls, and it does this through de-licensing, freer imports and more room for the private sector. R explains A.
71.tq: Ask whether the tools explain the aim.
n: Liberalisation removes or reduces domestic controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Liberalisation focuses on removing state controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Import deregulation is an instrument of Liberalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Private-sector expansion is an aspect of Liberalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xs: Both A and R are true, and **R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Liberalisation **removes or reduces domestic controls** by **focusing on removing state controls**.
Its tools — **de-licensing**, **import deregulation** and **private-sector expansion** — are how controls are reduced; R explains A.
xa: Liberalisation promotes **greater market orientation**; globalisation promotes **greater global integration**.
**MRTP** asset limits scrapped in **1991**; **SEBI** made statutory in **1992**.
RBI shifted from **regulator to facilitator**.

71.s: LPG reforms were associated with which of the following?
71.x: The LPG reforms opened the door to multinational corporations. Licensing, the joint sector and public-sector dominance belong to the pre-1991 policies.
71.tq: Discriminate pre- and post-1991 features.
n: LPG reforms were associated with multinational corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xs: **LPG reforms** were associated with **multinational corporations** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Globalisation facilitated **expanded entry and participation of MNCs**.
**Industrial licensing**, the **joint sector** and **public-sector** dominance belong to pre-1991 policy.
xa: Indian MNCs that went global: **Tata, Reliance, Infosys, Sun Pharma**.
Licensing abolished for all but **5-6** industries.
**Navratnas (1996)**: **9** PSUs; **Miniratnas**: **97** profit-making PSUs.

71.s: Which one of the following represents a long-term cause rather than an immediate trigger of the 1991 crisis?
o: Persistent fiscal profligacy and rising fiscal deficit
71.x: Persistent fiscal profligacy was a long-term domestic structural cause. The other three were immediate external-financing or geopolitical pressures.
71.tq: Find the structural domestic factor among short-term external shocks.
xs: **Persistent fiscal profligacy** is a **long-term cause** — option **(3)**.
**NRI deposit flight**, the **Gulf War** and **foreign banks stopping lending** were **immediate triggers**.
xa: Other long-term causes: **Licence-Permit-Quota Raj** (MRTP 1970), **PSU losses**, **weak exports**.
⚠ **9.4%** = Centre + States; **8.4%** = Centre's GFD.

71.s: The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced primarily to address which of the following?
o: Dominance of the public and joint sectors
Decline in agriculture's share of GDP
71.x: The 1991 New Economic Policy was a response to a severe balance-of-payments crisis, when foreign reserves covered only about two weeks of imports.
71.tq: Recall the trigger for the 1991 reforms.
n: The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced to address the severe 1991 Balance of Payments crisis. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xs: The **1991 New Economic Policy** was introduced to address the **severe 1991 Balance of Payments crisis** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Forex reserves had fallen to **$975 million (June 1991)** — about **two weeks** of imports.
SEZs, joint-sector dominance and agriculture's share were not its trigger.
xa: Crisis indicators: **high inflation**, **low forex reserves**, **large fiscal deficit** (APPSC 2025).
Triggers: **Gulf War (Aug 1990)**, political instability, **NRI deposit flight**.
**67 tonnes of gold** were pledged to the **Bank of England and UBS**.

71.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the causes of India's 1991 balance of payments crisis?
o: The Gulf War led to a doubling of oil prices.
Current account deficits had been financed by foreign borrowing since the 1980s.
Remittances from the Gulf region rose sharply.
71.x: Gulf remittances dried up rather than rising; the other three were causes of the crisis.
xa: Other trigger: **collapse of the Soviet Union** (**Dec 1991**) — a lost trading partner.
Political instability: **two changes of government** Dec 1989 - June 1991.
Long-term cause: **fiscal profligacy** — GFD **5.4%** (1981-82) to **8.0%** (1989-90).

71.s: The foreign exchange reserves of India in June 1991 were approximately
o: $975 million, sufficient for about two weeks of imports
$69.3 billion, sufficient for about one year of imports
$22.8 billion, sufficient for about three months of imports
$9.75 billion, sufficient for about six months of imports
71.x: India's foreign exchange reserves stood at approximately $975 million in June 1991, covering only about two weeks of imports.
71.tq: Match the crisis-year figure with its associated coverage period.
xs: Reserves were **$975 million** in **June 1991** — enough for about **two weeks** of imports — option **(1)**.
**$69.3 bn** was external debt; **$22.8 bn** was external debt in **1983-84**.
xa: Reserves later rose to **$701.4 bn** (~**11 months** of import cover).
⚠ Forex cover: **2 weeks (1991)** vs **over 11 months** now.
In **May 2026** the PM urged citizens to cut fuel, gold and foreign-travel spending — a step not taken even in **1991**.

71.s: The gross fiscal deficit of the Centre in 1990-91 was approximately
71.x: The Centre's gross fiscal deficit was 8.4 per cent of GDP in 1990-91, compared with 6.1 per cent in 1980-81. The 9.4 per cent figure refers to the combined Centre and States figure.
71.tq: Distinguish the Centre-only figure from the combined Centre and States figure.
xs: The Centre's GFD in 1990-91 was **8.4 per cent** of GDP — option **(4)**.
⚠ **9.4%** is the **combined Centre + States** figure; **3.2%** is the trade deficit/CAD share.
xa: Inflation about **12%**; GDP growth **1.1%**.
Govt internal debt reached **53%** of GDP (1990-91).

71.s: The Indian rupee became convertible on the current account in:
71.x: The rupee became market-determined in 1993 and current-account convertible in 1994; capital-account convertibility stayed partial.
xa: ⚠ Devaluation **1991** → market rate **1993** → convertibility **1994**.
**LERMS (March 1992)**: dual rate — **60%** at market rate, **40%** at official rate.
**WTO** founding member **1995**; **FERA → FEMA** in **1999**.

71.s: Which of the following was NOT a fiscal policy measure of 1991?
71.x: The tax net was widened, not contracted; expenditure control, subsidy cuts and better tax collection were part of the package.
xa: Also included: discipline in managing **Centre and State funds**.
Lower peak income/corporate tax rates (**Chelliah**).
Fiscal deficit (Centre + States) had reached **9.4%** of GDP.

71.s: Under the post-1991 liberalisation measures, tax rates were ____ and the tax base was ____.
71.x: Tax rates were cut and the base widened, alongside scrapping MRTP asset limits, deregulating interest rates and allowing private banks.
xa: **SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.
Industrial licensing abolished except for a few (**5-6**) industries.
Liberalisation = **reduction of state control**.

71.s: After the 1991 delicensing, delicensed firms got:
o: Freedom in pricing but curbs on expansion
Price controls and curbs on expansion
Price controls but no curbs on expansion
Freedom in pricing and no curbs on expansion
71.x: Delicensed firms gained pricing freedom and faced no expansion curbs; licensing stayed only for a few (5-6) industries.
xa: MRTP asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and merger controls were abolished.
Telecom, banking and civil aviation were **reshaped** by reforms.
**Dereservation**: public-sector-reserved industries cut sharply in **1991**.

71.s: Which of the following was NOT removed from the MRTP framework by the Industrial Policy of 1991?
71.x: The 1991 policy abolished MRTP asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and merger/expansion controls; SEBI's statutory status was a separate financial-market reform.
xa: In the 1980s the MRTP limit had been raised to **₹100 crore**.
**MRTP 1970** was part of the Licence-Permit-Quota Raj.
Licensing abolished for all but **5-6** industries.

71.s: When the Navratna scheme was introduced, how many public sector undertakings were given Navratna status?
71.x: The Navratna scheme initially covered nine PSUs, distinct from the 97 profit-making Miniratnas.
xa: ⚠ **9** Navratnas vs **97** Miniratnas.
PSU autonomy also via **MoUs**.
Disinvestment aims: **financial discipline, modernisation, FDI**.
71.fixed: Navratna scheme (9 PSUs) was introduced in 1997, not 1996

71.s: India removed its remaining quantitative restrictions on imports in:
71.x: The remaining QRs went in April 2001; average tariffs fell from about 125% to about 30% and general customs duty was later cut to 10%.
xa: Import licensing was dismantled; **EXIM scrips** and quotas removed.
**DGFT** changed from controller of trade to "**facilitator**".
Strategy shifted from **import substitution to export promotion**.

71.s: Disinvestment of PSU equity under the 1991 reforms was first undertaken mainly to:
71.x: Disinvestment was first used to bridge the fiscal deficit and only later for efficiency; nationalisation was not part of the NEP.
xa: **Dereservation** (1991) opened public-sector-reserved industries to private players.
**New PSE Policy (2021)** for **Atmanirbhar Bharat**.

71.s: After globalisation, India's imports:
71.x: Globalisation expanded trade and technology access, but imports grew faster than exports.
xa: India's world trade share had fallen from **1.78%** (1950) to **0.6%** (1995).
IT/outsourcing boom **cushioned the CAD**.
CAD peaked at **4.8%** of GDP (**FY13**).

71.s:
Assertion (A): Civil aviation saw the entry of private airlines after the 1991 reforms.
Reason (R): Power distribution underwent complete and uncontested privatisation.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
71.x: Private airlines did enter civil aviation, but power-distribution privatisation remained debated, so R is false.
xa: **Telecom** and **banking** were also reshaped.
**Railways** remained a state monopoly.
Source of the slow-sector notes: **LENS, May 2026**.

71.s: Which of the following was NOT an element of the Washington Consensus?
71.x: Privatisation, deregulation and property rights were among the ten Washington Consensus rules; expanding import quotas was not.
xa: It is blamed for the **1997** and **2008** crises.
It is now seen as **obsolete** (14 Mar 2026).
SAP conditions also included **currency devaluation** and **austerity**.

71.s: During the 1991 BoP crisis, about how many tonnes of gold were pledged to the Bank of England and UBS?
71.x: About 67 tonnes of gold were pledged, an IMF loan was taken, and the rupee was devalued in two steps (1 and 3 July 1991).
xa: Earlier IMF borrowings came in **July 1990** and **Jan 1991**.
Market-determined exchange rate came in **1993**.
⚠ **Demonetisation** was **not** part of 1991 (India's were in **1978** and **2016**).

71.s: The principal immediate purpose of the 1991 rupee devaluation was to:
o: Increase the price of Indian exports in foreign markets
Make Indian exports cheaper and help correct the balance of payments
Finance the fiscal deficit through currency expansion
71.x: Devaluation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper for foreign buyers and was undertaken to help address the balance of payments crisis.
71.tq: Apply the economic effect of devaluation rather than recall only its date.
xs: Devaluation aimed to **make Indian exports cheaper** and **correct the balance of payments** — option **(3)**.
This was the **APPSC 2024** key.
Option (1) is the opposite effect; capital account convertibility is still **not** full.
xa: Devaluation: about **20%**, in two steps on **1 and 3 July 1991**.
**Currency devaluation** is a standard **SAP** conditionality.
Strategy shift: **import substitution → export promotion**.

71.s: Stabilisation measures under the New Economic Policy are essentially:
71.x: Stabilisation corrects short-term imbalances (fiscal deficit, inflation, BoP) through demand management; structural adjustment is the supply side.
xa: Lead institutions: **IMF** (stabilisation) and **World Bank (IBRD)** (structural adjustment).
Stabilisation tools: subsidy cuts, **tight monetary policy** by RBI, **rupee devaluation**.
Some UPSC notes also list trade liberalisation under stabilisation.

71.s: Structural Adjustment Programmes are best described as
o: short-term central-bank operations for controlling currency circulation
domestic programmes confined to agricultural subsidies
WTO agreements dealing exclusively with customs valuation
IMF and World Bank loan packages intended to reduce fiscal imbalances and adjust economies for long-term growth
71.x: SAPs are IMF and World Bank loan packages designed to reduce fiscal imbalances and promote long-term economic adjustment and growth.
71.tq: Identify the defining combination of institutions, loans and long-term objectives.
xs: SAPs are **IMF/World Bank loan packages** to **reduce fiscal imbalances** and **adjust economies for long-term growth** — option **(4)**.
This is the **APPSC 2018** definition.
xa: Conditions: **austerity, privatisation, deregulation**, **currency devaluation**, better tax collection.
SAP outcomes raised poverty in the Global South — growth fell from **3.2% to 0.7%** a year.
The **Washington Consensus** (**10** rules) is now seen as obsolete.

71.s: Which plan began immediately after the phase of structural adjustment and macroeconomic stabilisation?
71.x: The Eighth Plan, covering 1992–97, began after structural adjustment and macroeconomic stabilisation.
71.tq: Link the plan period with the reform transition rather than with the preceding Annual Plans.
xs: The **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began right after structural adjustment and macro-stabilisation — option **(2)**.
The **Sixth** and **Seventh** Plans saw rising deficits — average GFD **6.3%** and **8.2%**.
xa: Average growth **6.8%** from **1993-94**.

71.s: Which one of the following pairs correctly identifies the lead institutions associated with stabilisation and structural adjustment respectively?
71.x: Stabilisation is linked with the IMF, whereas structural adjustment is linked with the World Bank, particularly the IBRD.
71.tq: Test the institutional pairing by keeping the order of the two reform components fixed.
xs: **IMF** leads stabilisation; **World Bank (IBRD)** leads structural adjustment — option **(3)**.
Option (4) reverses them; the **WTO** (1995) is a trade body.
xa: Stabilisation = **short-term, demand side**; structural adjustment = **long-term, supply side**.
India received an **IMF loan** of about **$7 bn** in 1991.
India was a **WTO** founding member in **1995** (successor to **GATT, 1948**).

71.s: Structural adjustment under the 1991 reforms is:
71.x: Structural adjustment is long-term and supply-side, while stabilisation is short-term and demand-side.
n: Stabilisation is short-term in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Stabilisation is demand-side in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Structural adjustment is long-term in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Structural adjustment is supply-side in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xa: Lead institution: stabilisation = **IMF**; structural adjustment = **World Bank (IBRD)**.
Stabilisation comes **first**; structural adjustment follows or runs alongside.
The **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began right after structural adjustment and stabilisation.

71.s: Which of the following best describes free trade?
o: Reduction or removal of trade barriers
Provision of an internationally competitive environment
Creation of a level playing field for exports
71.x: Free trade means reducing or removing trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas. The other options are SEZ objectives.
71.tq: Discriminate free trade from SEZ aims.
n: Free trade involves the reduction or removal of trade barriers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xs: **Free trade** = the **reduction or removal of trade barriers** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other options describe aims such as attracting investment and competitiveness, not the meaning of free trade.
xa: **Globalisation** involves the **reduction of import duties** on capital goods.
**Import substitution** gave way to **export promotion** after **1991**.
**WTO** founding member, **1995** — successor to **GATT** (**1948**, **23** countries).

71.s: Integration of the domestic economy with the world economy, with greater participation of MNCs, is called:
71.x: Globalisation linked India to the world economy through trade, FDI and technology flows and drew in more MNCs.
n: Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates expanded participation of Multinational Corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through foreign direct investment capital. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through cross-border technology. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates technology flows. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation promotes greater global integration. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates expanded entry of Multinational Corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xa: Globalisation also involves the **reduction of import duties on capital goods**.
**Liberalisation** and **privatisation** are strategies; **globalisation** is their outcome, with **outsourcing** a major feature.
**FERA → FEMA** (**1999**) was a globalisation measure.

71.s:
Arrange the following measures in the order in which they occurred during the initial 1991 reform sequence:
A. Industrial delicensing
B. Devaluation of the rupee
C. Removal of import quotas and EXIM scrips
D. Market-determined exchange rate
71.x: Devaluation came first in July 1991, followed by industrial delicensing, removal of EXIM scrips and import quotas, and the market-determined exchange rate in 1993.
71.tq: Fix the first and last events, then arrange the intervening reform measures.
xs: Order: **B, A, C, D** — devaluation, delicensing, import quota removal, market rate — option **(1)**.
**Devaluation (July 1991)** came first; then **industrial delicensing**.
Then **MRTP** limits abolished and **EXIM scrips** and quotas removed; market rate in **1993**.
xa: ⚠ Devaluation **1991** → market rate **1993** → convertibility **1994**.
**LERMS** (March 1992) was the dual-rate bridge.
Remaining **QRs** were removed only in **April 2001**.

71.s: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) was introduced in:
71.x: LERMS came in March 1992 (60% at market rate, 40% at official rate); a unified market rate followed in March 1993.
xa: ⚠ LERMS **1992** → unified rate **1993** → convertibility **1994** → WTO **1995** → FEMA **1999** → QRs removed **2001**.
The rupee was devalued about **20%** on **1 and 3 July 1991**.
Capital account is only **partly** convertible.

71.s: SEBI was given statutory status in:
71.x: SEBI received statutory status in 1992; FEMA replaced FERA in 1999.
xa: **LERMS** came in **March 1992**.
Current account convertibility: **1994**.
WTO founding member: **1995**.

71.s: The growth of India's IT and outsourcing exports after 1991 helped to:
71.x: IT and outsourcing generated services exports that helped cushion India's current account deficit.
xa: **1,800+ Global Capability Centres** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports in **July 2026**.
CAD was **0.8%** of GDP in **H1 FY26**; peak **4.8%** (FY13).
**ES 2025-26**: persistent CAD = structural cause of India's **high cost of capital**.

71.s: Which one of the following statements about the WTO and its predecessor is NOT correct?
o: GATT was associated with the year 1948.
India joined the WTO as a non-founding member in 2001.
71.x: India was a founding member of the WTO in 1995. The WTO succeeded GATT, which is associated with 1948 and 23 countries.
71.tq: Find the statement that contradicts the membership status and year.
xs: "India joined the WTO as a **non-founding member in 2001**" is NOT correct — option **(4)**.
India was a **founding member** of the **WTO** in **1995**.
The WTO succeeded **GATT** (**1948**, **23 countries**) — options (1)-(3) are correct.
xa: India signed **TRIPS, TRIMS and AoA**.
**2001** is the year remaining **QRs** were removed.

71.s: Which of the following was a feature of the economic groundwork laid during the 1980s?
o: Complete abolition of all industrial licensing
Broad-banding of licences and easier imports of capital goods
71.x: The 1980s saw broad-banding of licences, easier capital-goods imports, a higher MRTP limit and relaxation of FERA. Complete delicensing and FEMA came later.
71.tq: Distinguish preparatory 1980s measures from post-1991 reforms.
xs: The 1980s saw **broad-banding of licences** and **easier imports of capital goods** — option **(2)**.
Other 1980s steps: MRTP limit raised to **₹100 crore**; **FERA** eased.
Licensing was abolished (for all but **5-6** industries) only in **1991**; **FERA → FEMA** came in **1999**.
xa: This groundwork was under **Indira and Rajiv Gandhi** (**1984-89**).
Growth touched **5.5%**, breaking the Hindu rate, but was **debt-fuelled**.
⚠ **Full capital account convertibility** has still not been adopted.

71.s: Which of the following sets contains only structural adjustment measures?
o: Delicensing, tariff reduction and public-sector disinvestment
Subsidy cuts, tight money and devaluation
Inflation control, deficit reduction and tight money
Demand management, exchange control and subsidy expansion
71.x: Delicensing, tariff reduction and public-sector disinvestment are structural measures aimed at improving supply-side efficiency and long-term growth.
71.tq: Group measures by their policy objective instead of by the reform year.
xs: **Delicensing, tariff reduction and PSU disinvestment** are structural adjustment measures — option **(1)**.
Structural adjustment is **supply-side**, aimed at **long-term** efficiency and growth.
Subsidy cuts, **tight money**, **devaluation** and deficit reduction are **stabilisation** tools.
xa: Structural tools also include **MRTP relaxation**, **FDI opening**, **QR removal**, export promotion.
Lead institution for structural adjustment: **World Bank (IBRD)**.
The **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began right after structural adjustment and stabilisation.

71.s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the 1991 New Economic Policy?
71.x: Nationalisation was not a feature of the 1991 New Economic Policy. The policy instead promoted delicensing, disinvestment and greater foreign investment.
71.tq: Find the measure that reverses the reform direction.
xs: **Nationalisation** was NOT a 1991 NEP feature — option **(2)**.
It was the **odd one out** in **APPSC 2018**.
**Disinvestment**, **FDI liberalisation** and **delicensing** were NEP features.
xa: Also NOT NEP: strengthening the **License Raj/MRTP**, import substitution, more SSI reservation.
The economy was opened to foreign and private investment in **1991** (APPSC 2018).
FDI up to **100%** via automatic route in high-priority industries.

71.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 1991 New Economic Policy?
o: Full capital-account convertibility was not adopted.
Devaluation, tariff cuts and removal of import quotas were external-sector measures.
FDI was liberalised through an automatic route in high-priority industries.
Demonetisation formed part of the 1991 reform package.
71.x: Demonetisation was not part of the 1991 package; India's demonetisations were in 1978 and 2016.
xa: ⚠ **FDI in retail and defence** opened only much later.
**100% FDI in insurance** is now in place (May 2026).
**Nationalisation** was the odd one out (APPSC 2018).

71.s: Which of the following reflects the post-1991 reform direction?
o: Raising tariffs to protect domestic producers
Expanding the list of industries reserved for the public sector
Inviting FDI and FPI, with IT and services exports acting as a cushion
Restricting foreign investment to joint ventures with PSUs
71.x: The post-reform approach lowered tariffs, invited FDI and FPI, and benefited from IT and services exports as a cushion.
xa: Direction: **import substitution → export promotion**.
Economy moved to **enhanced global integration** (**PYQ 2025**).
**1,800+ GCCs** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports in July 2026.

71.s: A persistent current account deficit has been identified as a structural cause of India's:
71.x: Persistent CAD has been identified as a structural cause of India's high cost of capital.
xa: CAD was **0.8%** of GDP in **H1 FY26**; peaked at **4.8%** (FY13).
In 1991 the CAD was **3.1-3.2%** of GDP.
IT/services exports help **cushion the CAD**.

71.s: Which adverse outcome was associated with the pattern of growth after economic reforms?
o: Growth became entirely dependent on public-sector employment.
Agriculture received all investment and labour-intensive sectors disappeared.
Capital-intensive sectors generated more jobs than the available labour force.
Agriculture was neglected and capital-intensive growth generated too few jobs.
71.x: The pattern of growth was criticised for neglecting agriculture and concentrating growth in capital-intensive sectors, which created too few employment opportunities.
71.tq: Identify the stated distributional and employment consequence rather than the aggregate growth benefit.
xs: **Agriculture was neglected** and **capital-intensive** growth created **too few jobs** — option **(4)**.
This is the **Beyond GDP essay** criticism.
xa: **Jobless growth**: output rose faster than jobs; many graduates end in **gig work**.
**Agrarian neglect**: public investment in agriculture lagged.
**Crony capitalism**: gains concentrated among large, politically connected firms.

71.s: India's GDP growth in 1994–95 was about:
71.x: Growth was below 1% in 1991–92, about 5% in 1992–94 and 6.3% in 1994–95.
xa: Average growth: **5.18%** in the 1980s vs **6.8%** from **1993-94**.
GDP growth had been **1.1%** in **1990-91**.

71.s: Foreign-exchange reserves increased from approximately $975 million in 1991 to about
71.x: Foreign-exchange reserves rose from about $975 million in 1991 to approximately $701.4 billion, providing around 11 months of import cover as stated.
71.tq: Handle changes in units carefully when comparing a million figure with a billion figure.
xs: Reserves rose from **$975 million** (1991) to about **$701.4 billion** — option **(3)**.
That gives about **11 months** of import cover.
xa: ⚠ Forex cover: **2 weeks (1991)** vs **over 11 months** now.
In **1991** **67 tonnes of gold** had to be pledged abroad.
PM's **May 2026** appeal to save forex was not made even in 1991.

71.s: Which one of the following sectors remained largely a state monopoly after the reforms?
71.x: Railways remained a state monopoly, although modernisation continued to be pursued. The other sectors experienced greater private-sector participation or competition.
71.tq: Find the sector that was comparatively untouched among reform-exposed industries.
xs: **Railways** remained a **state monopoly** — option **(2)**.
Modernisation is still in progress (**LENS, May 2026**).
**Civil aviation**, **consumer electronics** and **telecom** saw private entry.
xa: Other slow sectors: **power distribution** (DISCOM privatisation debated), **agriculture**, **ports**.
**Civil aviation** saw **private airlines** enter.
Telecom: falling prices after private and foreign entry.

71.s: Which of the following best illustrates the criticism of crony capitalism?
o: Agricultural investment increases uniformly across regions
Small firms exclusively control public-sector disinvestment
All firms receive equal access to public resources
Gains are concentrated among large, politically connected firms
71.x: Crony capitalism is criticised because economic gains become concentrated among large firms with political connections.
71.tq: Recognise the concept through its distributional consequence.

74.s: What is the full form of EPCG?
74.x: The full form of EPCG is ‘Export Promotion Capital Goods’. EPCG scheme helps in facilitating the import of capital goods for manufacturing quality goods and to augment the competitiveness of India’s export. 74.s:
Consider the following statements about 'Rules of Origin':
1. Rules of Origin are the criteria needed to determine the national source of a product.
2. Rules of Origin help the custom agencies to know what regulations and fees apply to a given product.
3. These are used for the purpose of trade statistics.
4. Their importance is derived from the fact that duties and restrictions in several cases depend upon the sources of imports.
Which of the above statements are correct?
74.x: Rules of origin are the criteria needed to determine the national source of a product. Their importance is derived from the fact that duties and restrictions in several cases depend upon the source of imports. There is wide variation in the practice of governments with regard to the rules of origin. While the requirements of substantial transformation is universally recognized, some governments apply the criterion of change of tariff classification, others the ad valorem percentage criterion and yet others the criterion of manufacturing or processing operation. In a globalizing world it has become even more important that a degree of harmonization is achieved in these practices of members in implementing such a requirement. Rules of origin are used : ¾to implement measures and instruments of commercial policy such as anti-dumping duties and safeguard measures; ¾to determine whether imported products shall receive most-favoured-nation (MFN) treatment or preferential treatment; ¾for the purpose of trade statistics; ¾for the application of labelling and marking requirements; and ¾for government procurement. Hence, all of the given statements are correct.

75.s: Under the Balance of Payments framework, which of the following best distinguishes the presentation followed by the IMF from that generally followed by the Reserve Bank of India?
o: The IMF uses only current and capital accounts, whereas the RBI uses current, capital and financial accounts separately.
The IMF uses only trade and services accounts, whereas the RBI uses current and financial accounts.
The IMF uses current, capital and financial accounts, whereas the RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts.
Both the IMF and the RBI invariably present the Balance of Payments through exactly three separate accounts.
75.x: Under BPM6, the IMF distinguishes current, capital and financial accounts. The RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts under the heading ‘capital account’.
75.tq: Separate the IMF classification from the RBI presentation instead of treating the terms as identical.
xs: The **IMF (BPM6)** uses **three accounts — current, capital, financial**, while the **RBI combines** the last two as **"Capital Account"** — option **(3)**.
So the RBI does not keep them separate (option 1), and the two do not invariably use three accounts (option 4).
xa: **BoP** = systematic record of all transactions of residents with the rest of the world, on **double-entry** bookkeeping.
BoP has a **current account and a capital account** (PYQ 2025; APPSC-G2 2025 key).
Identity: Current + Capital + Financial + Net Errors & Omissions = **0**.

75.s: Which of the following correctly represents the Balance of Payments identity?
o: Current balance + capital balance + financial balance + errors and omissions = zero
Current balance + merchandise exports = financial balance
Current balance − capital balance = trade balance
75.x: The Balance of Payments identity is current balance plus capital balance plus financial balance plus errors and omissions equal to zero.
75.tq: Recall the complete identity rather than restricting the BoP to the trade balance.
xs: BoP identity: **Current + Capital + Financial + Net Errors & Omissions = 0** — option **(2)**.
BoP always **balances in accounting terms**; a surplus in one account = a deficit in another.
xa: BoP uses **double-entry** bookkeeping.
IMF **BPM6** has three accounts; RBI merges capital and financial into **"Capital Account"**.
**Overall BoP** positive → adds to reserves; negative → draws them down.

75.s: What is the usual effect of the overall balance of payments position on foreign exchange reserves?
o: The overall balance has no relationship with reserve movements.
A positive overall balance reduces reserves, while a negative balance increases them.
A positive overall balance adds to reserves, while a negative balance draws them down.
Both positive and negative balances increase reserves because the BoP always balances in accounting terms.
75.x: A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down. If reserves become insufficient, a balance of payments crisis may result.
75.tq: Use the direction of reserve movement to identify the correct surplus-deficit relationship.
xs: A **positive overall BoP adds to reserves**; a **negative** one **draws them down** — option **(3)**.
If reserves run short → **BoP crisis**.
xa: **July 2026**: overall BoP **$20.8 bn surplus**; capital account **$27.7 bn surplus**.
Forex reserves **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
Reserve components: **FCA**, **gold**, **SDRs**, **Reserve Tranche Position**.

75.s: The external-sector recovery in FY24 was mainly associated with:

75.s: Which of the following best defines the Balance of Payments (BoP)?
o: A complete record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world during a specified period
A systematic record of only goods exported and imported during a year
A record of only services and transfer payments between countries
A record of only cross-border capital movements during a specified period

n: Balance of Payments is a systematic record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments is a complete record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

The specified period for Balance of Payments is normally one year. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments covers all international economic transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xs: The **Balance of Payments** is a **complete record of all economic transactions** between **residents** of a country and the **rest of the world** during a **specified period** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It covers **goods**, **services**, **transfers** and **capital transactions**; the "only" options describe parts of it.
xa: The period is **normally one year**; BoP is kept on **double-entry** bookkeeping.
It has a **current account and a capital account** (APPSC-G2 2025 key).
IMF's **BPM6** uses three accounts; **RBI** combines capital and financial as "Capital Account".

75.s: The Balance of Trade covers:

Balance of Trade is visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments includes goods, services, transfers, and capital transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments is the broader external account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

xa: **Full current account convertibility** came in **August 1994** (IMF **Article VIII**).

n: Current Account contains visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Visible trade consists of exports and imports of goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account contains invisible transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

xs: The incorrect statement is that **FDI is included in the Current Account** — so option **(2)** is the answer.

The **Current Account** has **visible trade** (goods) and **invisibles** — **services**, **transfer payments**, **net income**; options 1, 3, 4 are correct.

75.s:
Assertion (A): Current Account Deficit occurs when payments exceed receipts from goods, services, transfers and net income.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

n: Current Account contains visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Visible trade consists of exports and imports of goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account contains invisible transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Invisible transactions consist of services, transfer payments, and net income. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from services. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from transfers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from net income. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xs: Both A and R are true, and **R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **Current Account Deficit** arises when **payments exceed receipts** from **goods, services, transfers and net income**.
Those are exactly the Current Account's items — **visible trade** and **invisible transactions** — so R explains A.
xa: A **CAD** must be financed by a capital account surplus or by drawing down reserves.

75.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Balance of Trade covers only goods or visible trade.
A Balance of Trade deficit occurs when goods imports exceed goods exports.
Balance of Trade is the complete record of economic transactions with the rest of the world.
A Balance of Trade surplus occurs when goods exports exceed goods imports.
75.x: Option C is incorrect: the full record of transactions with the world is the balance of payments. The balance of trade covers only goods.
