Informal credit markets are fully within the reach of RBI policy
82.x: Informal credit markets remain outside the full reach of RBI policy, which is itself an obstacle to transmission.
xa: Other obstacles: **NPAs**, **structural rigidities**, **liquidity mismatches**.
GNPA is at a **multi-decadal low** of **2.2%** (Sep **2025**).

82.s: Which of the following influence Indian government-security yields?
o: US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions, and domestic inflation and short-term rates
82.x: G-sec yields are influenced by all three: US Fed actions, RBI actions, and domestic inflation and short-term interest rates.
xa: **OMO purchases** (**₹1 lakh crore**, Dec **2025**) were meant to **stabilise bond yields**.
A narrower **sovereign spread** over US bonds → lower borrowing costs.
**S&P** upgraded India from **BBB- to BBB** (**2025-26**).

82.s: If the repo rate is 5.25 per cent, the MSF rate under the current corridor would be:
82.x: The MSF rate is 25 basis points above repo (5.50%), and the SDF rate 25 basis points below it (5.00%).
xa: The corridor is **50 bps** wide (**5.00-5.50%**).
The **bank rate** equals the MSF.
⚠ MSF began in **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**.

82.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Bank Rate – RBI absorbs liquidity from banks
Repo Rate – RBI buys or sells government securities
Reverse Repo – RBI lends to banks against securities
OMO – RBI buys or sells government securities
82.x: OMO is the RBI buying or selling government securities. Bank rate is its lending rate, repo is lending against securities and reverse repo absorbs liquidity.
n: Bank Rate is the RBI’s lending or discount rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 12-13]
Repo Rate is lending by the RBI to banks against securities. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 12-13]
Reverse Repo enables the RBI to absorb liquidity from banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 12-13]
OMO involves the RBI buying or selling government securities. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 12-13]
xa: Current rates: **Repo 5.25%**, **Bank Rate 5.50%**, **Reverse Repo 3.35%** (May 2026).
**MSF** = repo + **25 bps** — the **ceiling** of the corridor; **SDF** (**5.00%**) is the **floor**.
⚠ **Fiscal deficit** belongs to **fiscal policy**, not monetary policy instruments.

82.s: Central bank policy rates directly regulate which of the following?
o: The order of liquidity among deposits
The difference between M3 and M1
The composition of narrow money only
82.x: Policy rates directly control how much credit banks can create. The other options are definitions of money measures.
82.tq: Recall what policy rates act on.
n: Central bank policy rates directly regulate the capacity for credit creation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xs: Central bank policy rates **directly regulate** **the capacity for credit creation** — option **(3)**.
A **lower bank rate** **expands liquidity**; a **higher bank rate** **contracts liquidity**.
The other options describe money measures: the **liquidity order** of deposits and **M3 minus M1** (= **time deposits**) are not set by policy rates.
xa: **Lower bank rate** = **expansionary stance**; **higher bank rate** = **tight stance**.
**MSF** began **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**; now **25 bps above repo**.
⚠ MSF borrowing limit: **1%** of NDTL (2011) vs **2%** now.

82.s: Which of the following about the Reverse Repo is NOT correct?
o: Under it, banks borrow from the RBI
It is used to absorb surplus liquidity
It is a monetary policy tool
Under it, the RBI borrows from banks
82.x: Under reverse repo the RBI borrows from banks to absorb surplus liquidity; banks borrowing from the RBI is repo.
n: The Reverse Repo Rate is the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
A bank parks money with the RBI under the Reverse Repo Rate mechanism. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
The Reverse Repo Rate is used to absorb surplus liquidity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
The Reverse Repo Rate is associated with monetary policy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
xa: Under **repo**, a **bank borrows** from the RBI — **liquidity injection**.
**Reverse repo rate** = **3.35%** (May 2026); used at RBI's discretion since **SDF**.
**SDF** absorbs surplus **without collateral** — floor of the LAF corridor at **5.00%**.

82.s: The RBI's principal policy lending rate is the:
82.x: Repo is the main policy lending rate and the tool for regular liquidity; MSF is for emergency, marginal needs.
n: Repo is the principal policy lending rate in the source framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is used for marginal or short-term liquidity needs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: MSF is an **overnight borrowing facility** that can involve **dipping** into the **SLR portfolio**.
**MSF** traditionally costs **more** than repo; now repo + **25 bps**.
The **policy repo rate** is the **main instrument** — the single operating policy rate under **FIT**.

82.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Repo – principal policy rate for regular liquidity management
Marginal Standing Facility – absorbs surplus liquidity from banks without collateral
Bank Rate – rate at which the RBI rediscounts bills of exchange
Standing Deposit Facility – absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral
82.x: MSF is overnight emergency borrowing above the repo rate that lets banks dip into SLR; absorbing surplus liquidity without collateral is the SDF.
n: The MSF rate traditionally carries a higher cost than the repo rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) can involve dipping into the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) portfolio. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is the principal policy lending rate in the source framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: **SDF** began **April 2022**, enabled by **Budget 2018-19**; first proposed in **2015**.
Rates: **SDF 5.00%**, **repo 5.25%**, **MSF = bank rate 5.50%**.
Corridor order: **SDF** (floor) < **repo** < **MSF = bank rate** (ceiling).

82.s: Open Market Operations (OMO) are associated with which of the following?
82.x: Open market operations, the RBI buying and selling government securities, are a monetary-policy tool. Public revenue belongs to fiscal policy.
82.tq: Discriminate monetary from fiscal tools.
n: OMO is a monetary policy instrument. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 75-77]
xs: **Open Market Operations** are associated with **monetary policy** — option **(1)**.
OMO means the **RBI buying or selling government securities**; a **sale absorbs** and a **purchase injects** liquidity.
⚠ **Public revenue** is associated with **fiscal policy**, which uses **spending, taxes, subsidies and borrowing**.
xa: **OMOs** are the main tool for **durable** liquidity — e.g. **₹1 lakh crore** of purchases in **Dec 2025**.
FY26 OMO purchases: **₹2.39 lakh crore** (**Apr-May 2025**).
A **decrease** in the **Bank Rate** **increases liquidity**; an increase is **contractionary**.
To control inflation (**dear money**), the RBI **sells G-secs**; to boost growth, it **buys G-secs**.

82.s: A bank is allowed to lend ₹70 against a security valued at ₹100. If the margin requirement is raised, the immediate effect will generally be to
o: increase the value of the security automatically
convert the loan into an equity investment
reduce the loan available against the same security
increase the loan available against the same security
82.x: The margin is the gap between the value of the security and the loan. Raising the margin reduces the amount that can be borrowed against the same security.
82.tq: Apply the inverse relationship between margin requirements and credit availability.
xs: Raising the margin will **reduce the loan available against the same security** — option **(3)**.
**Margin** = gap between the **value of the security** and the **loan**.
Higher margin = **smaller loan** → cuts credit against that security.
xa: Margin requirement is a **qualitative (selective)** tool.
⚠ **Moral suasion**, **margin requirements**, **direct action** = qualitative; **CRR, SLR, OMO** = quantitative.

82.s: Why do interest rates on outstanding MCLR-linked loans generally respond more slowly than rates on EBLR-linked loans?
o: MCLR-linked loans reset only periodically, whereas EBLR-linked loans reprice quickly
MCLR-linked loans are unrelated to bank funding costs
Outstanding loans are excluded from monetary transmission
EBLR-linked loans are reset only once a year by law
82.x: MCLR-linked loans reset at periodic intervals, creating a lag. EBLR-linked loans are directly linked to an external benchmark and reprice more quickly.
82.tq: Discriminate between periodic reset behaviour and rapid external-benchmark repricing.
xs: **MCLR-linked loans reset only periodically**, whereas **EBLR-linked loans reprice quickly** — option **(1)**.
That is why outstanding-loan WALR (**9.26%**) lagged fresh-loan WALR (**8.5%**) in Sep **2025**.
xa: **Deposit rates** and **MCLR** adjust slowly.
WALR on fresh loans fell **64 bps** in **FY26** (ES **2025-26**).

82.s: ‘Repurchase Option’ is used :
o: to reduce the heavy sell off pressure of rupee in
to increase the sell off pressure of rupee in Exchange
to reduce the value of rupee in Exchange market
82.x: ‘Repurchase Option’ (or Repo Rate) is used by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to regulate the money supply and inflation in the economy. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

82.s: The gradual reduction in the SLR from its 1991-92 level was undertaken on the advice of the
82.x: The SLR was gradually reduced after the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee on financial-sector reforms.
82.tq: Use the committee-recommendation trap by matching the reform with the correct committee.
xs: SLR was cut gradually on the **Narasimham Committee**'s advice — option **(2)**.
It fell from **38.5%** of NDTL (**1991-92**) to **18%** now.
xa: SLR statutory range: **0-40%**; the **25%** floor went in **2007**.
SLR is governed by **Sec 24** of the **BR Act, 1949**.

82.s: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is governed by which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
82.x: CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act; SLR by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
xa: CRR now **3%** of NDTL; SLR **18%**.
"Required reserve ratio" = **CRR** (APPSC **2023**).

82.s: The SLR, which was 38.5 per cent in 1991–92, stood at what level in September 2023?
82.x: The SLR was 18 per cent in September 2023, down from 38.5 per cent in 1991–92.
xa: SLR was cut gradually on the **Narasimham** Committee's advice.
SLR statutory range **0-40%**; **25%** floor removed in **2007**.
CRR was **4%** before the **2025** cuts → **3%** now.

82.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Quantitative tools — Margin requirements and moral suasion
Quantitative tools — Change the volume and cost of total credit
Qualitative tools — Direct the flow of credit among sectors or borrowers
82.x: Margin requirements and moral suasion are qualitative or selective tools. Quantitative tools include repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR and SLR.
82.tq: Separate tools by whether they alter total credit or direct credit to selected borrowers.
xs: **Quantitative tools — margin requirements and moral suasion** is wrong — option **(1)**.
**Margin requirements** and **moral suasion** are **qualitative (selective)** tools.
Quantitative tools: **bank rate, repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR, SLR**; they act on the **volume and cost** of total credit.
xa: Qualitative tools **direct credit to sectors or borrowers**; also called **selective credit control**.
Quantitative tools are also called **traditional methods of control**.
Other qualitative tools: **credit rationing**, **direct action**, consumer credit regulation.

82.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the monetary policy framework followed in India during 1985–1998?
82.x: During 1985–1998, India followed monetary targeting with feedback, with M3 as the principal monetary aggregate.
82.tq: Directly identify the framework associated with the given period.
xs: During **1985-1998** India followed **monetary targeting with feedback** (using **M3**) — option **(3)**.
The **multiple indicator approach** came in **1998-2016**; **flexible inflation targeting** from **2016**.
xa: Landmarks of that phase: **Chakravarty Committee 1985**, **Vaghul Committee 1987** (money market).
Multiple-indicator landmarks: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **Base Rate 2010**, **MSF 2011**, **MCLR 2016**.
**Shaktikanta Das** traced these phases in "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" (**24 Jan 2020**).

82.s: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) was introduced in:
82.x: MSF came in 2011, after LAF (2000) and MSS (2004), and before MCLR (2016).
xa: **Base Rate** came in **2010**, between MSS and MSF.
**SDF** began in **April 2022**, under the FIT phase.
All four belong to the **1998-2016** multiple indicator era (MCLR at its end).

82.s: India's flexible inflation-targeting framework is based on the recommendations of which committee?
82.x: The Urjit Patel Committee reported in 2014, the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement followed in 2015 and the RBI Act was amended in 2016.
xa: **SDF** (**2022**) is a later landmark of the FIT phase.
Under FIT, the **repo rate** is the **single operating policy rate**.
**Price stability** is the paramount objective.

82.s: India adopted the flexible inflation-targeting framework in:
82.x: Flexible inflation targeting began in 2016, after the multiple indicator approach of 1998–2016.
xa: **Money supply (M3)** targeting was the **1985-1998** framework.
The approach was dropped for being **opaque**.
Landmarks of the era: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **MSF 2011**.

82.s: Which of the following rates is correctly classified as a rate fixed by the RBI or the Monetary Policy Committee rather than by an individual bank or the market?
o: Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate
82.x: The MSF rate is fixed by the RBI/MPC. MCLR is computed by each bank, EBLR is linked to an external benchmark, and the call money rate is market-determined.
82.tq: Separate official policy rates from bank-specific benchmarks and market-determined rates.
xs: The **Marginal Standing Facility rate** is fixed by **RBI/MPC** — option **(3)**.
**MCLR** is set by **each bank**; **EBLR** is a bank's spread over an external benchmark.
The **call money rate** (WACR) is **market-determined**.
xa: RBI/MPC also fix **repo, SDF, bank rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR**.
⚠ **SLR** and **CRR** are set by RBI, not by banks.

82.s: The Base Rate system of bank lending was introduced on:
82.x: The Base Rate came on 1 July 2010 and was based on the average cost of funds; MCLR (2016) uses the marginal cost of funds.
xa: Base Rate gave **slow transmission**.
**EBLR** from **1 October 2019**.

82.s: MCLR was introduced on
82.x: The Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate system was introduced on 1 April 2016.
82.tq: Test the close dates of successive lending-rate benchmark reforms.
xs: **MCLR** was introduced on **1 April 2016** — option **(2)**.
**1 July 2010** is the **Base Rate**; **1 October 2019** is **EBLR**.
xa: MCLR is based on the **marginal cost of funds** + CRR/SLR carry + operating cost + **tenor premium**.
**Janak Raj** group (**2017**) found MCLR transmission weak.
MCLR came at the end of the **1998-2016** multiple-indicator phase.

82.s: From 1 October 2019, new floating-rate personal, retail and micro, small and medium enterprise loans were required to be linked to
o: an external benchmark such as the repo rate or specified Treasury-bill yield
the BPLR fixed by the RBI
the average call money rate of the preceding financial year
an internal benchmark selected by the borrowing customer
82.x: From 1 October 2019, such loans had to be linked to an external benchmark, including the repo rate, the three- or six-month Treasury-bill yield, or an FBIL-published rate.
82.tq: Apply the external-benchmark rule to the specified category of floating-rate loans.
xs: From **1 October 2019**, such loans must link to **an external benchmark such as the repo rate or T-bill yield** — option **(1)**.
Benchmarks: **repo rate**, **3-month** or **6-month** T-bill yield, or an **FBIL**-published rate.
**BPLR** was an old bank-set benchmark; the choice is not the borrower's internal pick.
xa: Loans linked directly to repo are the **fastest route** of transmission.
The mandate followed the **Janak Raj** Internal Study Group (**2017**).

82.s: Which of the following best distinguishes the Base Rate system from the MCLR system?
o: Base Rate used average cost of funds, whereas MCLR uses marginal cost of funds
Base Rate used marginal cost of funds, whereas MCLR used average cost of funds
Base Rate is applicable only to government securities, whereas MCLR applies only to deposits
Both Base Rate and MCLR are directly linked to the repo rate
82.x: The Base Rate was based on the average cost of funds and therefore transmitted policy changes slowly. MCLR uses marginal cost components, including marginal deposit costs, CRR/SLR carry, operating cost and tenor premium.
82.tq: Discriminate between two closely related benchmark-rate systems by their cost-of-funds basis.
xs: **Base Rate used average cost of funds**, whereas **MCLR uses marginal cost of funds** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses them.
Neither is directly linked to repo; that is **EBLR** — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Base Rate: **1 July 2010**; MCLR: **1 April 2016**.
MCLR adds **CRR/SLR carry**, **operating cost** and **tenor premium**.

82.s: Which one of the following represents the fastest route of monetary-policy transmission to lending rates?
o: Loans linked to fixed small-savings rates
Loans linked to the Base Rate
82.x: EBLR links lending rates directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, allowing loans to reprice more quickly than Base Rate or MCLR loans.
82.tq: Identify the institutional mechanism that transmits a policy-rate change most directly.
xs: **Loans linked to EBLR** are the fastest transmission route — option **(1)**.
EBLR loans linked directly to **repo** **reprice quickly**.
**MCLR** and deposit rates adjust **slowly**; **Base Rate** was slow too.
xa: **Administered small-savings rates** hold deposit rates up — an obstacle to transmission.
Outstanding-loan WALR (**9.26%**) lags fresh loans (**8.5%**) because MCLR loans reset periodically.

82.s: The Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system, constituted by the RBI in 2017, was chaired by whom?
82.x: The RBI’s Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system was chaired by Janak Raj in 2017.
82.tq: Use the committee-chairperson association to identify the correct answer.
xs: The **2017** Internal Study Group on MCLR was chaired by **Janak Raj** — option **(2)**.
It found **MCLR transmission weak** and recommended an **external benchmark**.
xa: Outcome: **EBLR mandate from 1 Oct 2019**.
⚠ **Urjit Patel Committee** (**2014**) led to **flexible inflation targeting**, not EBLR.

82.s: Following the RBI's Internal Study Group on MCLR, the external benchmark-based lending rate (EBLR) became mandatory from:
82.x: The study group found weak MCLR transmission and recommended an external benchmark, leading to the EBLR mandate from 1 October 2019.
xa: EBLR benchmarks: **repo**, **3-month**/**6-month** T-bill yield, or an **FBIL** rate.
EBLR covers new floating **personal/retail and MSME** loans.

82.s: Which of the following about the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is NOT correct?
o: It is an overnight borrowing facility
Banks borrow from the RBI under it
Its rate is usually repo plus 0.25%
Its rate is lower than the repo rate
82.x: MSF costs more than repo, usually repo plus 0.25%; it is an overnight emergency window, while repo is for regular liquidity.
n: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is an overnight borrowing facility. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Banks borrow from the RBI through the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF). [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The MSF rate traditionally carries a higher cost than the repo rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: Under MSF banks can **dip into** their **SLR portfolio** up to **2%** of NDTL.
MSF began **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**, up to **1%** of NDTL.
Corridor: **SDF (5.00%)** floor, **MSF (5.50%)** ceiling — **50 bps** wide.

82.s: The Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), introduced in April 2004, was meant to:
o: Sterilise excess liquidity created by foreign-exchange purchases
Replace the repo for daily liquidity adjustment
82.x: Under the MSS the RBI issues Treasury Bills and securities to absorb rupees created by forex purchases; the proceeds sit in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
xa: **MSS** securities count towards banks' **SLR**.
Sterilisation tools: **OMO/MSS** sales and **VRRRs**.

82.s: Sterilisation by the Reserve Bank of India refers to:
o: Increasing currency circulation after a fall in exports
Absorbing or offsetting excess rupee liquidity created by foreign-exchange inflows
Replacing open market operations with fiscal expenditure
Converting all foreign-exchange reserves into gold
82.x: When foreign-exchange inflows increase rupee liquidity, the RBI may sell government securities or conduct liquidity-absorption operations to offset the impact. This process is called sterilisation.
82.tq: Identify the policy operation by linking foreign-exchange inflows with offsetting domestic liquidity action.
xs: **Sterilisation** = **absorbing or offsetting excess rupee liquidity created by forex inflows** — option **(2)**.
RBI sells G-secs (**OMO/MSS**) or runs **VRRRs** to offset it.
xa: Sep **2026** case: **FCNR(B)** inflows of **$127.23 bn**.
**MSS** began in **April 2004**.
Under an **open capital account**, flows move liquidity and the rupee.

82.s: The policy repo rate is regarded as the main monetary-policy instrument because the Monetary Policy Committee sets it primarily to
o: achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates
determine the annual SLR ceiling of 40 per cent
fix the exchange rate of the Indian rupee permanently
82.x: The MPC sets the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target, while liquidity operations help keep money-market rates close to that rate.
82.tq: Connect the policy instrument with the objective it is designed to achieve.
xs: The MPC sets the repo rate to **achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates** — option **(1)**.
Liquidity is managed so **money-market rates stay near** the repo rate.
The **SLR ceiling of 40%** is statutory, not set via the repo rate.
xa: The repo is the **single operating policy rate** under **FIT** and the **most-watched signal**.
**OMOs** are the main tool for **durable** liquidity.

82.s: When the RBI raises the repo rate, the first effect in the transmission sequence is:
82.x: The sequence is higher money-market rates, then costlier credit, then lower consumption and investment, and finally lower aggregate demand.
xa: A rate cut **increases investment expenditure** (UPSC **2014**).
⚠ A rate cut does not raise savings or tax collection.
Transmission channels: **interest rate, credit, exchange rate, asset price, expectations**.

82.s: Surplus liquidity in the banking system generally pulls market rates:
o: Below the repo rate, speeding up transmission
Above the repo rate, speeding up transmission
Above the repo rate, weakening transmission
Below the repo rate, weakening transmission
82.x: Surplus liquidity can lower market rates below the repo rate and aid transmission; deficit liquidity tends to weaken it.
xa: By **3 Sep 2026** surplus of about **₹10.32 lakh crore** had pushed the **call rate below repo**.
RBI drained it via **VRRR**.
Governor (Feb **2026**): RBI to keep "**sufficient liquidity**" for transmission.

82.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Exchange-rate channel — lower rates can weaken the rupee and support exports
Asset-price channel — higher bond and equity prices can create a wealth effect
Expectations channel — a credible target necessarily removes all uncertainty about inflation
Credit channel — greater bank funds and increased lending
82.x: A credible target anchors inflation expectations; it does not necessarily remove all uncertainty. The other three channel descriptions are correct.
82.tq: Find the overstatement in an otherwise accurate list of transmission-channel effects.
xs: **Expectations channel — a credible target removes all uncertainty** is NOT correct — option **(3)**.
A credible target only **anchors inflation expectations**.
The **exchange-rate**, **asset-price** and **credit** channel descriptions are correct.
xa: **Interest rate** channel: cheaper loans raise consumption and **investment**.
Under **FIT**, the MPC sets the repo to hit the inflation target.

82.s: The RBI may sterilise the liquidity effects of capital flows through MSS, OMO and:
82.x: Under an open capital account, flows alter liquidity and the rupee, and the RBI can sterilise them through MSS, OMO and VRRR.
xa: Example: **FCNR(B)** inflows of **$127.23 bn** (Sep **2026**).
**MSS** (April **2004**) proceeds sit in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
By **4 Sep 2026** RBI absorbed about **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two **3-day** VRRRs.

82.s: Which of the following monetary-policy stances is INCORRECTLY described?
o: Neutral – rates can move either way, depending on the data
Accommodative – supports growth with ample liquidity; rate cuts likely
Calibrated tightening – no cuts; hikes measured, not at every meeting
Hawkish – worried about growth, with a bias towards easing
82.x: A hawkish stance worries about inflation and tightens; concern for growth with an easing bias is dovish.
xa: Stance path: neutral → **accommodative** (Apr **2025**) → **neutral** (**June 2025**) → retained through Aug **2026**.
**Hawkish** stance tightens: **raises rates** and **drains liquidity**.

82.s: A rise in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) generally:
o: Raises demand for goods and services
82.x: A higher CRR withdraws lendable funds, reducing money in circulation and demand.
xa: CRR = share of **NDTL** kept as **cash with RBI**, earning **no interest**.
CRR is now **3%** of NDTL after a **100 bps** cut.
To control inflation (dear money): **raise** CRR, SLR, repo; **sell** G-secs.

82.s: The RBI's primary window for managing day-to-day liquidity through repo, reverse repo and SDF operations is the:
82.x: LAF is the framework through which the RBI injects liquidity via repo and absorbs it via reverse repo and SDF on a day-to-day basis.
xa: LAF was introduced in **2000**.
The LAF corridor: **SDF (5.00%)** floor, **MSF (5.50%)** ceiling — **50 bps** wide.
**VRR/VRRR** are auction-based LAF tools.

82.s: Which LAF instrument absorbs surplus liquidity for maturities longer than the overnight SDF?
82.x: VRRR is an auction-based tool that absorbs liquidity for maturities longer than the overnight SDF, while VRR injects liquidity.
xa: They keep **short rates near repo**.
By **4 Sep 2026** RBI absorbed about **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two **3-day** VRRRs.

82.s: Fine-tuning operations of the Reserve Bank of India are primarily conducted to
o: keep system liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance
determine the annual financial statements of banks
fix the statutory floor for the SLR
replace all permanent open market operations
82.x: Fine-tuning operations, generally involving short-term VRR or VRRR auctions, are conducted to align liquidity conditions with the prevailing monetary policy stance.
82.tq: Match a specialised operational tool with its precise policy objective.
xs: Fine-tuning operations aim to **keep liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance** — option **(1)**.
They are **short VRR/VRRR auctions**.
xa: RBI ran **49** fine-tuning operations in **FY2024** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**OMOs** remain the main tool for **durable** liquidity — fine-tuning does not replace them.
Stance was **neutral** through Aug **2026**.

82.s: The temporary incremental CRR (I-CRR) announced by the RBI on 10 August 2023 was:
82.x: The temporary I-CRR was 10%, announced on 10 August 2023; it impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore.
xa: In APPSC-G2 **2025**, both I-CRR statements asked were correct.
Regular **CRR** is now **3%** of NDTL.
**Fine-tuning operations**: **49** in **FY2024**.

82.s: Open Market Operations (OMO) of the RBI involve outright purchase or sale of:
82.x: OMO is the outright purchase or sale of government securities to manage durable liquidity, conducted through banks.
xa: FY26 injections: **₹2.39 lakh crore** OMO purchases (Apr-May **2025**).

82.x: ‘Sterilization’ refers to the process by which the RBI takes away money from the banking system to neutralize the fresh money that enters the system. To ease the threat of currency appreciation or inflation, Central Banks often attempt what is knwon as the ‘sterilization’ of capital flows. In a successful sterilization operation, the domestic component of the monetary base (bank reserves plus currency) is reduced to offset the reserve inflow, at least temporarily. The classical form of sterilization has been through the use of open market operations, that is, selling Treasury bills and other instruments to reduce the domestic component of the monetary base. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

A Committee of Bankers on Branch Expansion Programme of Public Sector Banks appointed by the Reserve Bank of India under the Chairmanship of F.K.F. Nariman (Nariman Committee) endorsed the idea of an ‘Area Approach’ in its report (November, 1969), recommending that in order to enable the Public Sector Banks to discharge their social responsibilities, each bank should concentrate on certain districts where it should act as a ‘Lead Bank’. The Scheme aims at coordinating the activities of banks and other developmental agencies through various fora in order to achieve the objective of enhancing the flow of bank finance to the priority sector and other sectors and to promote banks’ role in the overall development of the rural sector. For coordinating the activities in the district, a particular bank is assigned ‘Lead Bank’ responsibility of the district. 84.s: Which one of the following is different from others?
84.x: According to Companies Act 2013, a company that is limited by shares refers to a company that has the liability of the members (shareholders) limited by such an amount that is unpaid on their respectively held shares. The company can enact this liability while the company is in existence or as it is ending. When incorporating a company limited by shares, the total share capital consists of all of the shares held by each member at incorporation. Those shares can either be : fully paid; partly paid; or unpaid. Partly paid or unpaid shares are shares where a member is due to pay the company. In contrast, fully paid shares are where the full value of the shares have been paid to the company. In companies limited by shares, the liability of members is limited to any unpaid amount of shares that they hold. If a member has fully paid for their shares, they should have no further liabilities as a member.

84.s: The Service Area Approach was implemented under the purview of :
84.x: The Service Area Approach (SAA) was implemented under the purview of Lead Bank Scheme (LBS).The Service Area Approach (SAA) introduced in April, 1989 for planned and orderly development of rural and semi-urban areas was applicable to all scheduled commercial banks including Regional Rural Banks. Under SAA, each bank branch in rural and semi-urban area was designated to serve an area of 15 to 25 villages and the branch was responsible for meeting the needs of bank credit of its service area. The primary objective of SAA was to increase productive lending and forge effective linkages between bank credit, production, productivity and increase in income levels. The SAA scheme was reviewed from time to time and appropriate changes were made in the scheme to make it more effective. The Service Area Approach scheme was last reviewed in December, 2004 and it was decided to dispense with the restrictive provisions of the scheme while retaining the positive features of the SAA such as credit planning and monitoring of the credit purveyance. Accordingly, under SAA the allocation of villages among the rural and semi-urban branches of banks were made not applicable for lending except under Government Sponsored schemes. Thus, while the commercial banks and RRBs are free to lend in any rural and semi-urban area, the borrowers have the choice of approaching any branch for their credit requirements. SCB GNPA was **4.28%** in **March 2015**, before the AQR.

86.s: The Government's 4R strategy in response to the banking-sector stress consisted of:
86.x: The four Rs were Recognise, Resolve, Recapitalise and Reform. The response included the IBC, recapitalisation and NARCL.
86.tq: Recall the exact expansion of a policy framework acronym.
xs: The **4R strategy** = **Recognise, Resolve, Recapitalise, Reform** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Restructure, Refinance, Recover and the like are not among the 4Rs.
xa: Tools used: **IBC**, recapitalisation and **NARCL**.
The **AQR (2015)** forced recognition.
GNPA has fallen for **eight straight years**.

86.s: Following the RBI's Asset Quality Review, NPA levels of banks peaked in:
86.x: The AQR sharply raised disclosed NPAs, which peaked in 2018, and exposed the twin balance sheet problem.
xa: It led on to the **IBC** and recapitalisation.

86.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the new borrower-level NPA tagging system?
o: Banks must identify NPAs through automated systems
It is to be effective from 1 April 2027
If one loan of a borrower becomes an NPA, all its loans at that bank become NPAs
An account can be upgraded even if arrears on one facility remain unpaid
86.x: An account is upgraded only after all arrears on every facility are paid.
xa: The **90-day** overdue test stays.
RBI is moving to a 3-stage **ECL** model.

86.s: Under its new provisioning framework, the RBI is moving from which approach to which approach?
o: From a 3-stage ECL model to a 2-stage incurred-loss model
From incurred-loss model to a 3-stage Expected Credit Loss model
From a 90-day overdue test to a 180-day overdue test
86.x: The RBI is shifting from the incurred-loss model to a forward-looking 3-stage Expected Credit Loss (ECL) model; the 90-day overdue test stays.
86.tq: Provide before the loss happens: incurred → expected.
xs: RBI is moving **from the incurred-loss model to a 3-stage ECL model** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses it; the **90-day** test is unchanged.
xa: Stage 1 = **12-month** loss; Stage 2 = lifetime; Stage 3 = full lifetime provision.
Loss allowances use the **effective interest rate (EIR)** method.
ECL may cut Tier-1 ratios — a capital concern.

86.s:
Assertion (A): Under the Expected Credit Loss model, Stage 2 assets require provisioning for lifetime expected loss.
Reason (R): Under the same model, Stage 1 assets require provisioning for 12-month expected loss.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
86.x: Both are true (Stage 2 lifetime loss, Stage 1 12-month loss), but the Stage 1 treatment does not explain the Stage 2 treatment.
xa: ECL replaces the **incurred-loss** model from **1 April 2027**.
Criticism: ECL **raises capital needs**.

86.s: The GNPA ratio of Scheduled Commercial Banks reached an approximate peak of 11.2 per cent in:
86.x: SCB GNPA peaked at approximately 11.2 per cent in March 2018, after the Asset Quality Review.
86.tq: Use the peak-year clue to distinguish pre-AQR, post-AQR and recovery-period figures.
xs: SCB GNPA peaked at **~11.2%** in **March 2018** — so option **(1)** is correct.
That peak came after the **AQR (2015)** forced recognition.
xa: **Sep 2025**: **2.15%**, a historic low below the 2010-11 level.
GNPA has fallen for **eight straight years**.

86.s: The GNPA of Scheduled Commercial Banks in March 2026, together with the corresponding NNPA, was:
86.x: In March 2026, GNPA was 1.93 per cent and NNPA was 0.39 per cent, described as a decadal low.
86.tq: Pair the two related ratios with the same reporting date.
xs: In **March 2026**, SCB GNPA was **1.93 per cent** and NNPA **0.39 per cent** — so option **(3)** is correct (a decadal low).
xa: March 2025 GNPA: **2.2-2.3%**, lowest since 2011-12.
Large private banks (June 2026): HDFC **1.17%**, ICICI **1.38%**, Axis **1.28%**.

86.s: Credit of Scheduled Commercial Banks rose from about ₹67 lakh crore in 2015 to about ____ in 2025.
86.x: SCB credit nearly tripled from about ₹67 lakh crore (2015) to about ₹181 lakh crore (2025), with CRAR at about 17.3%.
xa: GNPA fell to **1.93%** (March 2026).
GNPA has fallen for **eight straight years**.

86.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank in FY26:
1. Its GNPA was reported at 0.91%.
2. Its NNPA was reported as nil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Both statements are correct: Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank reported GNPA of 0.91% and NNPA as nil in FY26.
86.tq: Verify each numerical statement independently before choosing the combined code.
xs: Both statements are correct — so option **(3) Both 1 and 2** is correct.
**Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank** reported GNPA **0.91%** and NNPA **nil** in **FY26**.
xa: National SCB GNPA in March 2026: **1.93%**.
National NNPA: **0.39%** (March 2026).

86.s: Non-performing assets in commercial banks mean:
o: Bank deposits which are not invested
Loans in which interest or principal amount is not
86.x: A non-performing asset (NPA) refers to classification for loans or advances that are in default or in arrears. A loan is an arrears when its principal or interest payments are missed. As per the RBI guidelines, any advance or loan is classified as non-performing asset when its interest and/or installment of principal remain overdue for a period of more than 90 days.

87.s: Debt Recovery Tribunals were set up under:
o: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
87.x: DRTs were established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993; they are also used under SARFAESI.
xa: **39 DRTs** and **5 DRATs**; debts **above ₹20 lakh**.
**e-DRT** launched **1 Oct 2018**; e-filing mandatory from **1 Feb 2023**.
⚠ **1987** = Lok Adalats; **1993** = DRTs; **2002** = SARFAESI.

87.s: Debt Recovery Tribunals deal with debts due to banks and financial institutions above:
87.x: The DRTs and DRATs handle debts above ₹20 lakh under the stated framework.
87.tq: Use ascending monetary thresholds to distinguish DRT jurisdiction from the CIRP default threshold.
xs: DRTs handle debts **above ₹20 lakh** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**₹1 crore** is the minimum default for triggering **CIRP** under the IBC.
xa: DRTs were set up under the **RDDBFI Act, 1993**.
**Lok Adalats** handle **small NPAs** only.
**e-DRT**: launched **1 Oct 2018**.

87.s: Which mechanism accounted for the largest share of bank recoveries in FY 2024?
87.x: In FY 2024, IBC accounted for 48% of recoveries, SARFAESI 32%, DRTs 17% and Lok Adalats 3%.
xa: **Lok Adalats** handle small NPAs only.
Comparison: **SARFAESI** (secured lenders, no court) vs **IBC** (collective, NCLT-led) vs **DRT** (tribunal recovery).
FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value.

87.s: The Lok Adalats that facilitate settlement of small non-performing assets derive their statutory status from which enactment?
o: The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
87.x: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
87.tq: Identify the statute specifically associated with the forum.
xs: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**1993** is the **RDDBFI Act** (DRTs); **2002** is **SARFAESI**; **2016** is the **IBC**.
xa: They offer **quick, fee-free settlement** of small loans by compromise.
**National Lok Adalat (13 Sep 2026)**: **DRT Visakhapatnam bench** settled **13** cases worth **₹46.11 crore**.
Lok Adalats delivered **3%** of FY24 bank recoveries.

87.s: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) replaced the Company Law Board, the BIFR and the:
87.x: NCLT replaced the Company Law Board, BIFR and AAIFR; it did not replace the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
xa: **BIFR** was dissolved on **1 Dec 2016**; cases went to NCLT/NCLAT.
The IBC replaced **SICA 1985/BIFR** and scattered Companies Act provisions.
NCLT/NCLAT constituted **1 June 2016**.

87.s: Which authority is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?
87.x: The NCLT is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the IBC, 2016. The DRT is the authority for individuals and partnership firms.
87.tq: Ask which body would handle the dispute by distinguishing corporate from individual insolvency.
xs: The **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)** is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency (**companies and LLPs**) — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC GS 2019 key).
The **DRT** handles **individuals and partnership firms**; the **NCLAT** hears appeals.
xa: NCLT also handles **personal guarantors of corporate debtors**.
CIRP is triggered by a default of at least **₹1 crore**.
⚠ NCLT = **companies and LLPs**; DRT = **individuals and partnership firms**.

87.s: Recovery by secured lenders without court intervention is the principal feature of:
87.x: SARFAESI allows secured lenders to recover without courts; IBC is collective, NCLT-led resolution and DRTs are tribunal-based recovery.
xa: FY24 recovery shares: **IBC 48%**, **SARFAESI 32%**, **DRTs 17%**.

87.s: Under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework, capital infusion, a change of management or a merger may be ordered by the:
87.x: Under PCA, the RBI may restrict lending, branch expansion, dividends and pay, and may order capital infusion, a management change or a merger.
xa: Curbs last until capital and asset quality improve.
PCA was introduced in **2002**; full form **Prompt Corrective Action**.

87.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the NCLT bench is located at:
87.x: The NCLT bench sits at Amaravati, while the DRT bench is at Visakhapatnam.
xa: **13 Sep 2026** National Lok Adalat: DRT Visakhapatnam settled **13** cases worth **₹46.11 crore**.

87.s: An Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR) below 1 means the firm:
o: Cannot service its interest from earnings
87.x: ICR = EBIT ÷ interest payable; below 1, earnings do not cover interest.
xa: Lenders use ICR to judge a borrower's **present and emerging risk**.
**PCR** = provisions / gross NPA; higher PCR → more resilient bank.
**Twin Balance Sheet problem**: over-leveraged corporates + capital-starved banks.

87.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
o: Lenders holding 60% of the dues can issue a 60-day notice under Section 13(2)
The threshold was 75% of dues before the 2016 amendment
Under Section 13(4), lenders can take possession of the secured asset, take over management or sell it
Under Section 13(8), the borrower can redeem the asset after the auction notice by paying 25% of the dues
87.x: Under Section 13(8) the borrower can redeem only by paying the full dues, not 25%.
xa: **Sec 17**: appeal to the **DRT** within **45 days**; **Sec 18** bars civil courts.

87.s: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 was based on the recommendations of the:
87.x: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 was based on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee.
xa: Core feature: banks enforce security on NPAs **without court intervention**.
⚠ The **IBC** was based on the **T.K. Viswanathan Committee (2015)**, not Narasimham.
**ARCs** under SARFAESI are registered with and regulated by **RBI**.

87.s: Under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act, an appeal lies to the DRT within:
87.x: Section 17 allows an appeal to the DRT within 45 days; the Section 13(2) demand notice is of 60 days.
xa: ⚠ **60%** of lenders + **60-day** notice; appeal within **45 days**.

87.s: The NCLAT hears appeals against orders of the NCLT, IBBI, CCI and:
87.x: NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT, IBBI, CCI (from 26 May 2017) and NFRA (from 7 May 2018).
xa: Further appeal from NCLAT lies to the **Supreme Court**.
NCLAT sits at **New Delhi** (Principal Bench) and **Chennai**.

87.s: Under the IBC waterfall mechanism, which of the following ranks above government dues?
87.x: Resolution costs, workmen's dues and secured creditors' claims are placed above government dues in the IBC waterfall.
xa: The **2026** amendment cut liquidation to **180 + 90 days**.
FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value; "not a debt-recovery tool".
Criticism: **deep haircuts** and guarantor liability.

87.s:
Consider the following about Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs):
1. They acquire NPAs, generally at a discount.
2. They are regulated by SEBI.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
87.x: ARCs acquire NPAs, generally at a discount, and are regulated by the RBI, not SEBI.
xa: **NARCL**, India's "bad bank", pays **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts**.
SARFAESI is based on the **Narasimham Committee**.

87.s:
Arrange the following earlier debt-resolution mechanisms in chronological order of their introduction:
A. Strategic Debt Restructuring
B. Corporate Debt Restructuring
C. S4A
D. 5/25 scheme
87.x: Corporate Debt Restructuring was introduced in 2001, followed by the 5/25 scheme in 2014, Strategic Debt Restructuring in 2015 and S4A in 2016.
87.tq: Fix the earliest and latest items first, then arrange the intervening years.
xs: CDR is the oldest; S4A, the newest of the four, split debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts.
xa: **Project Sashakt** (Inter-Creditor Agreement) followed in **2018**.
**Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets**: **7 June 2019**.
The **IBC** was enacted in **2016**, the same year as S4A.

87.s: The Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A) was introduced by the RBI in:
87.x: S4A came in 2016 and split a stressed firm's debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts; 2018 is Project Sashakt.
xa: S4A was an **RBI** scheme to rework the financial structure of stressed firms.
**SDR (2015)** preceded it.

87.s: Project Sashakt (2018) for resolving stressed assets was based on the recommendations of the:
87.x: Project Sashakt came from the Sunil Mehta Committee; its plan binds all lenders once 66% approve, with the lead bank driving it.
xa: Its **Inter-Creditor Agreement** aimed at **faster resolution of stressed assets** (UPSC 2019 key).
The **Prudential Framework (2019)** made the ICA mandatory.

87.s: The deterrent effect of the IBC is shown mainly by:
o: Completion of all cases by NCLT within 330 days
Settlement of a large number of cases before admission
Transfer of all recovery cases to Lok Adalats
87.x: The settlement of 30,310 cases worth ₹13.78 lakh crore before admission was cited as evidence of the IBC's deterrent effect.
xa: FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value; "not a debt-recovery tool".
IBC delivered **48%** of bank recoveries in FY24.

87.s:
Consider the following about the RBI's Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets:
1. Signing an Inter-Creditor Agreement is voluntary.
2. Lenders must review the borrower account within 30 days of default.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
87.x: The framework requires a 30-day review after default and makes the Inter-Creditor Agreement mandatory, with resolution envisaged within 180 days.
xa: The **ICA** came from **Project Sashakt (2018)**.
⚠ **180 days** is also the basic **CIRP** period under the IBC.

87.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: ARCs — registered with RBI under SARFAESI
CDR — restructuring outside court for large multi-bank borrowers
Lok Adalats — conversion of lender debt into a 51 per cent equity stake
ARCs — purchase bad loans against security receipts
87.x: Conversion of lender debt into a 51 per cent or more equity stake is associated with Strategic Debt Restructuring, not Lok Adalats. ARCs, CDR and Lok Adalats have the other stated functions.
87.tq: Find the wrong mechanism-feature pairing by checking who performs the action.
xs: **Lok Adalats — 51% equity conversion** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
Converting debt into a **51%+** equity stake is **SDR (2015)**; Lok Adalats settle small loans by compromise.
The rest are right: **ARCs** are registered with RBI and buy bad loans against **security receipts**; **CDR** restructures large multi-bank loans out of court.
xa: Lok Adalats are statutory under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
ARCs buy NPAs **at a discount**.

87.s: A higher Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR) indicates a bank that is:
87.x: PCR = provisions ÷ gross NPA; a higher PCR means more bad loans are provided for, so the bank is more resilient.
xa: SCB PCR: **76.3%** (Mar 2025, FSR basis).
Govt data gives **93.14%** for SCBs — a different basis.

87.s: The March 2026 SCB Gross NPA ratio of 1.93 per cent was characterised as a:
87.x: The March 2026 Gross NPA ratio of 1.93 per cent was described as a decadal low.
87.tq: Match the latest numerical value with its stated trend description.
xs: SCB GNPA of **1.93%** in **Mar 2026** was a **decadal low** — so option **(3)** is correct.
NNPA was **0.39%**.
xa: Up next: **ECL** provisioning and higher risk weights on unsecured consumer credit + NBFC exposures.

87.s: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was based on the recommendations of the:
87.x: The IBC came from the T.K. Viswanathan (Bankruptcy Law Reforms) Committee, 2015; Narasimham is linked to SARFAESI.
xa: ⚠ PYQ: "September assent" and "13-member IBBI" were both wrong (IBBI has **10** members).
IBC completed **10 years** in May 2026.

87.s: Which change in the control structure of insolvency proceedings was introduced by the IBC?
87.x: The IBC shifted the framework from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control.
87.tq: Test a paired conceptual comparison by identifying the direction of institutional change.
xs: The IBC shifted control **from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the change.
xa: It created a single, **time-bound** process — a structural reform.
The **2026** amendment's **CIIRP** is a hybrid of debtor-in-possession + creditor-in-control.
The **Committee of Creditors** (financial creditors) votes on resolution plans.

87.s: A promoter classified as a wilful defaulter, or a promoter associated with an NPA, is generally barred from bidding under which provision of the IBC?
87.x: Section 29A prevents wilful defaulters and promoters of NPAs from submitting resolution bids, subject to the statutory framework.
87.tq: Direct recall of the relevant statutory provision.
xs: **Section 29A** bars **wilful defaulters**/NPA promoters from bidding for their own firms — so option **(2)** is correct.
They are **barred from bidding under IBC** (May 2026), so they cannot regain the firm cheaply.
xa: The **Committee of Creditors** votes on resolution plans.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)**: **personal guarantors** stay liable after plan approval.
The **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018** covers cases of **₹100 crore** and above.

87.s: The minimum default required to trigger the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) is:
87.x: CIRP needs a default of at least Rs 1 crore; it can be triggered by financial or operational creditors.
xa: CIRP timeline: **180 days** + **90 days**; outer limit **330 days** incl. litigation.
**Sec 29A**: wilful defaulters/NPA promoters cannot bid for their own firms.
NCLT is the adjudicating authority for **companies and LLPs**.

87.s: The outer time limit for completing CIRP, including litigation, is:
87.x: CIRP ordinarily runs 180 days with extension, with an outer limit of 330 days including litigation; actual cases have often taken longer.
xa: **67%** of cases exceed the timeline (ES 2025-26).
Causes: protracted litigation, NCLT capacity/staff shortages.

87.s: The Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process for MSMEs was introduced in:
87.x: The PPIRP for MSMEs was introduced in 2021 and has a 120-day limit.
87.tq: Combine the launch year and time limit to distinguish the pre-pack process from ordinary CIRP.
xs: **PPIRP** for **MSMEs** came in **2021** with a **120-day** limit — so option **(4)** is correct.
**180 days** is the CIRP period; **330 days** is the CIRP outer limit.
xa: Only **14 admissions in 4 years** under PPIRP (ES 2025-26).
⚠ Timelines: CIRP **180 + 90** (outer **330**); PPIRP **120**; CIIRP **150**.

87.s: Under the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, the liquidation timeline has been cut to:
87.x: Liquidation is cut to 180 + 90 days; the Act also adds the hybrid Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (Secs 54C–54P).
xa: CIIRP: **150 days**, needs **51%** by value of notified financial creditors.
Criticism: **limits on who can start CIIRP**.

87.s: Under which provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 are the NCLT and NCLAT respectively set up?
87.x: NCLT is established under Section 408 and NCLAT under Section 410 of the Companies Act, 2013.
87.tq: Check the order of the statutory provisions instead of treating the two tribunals as interchangeable.
xs: NCLT is set up under **Sections 408** and NCLAT under **410** of the **Companies Act 2013** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses them; **Sec 61** (IBC) is the NCLAT appeal provision; **Secs 202 and 211** relate to IBBI.
xa: Both were constituted on **1 June 2016**.
NCLT has **16 benches**, incl. **Amaravati** and **Hyderabad**.
NCLAT: Principal Bench **New Delhi** + a bench at **Chennai**.

87.s: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) sits at:
87.x: NCLAT sits in New Delhi and Chennai and hears appeals from NCLT under Section 61 of the IBC.
xa: NCLT has **16 benches**, incl. **Amaravati** and **Hyderabad**.
Further appeal lies to the **Supreme Court**.

87.s: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) regulates:
87.x: IBBI regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies, information utilities and registered valuers.
xa: IBBI (**2016**) is the apex statutory regulator; it has **10** members.
IBBI proposed stronger safeguards for **guarantor insolvency** (**16 Sep 2026**).

87.s:
Which of the following are cited as reasons for the decline in banks' NPAs?
1. The 4R strategy and higher provisioning
2. The IBC and NARCL
3. Lower provisioning requirements
87.x: The decline in NPAs is attributed to the 4R strategy, higher (not lower) provisioning, the IBC and NARCL.
xa: **IBC** delivered **48%** of bank recoveries in FY24.
**NARCL** aggregates stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**.

87.s:
Assertion (A): Under the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, the NCLT must admit or reject a CIRP plea within 14 days.
Reason (R): Under the same Act, the NCLT must rule on resolution plans within 90 days.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
87.x: A is true: admission must be decided within 14 days. R is false: the NCLT must rule on resolution plans within 30 days.
xa: CIIRP sits in **Secs 54C-54P**; a hybrid of debtor-in-possession + creditor-in-control.
Liquidation cut to **180 + 90 days**.

87.s: The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 changed 'may' to 'shall' in Section 7(5)(a) of the Code. This change overturned the ruling in:
o: Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India
Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India
87.x: The change from 'may' to 'shall' in Sec 7(5)(a) makes admission of a financial creditor's CIRP plea mandatory once default is proved, overturning the Vidarbha Industries ruling, which had read 'may' as giving the NCLT discretion. Lalit Kumar Jain (2021) concerns personal guarantors' liability; Swiss Ribbons and Essar Steel are other IBC judgments not affected by this change.
xs: Changing "may" to "**shall**" in **Sec 7(5)(a)** overturned the **Vidarbha Industries** ruling — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)** is about **personal guarantors** staying liable after plan approval.
xa: Other 2026 changes: NCLT admission within **14 days**, plan ruling within **30 days**.
New **CIIRP**: **150 days**, **51%** of notified financial creditors.
Clean-slate protection + cross-border insolvency framework.

87.s: NARCL, described as India’s ‘bad bank’, was announced in which Budget?
87.x: The National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) was announced in Budget 2021–22.
87.tq: Use the announcement-year distinction among closely placed Budgets.
xs: **NARCL**, India's "bad bank", was announced in **Budget 2021-22** — so option **(2)** is correct.
NARCL was one of the cited reasons for the fall in NPAs, alongside the **4R strategy** and **IBC**.
xa: It aggregates large stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**, targeting about **₹2 lakh crore**.
**IDRCL** resolves the assets, incl. by sale to **AIFs**.
Funding: **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts**.

87.s: NARCL pays for stressed assets ____ in cash and the rest in Security Receipts.
87.x: NARCL pays 15% in cash and 85% in Security Receipts; the Government guarantee of Rs 30,600 crore runs for 5 years.
xa: NARCL targets about **₹2 lakh crore** of fully or partly provided assets, in phases.
**₹2,410 crore** recovered by **30 Jun 2025**.

87.s: NARCL primarily targets stressed loans above which threshold and an aggregate asset value of approximately what amount?
87.x: NARCL takes over large stressed loans above ₹500 crore, targeting about ₹2 lakh crore of fully or partly provided assets.
87.tq: Combine the eligibility threshold with the aggregate target.
xs: NARCL targets stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**, about **₹2 lakh crore** in all — so option **(3)** is correct.
These are **fully or partly provided** assets, taken in phases.
xa: By **30 Jun 2025**: **27 accounts**, **₹1,57,215 crore** exposure.
**IDRCL** resolves them; IDRCL is majority private.

87.s: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 applies to offenders in cases involving amounts of:
87.x: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 covers offenders in cases involving ₹100 crore or more.
87.tq: Recall the statutory monetary threshold without confusing it with NARCL’s loan threshold.
xs: The **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018** covers cases of **₹100 crore** and above — so option **(1)** is correct.
The ₹500, ₹50 and ₹10 crore figures are not the Act's threshold.
xa: **FIU-IND**: suspicious transaction reports up **45%**.
**Sec 29A** of the IBC bars wilful defaulters from bidding.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)**: personal guarantors remain liable.

87.s: What is meant by ‘evergreening’ of loans?
o: Writing off an old loan after full recovery
Giving a fresh loan to repay an old loan so that the NPA remains hidden
Increasing the maturity of a standard loan without any new borrowing
Converting every NPA into a government-guaranteed bond
87.x: Evergreening occurs when fresh loans are used to repay old loans, thereby concealing the underlying NPA.
87.tq: Discriminate between concealment through fresh lending and genuine recovery.
xs: **Evergreening** = a **fresh loan to repay an old loan**, so the **NPA stays hidden** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **AQR** exposed this practice.
xa: Other causes of NPAs: **loan frauds and diversion of funds**, weak credit appraisal, slow recovery machinery, corporate over-leverage.
The **twin balance sheet problem** stalls private capex and squeezes **MSME** credit.
**ICR** below **1** → the firm cannot service its interest.

87.s: In the context of banking supervision, PCA stands for:
87.x: PCA stands for Prompt Corrective Action, a framework used by the Reserve Bank of India to intervene in banks with weakening financial health.
87.tq: Test the exact expansion of a frequently confused institutional acronym.

87.x: The Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) for resolution of stressed Assets was signed in July, 2018 by 33 banks / financial institutions. 87.s:
Consider the following statements regarding insolvency and bankruptcy :
1. Bankruptcy refers to a financial state in which an individual or entity is unable to pay off their debts as they become due.
2. Insolvency refers to a legal process, where the assets of the debtor are liquidated or reorganized for the benefit of creditors.
3. Bankruptcy is a state whereas insolvency is the conclusion.
4. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) is the regulatory body responsible for overseeing insolvency and bankruptcy proceedings.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
87.x: Insolvency refers to a financial state in which an individual or entity is unable to pay off their debts as they become due. While bankruptcy refers to a legal process, where the assets of the debtor are liquidated or reorganized for the benefit of creditors.Though both terms deal with excessive debts, insolvency is a state that can lead to declaring bankruptcy. Thus, insolvency is a state whereas bankruptcy is the conclusion. Hence, statements 1, 2 and 3 are incorrect. Statement 4 is correct as the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) is the regulatory body responsible for overseeing insolvency and bankruptcy proceedings. It was established on 1 October, 2016 and given statutory powers through the ‘Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.’ 4. 88.x: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) is a scheme launched by the Prime Minister Narendra Modi on April 8, 2015 for providing loans upto Rs.10 lakh to the non-corporate, non-farm small/micro enterprises. To strengthen support for aspiring entrepreneurs, the finance minister announced an increase in loan limit to Rs. 20 lakh during the Union Budget 2024-25 in July, 2024. This new limit took effect from 24 October, 2024. These loans are classified as MUDRA(Micro Units Development & Refinance Agency Ltd.) loans under PMMY. These loans are given by Commercial Banks, RRBs, Small Finance Banks, MFIs and NBFCs, while MUDRA will refinance these institutions. The borrower can approach any of the lending institutions mentioned above or can apply online through the portal www.udyamimitra.in . Under the aegis of PMMY, MUDRA has earlier created three products namely ‘Shishu’ (for loans upto Rs. 50,000), ‘Kishore’ (for loans of Rs. 50,001 upto Rs. 5 lakh) and ‘Tarun’ (for loans above Rs. 5 lakh and up to Rs. 10 lakh) to signify the stage of growth/development and funding needs of the beneficiary micro unit/entrepreneur and also provide a reference point for the next phase of graduation/growth. As per the announcement of Union Budget 2024-25, a new loan category 'Tarun Plus' (for loans above Rs. 10 lakh and upto Rs. 20 lakh) is also added, which is designed specifically for those who have previously availed and successfully repaid loans under the Tarun category.

89.x: A collateralised borrowing and lending obligation (CBLO) is a money market instrument in India that connects borrowers and lenders for short-term funds. 89.x: The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd. (CCIL) has developed and introduced with effect from January 20, 2003 a money market instrument called Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation (CBLO). CBLO represents an obligation between a borrower and a lender concerning the terms and conditions of a loan. The instrument works like a bond where the lender buys the CBLO and a borrower sells the money market instrument with interest. CBLOs allow short-term loans to be secured by financial institutions, helping to cover their transactions. To access these funds, the institution must provide eligible securities as collateral – such as Treasury Bills.

Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: If the United States of America (USA) were to default on its debt, holders of US Treasury Bonds will not be able to exercise their claims to receive payment.
Statement-II: The USA Government debt is not backed by any hard assets, but only by the faith of the Government. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
89.x: If the USA were to default on its debt, it does not necessarily mean that holders of US Treasury Bonds would have no recourse to exercise their claims. Default means that the government is failing to meet its payment obligations as scheduled, but it does not nullify the legal claims of the bondholders. If the USA Government misses a payment, American debt holders who wanted to litigate would presumably sue in US courts while foreign owners of US debt could sue the USA Government in their own courts and even attempt to enforce judgment against the United States by seizing US assets. Hence, Statement-I is incorrect. The debt issued by the USA Government, including US Treasury Bonds, is indeed not backed by any hard assets like gold, but rather by the full faith and credit of the government, meaning that the government promises to raise money by any legally available means (e.g. tax) to repay them. Hence, Statement-II is correct.

89.s: Capital Market means :
89.x: Capital market is a place where buyers and sellers indulge in trade (buying/selling) of financial securities like bonds, stocks, etc. The trading is undertaken by participants such as individuals and institutions. Capital market trades mostly in long-term securities. The magnitude of a nation’s capital markets is directly interconnected to the size of its economy which means that ripples in one corner can cause major waves somewhere else. Capital market consists of two types i.e. Primary and Secondary. Primary Market : Primary market is the market for new shares or securities. A primary market is one in which a company issues new securities in exchange for cash from an investor (buyer). It deals with trade of new issues of stocks and other securities sold to the investors. Secondary Market : Secondary market deals with the exchange of prevailing or previously-issued securities among investors. Once new securities have been sold in the primary market, an efficient manner must exist for their resale. Secondary markets give investors the means to resell/trade existing securities. Another important division in the capital market is made on the basis of the nature of security sold or bought, i.e. stock market and bond market.

90.s: Terms ‘Bull’ and ‘Bear’ are associated with which branch of commercial activity:
90.x: In investing world, the terms ‘bull’ and ‘bear’ are frequently used to refer to stock market conditions. Bull market and bear market are said to be two opposite phases in a stock market. In a bull market, stock prices continue to rise over a period of time, whereas in a bear market, prices continue to decline over a period of time. The market rise can be attributed to several factors such as a positive economic outlook, strong corporate earnings, etc. and vice versa in the case of a declining market. One of the commonly accepted definitions of bull and bear market phases is that when the stock price rises 20% or more from its recent low or 52-week low, it is said to have entered a bull phase. On the other hand, as and when a stock falls 20% or more from its recent peak or 52-week high, it is said to have entered a bear phase.

91.s: Insider trading is related to :
91.x: Insider trading is related to share market. It is the buying or selling of a publicly traded company’s stock in share market by someone who has non-public, material information about that stock. Insider trading is an unfair and illegal practice in the stock market, wherein other investors are at a great disadvantage due to the lack of important insider non-public information about a company.

91.s: Private Sector Mutual Funds in India were permitted in :
91.x: The mutual fund industry in India started in 1964 with the formation of Unit Trust of India, at the initiative of the Government of India and Reserve Bank of India. Unit Trust of India (UTI) was established on 1 February, 1964 under the UTI Act, 1963 of the Parliament. It was set up by the Reserve Bank of India and functioned under the regulatory and administrative control of the Reserve Bank of India. In 1978, UTI was de-linked from the RBI and the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) took over the regulatory and administrative control in place of RBI. The first scheme launched by UTI was Unit Scheme (US) 1964. 1987 marked the entry of non-UTI, public sector mutual funds set up by public sector banks and Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) and General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC). SBI Mutual Fund was the first non-UTI Mutual Fund established in June,1987. LIC established its mutual fund in June, 1989 while GIC had set up its mutual fund in December, 1990. With the entry of private sector funds in 1993, a new era started in the Indian mutual fund industry, giving the Indian investors a wider choice of fund families. Also, 1993 was the year in which the first Mutual Funds Regulations came into being, under which all mutual funds, except UTI were to be registered and governed. Consider the following statements :

91.x: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) is a disclosure framework introduced in India by SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India), not by the RBI. Therefore, (i) the regulator is SEBI, not the RBI, and (ii) BRSR is not mandatory for all listed companies; it is mandatory mainly for the top 1,000 listed entities (i.e., the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalization). Hence, Statement I is factually incorrect. The information to be disclosed under BRSR is mainly Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) in nature– i.e., it is predominantly nonfinancial. This is what Statement II says, so it is correct. Thus, only Statement II is correct.

93.s: Which one of the following statements is an appropriate description of deflation?
o: It is a sudden fall in the value of a currency against other currencies
It is a persistent recession in both the financial and real sectors of the economy
It is a persistent fall in the general price level of goods and services
It is a fall in the rate of inflation over a period of time
93.x: Deflation is defined in standard economics texts as a sustained decrease in the general price level of goods and services over a period of time. It reflects negative inflation and is associated with reduced consumer spending, falling demand and economic slowdown. A sudden fall in the value of a currency against other currencies refers to depreciation, not deflation. A persistent recession refers to a decline in economic activity, not prices. A fall in the rate of inflation means disinflation, not deflation.

93.s: Economic growth is usually coupled with
93.x: Economic growth usually involves a rise in production and income, which boosts the demand for goods and services. This increased demand tends to push prices upward, causing moderate inflation. Although inflation often accompanies growth, central banks work to manage and control it through monetary policy.

93.s: Inflation is beneficial to which of the following section of economy?
93.x: Inflation occurs when there is a general increase in the price of goods and services and a fall in purchasing value of money. Inflation allows debtors (borrowers) to pay credtitors (lenders) back with money worth less than when it was originally borrowed, which benefits debtors. Thus, inflation brings about a redistribution of real wealth in favour of debtors at the cost of creditors. Investors in bonds and securities with fixed interest rates, consumers, fixed income groups pensioners etc. also lose in real terms during inflation.

93.x: Expansionary policies are correct: Demand-pull inflation is the upward pressure on prices that follows a shortage of supply, where too much money chases too few goods. Expansionary monetary or fiscal policies aim to increase aggregate demand by lowering interest rates or increasing government spending. This can boost consumer and business spending, leading to higher demand for goods and services. As demand outstrips supply, it results in demand-pull inflation. Fiscal stimulus is correct: Fiscal stimulus involves increasing government spending or reducing taxes to boost economic activity. This increases disposable income and encourages spending, which can lead to higher aggregate demand and, consequently, demand-pull inflation. Inflation-indexing wages is incorrect: Inflation-indexing wages means adjusting wages based on the rate of inflation. This can lead to cost-push inflation rather than demand-pull inflation. Workers receive higher wages to compensate for rising prices, which can increase production costs and cause cost-push inflation, but it does not directly impact demand-pull inflation. Higher purchasing power is correct: Higher purchasing power means that consumers have more money to spend, which increases aggregate demand. The base year of CPI-IW has been revised from 2001 to 2016 with effect from September, 2020 to reflect the changing consumption pattern. The job of compilation and maintenance of CPI-IW was taken over by the Central Government in 1941. After that, the Labour Bureau has been compiling and maintaining the CPI-IW since 1944. However, All India CPI-IW was first introduced on uniform and scientific lines with base year 1960 = 100 which was based on the results of Family Living Survey conducted in 1958-59. The series was then updated in 1988 on base year 1982 = 100 and a revision in 2006 has further updated the base year to 2001 = 100. 94.s: A redistribution of income in a country can be best brought about through :
94.x: Redistribution of income and wealth are respectively the transfer of income and wealth (including physical property) from some individuals to others by means of taxation, monetary policies, welfare policies, public services, land reforms etc. This can be achieved with a combination of progressive taxation and progressive expenditure. A progressive tax is one where the average tax burden increases with income. It applies higher tax rates to higher levels of income. High-income families pay a disproportionate high share of the tax burden, while low-and middle-income taxpayers shoulder a relatively small tax burden. Regarding the distributive impact of public expenditure, the principle of maximum social welfare should be the underlying criteria of public spending. Therefore, progressive public expenditure (like free medical aid, free education, subsidized houses etc. to poors) is the best antidote to reduce income inequality existing in the society.

94.x: Direct Taxes : A direct tax is a kind of charge, which is imposed directly on the taxpayer and paid directly to the government by the persons/entities on whom it imposed. Examples : Income Tax, Corporation Tax, Property Tax, Wealth Tax, Gift Tax etc. Indirect Taxes : An indirect tax is a tax collected by an intermediary (such as a retail store) from the person who bears the ultimate economic burden of the tax (such as the customer). An indirect tax is one that can be shifted by the taxpayer to someone else. An indirect tax may increase the price of a good so that consumers are actually paying the tax by paying more for the products. Examples : Customs Duty, Central Excise Duty, Service Tax, Sales Tax, GST, Value Added Tax (VAT) etc.

94.s: MODVAT is related to :
94.x: MODVAT (Modified Value Added Tax) is basically related to the excise duties. In the mid 1980s, the excise duty reforms focused on relieving tax cascading, rationalization of duty rates, and simplification of rules and procedures. As a first step towards mitigating tax cascading, MODVAT was incorporated in the Indian tax system in the year 1986, covering a few limited commodities initially. This permitted the manufacturers to avail of tax credit for the excise duty paid on their purchase of specified raw materials (and not capital goods) used in the manufacturing of specified goods. After being in froce for around 15 years, MODVAT was replaced by CENVAT (Central Value Added Tax) from 1 April, 2000. MODVAT/CENVAT is different from the VAT as under MODVAT/CENVAT, excise is levied on final value and then rebate is given on inputs while under VAT, tax is levied on value addition at each stage of transaction in the production-distribution chain.

94.x: During the question period, Sales tax was a form of indirect tax imposed on the sale and purchase of goods within India. The tax imposed on the sale and purchase of goods within the State was called Sales Tax while the Central Sales Tax was charged by the Central Government for the inter-state transfers. Hence, the sales tax we had to pay while purchasing a toothpaste during the question period, was a tax imposed and collected by the State Government. Sales tax (or VAT) has been replaced by the Goods and Services Tax (GST) since 1 July, 2017. Under the GST regime, when the supply of goods or services happens within a State called intra-state transactions, then both the CGST (Central GST) and SGST (State GST) will be collected. Whereas if the supply of goods or services happens between the States called as inter-state transactions, then only IGST (Integrated GST) will be collected. Under the GST law, the Central Government would levy and collect CGST and IGST, while the State Governments would levy and collect SGST.

The DTC was planned to replace the Income Tax Act, 1961 and other direct tax legislations like the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The first Direct Tax Code Bill was introduced in the Parliament in 2010, but it was lapsed. In 2017, the government set up a task force (headed by Akhilesh Ranjan) to draft a new DTC. The report of the task force on DTC was submitted to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in August, 2019. 95.s: The Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) was introduced in the Budget of the Government of India for the year:
95.x: The Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) is a tax first introduced in India by the Union Budget 1987-88 (Finance Act, 1987) with effect from assessment year 1988-89. Later on, it was withdrawn by the Finance Act, 1990 and then reintroduced by the Union Budget 1996-97 (Finance Act, 1996) with effect from 1 April, 1997. The objective of introduction of MAT is to bring into the tax net 'zero tax companies' which in spite of having earned substantial book profits and having paid handsome dividends, do not pay any tax due to various tax concessions and incentives provided under the Income Tax Law. At present, MAT is computed by 15% (plus surcharge and cess as applicable) on book profit. It is levied at the rate of 9% (plus surcharge and cess as applicable) in case of a company being a unit of an International Financial Services Centre and deriving its income solely in convertible foreign exchange.
