Under Section 56 (ii) of the Income Tax Act, there is no inheritance tax applicable in India irrespective of the cost of the inherited property. However, if the person who inherited the asset decides to sell it, capital gains tax will be applicable.

95.x: Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) refers to tax planning strategies used by multinational enterprises that exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to make profit 'disappear' for tax purpose or to shift profits to locations where there is little or no real activity but taxes are low, resulting in little or no overall corporate tax being paid. xs: Setting off input tax against output tax is **Input Tax Credit (ITC)** — option **(2)**.
**RCM** shifts liability to the recipient; **anti-profiteering** passes benefits to consumers; **destination principle** assigns revenue to the consuming State.
xa: ITC ends **cascading** (tax on tax); blocked-ITC rules apply.
**Zero-rated** supplies get a **full ITC refund**; nil-rated/exempt get none.
**E-invoicing** helps verify ITC and curb fake invoices.

96.s: Which Article of the Constitution deals with inter-State GST?
96.x: Article 269A concerns inter-State GST; 246A gives GST law-making power and 279A provides for the GST Council.
xa: ⚠ Council = **Article 279A**, not 269A (**APPSC G2 2025**).
Under 246A, **Parliament alone** legislates on **inter-State supply**.
Also amended: Arts. **248, 249, 250, 268, 269, 270, 271, 286, 366, 368** + Sixth and Seventh Schedules.

96.s: Under Article 246A, Parliament alone has the power to make laws concerning GST when the supply is:
o: Made by a local authority only
96.x: Article 246A gives Parliament and State Legislatures concurrent GST legislative power, but Parliament alone legislates in relation to inter-State supplies.
96.tq: Apply the constitutional division of legislative power to an inter-State supply.
xs: Under **Art. 246A**, **Parliament alone** makes GST laws on **inter-State** supply — option **(4)**.
For other supplies, **Parliament and State legislatures** both legislate (concurrent GST power).
xa: Only **Parliament** legislates on **IGST**.
**Art. 269A**: IGST levied by the Union, apportioned on Council advice.
**Mohit Minerals (2022)**: Parliament and States have **simultaneous power** to legislate on GST.

96.s: Who constitutes the GST Council?
96.x: The GST Council is formed by the President under Article 279A of the Constitution.
96.tq: Ask which constitutional authority performs the formal constituting function.
xs: The **GST Council** is formed by the **President** (September **2016**) — option **(2)**.
It is a **constitutional body** under **Art. 279A**, not created by ordinary legislation.
xa: It was **never a statutory body** (APPSC G1 2024).
Chair: **Union Finance Minister**; first chair **Arun Jaitley**.
**55th** meeting: **21 Dec 2024**, Jaisalmer; GST 2.0 approved at the **56th** (3-4 Sep **2025**).

96.s: The principal purpose of e-invoicing is to:
o: Replace all GST returns with paper invoices
Digitally report invoices, curb fake invoices and verify input-tax credit
Set the GST Council’s voting weights
Determine the annual borrowing limit of States
96.x: E-invoicing digitally reports invoices, helps curb fake invoices and supports verification of input-tax credit.
96.tq: Connect the digital mechanism with its compliance objectives.
xs: **E-invoicing** means **digital reporting of invoices** to **curb fake invoices** and **verify ITC** — option **(2)**.
It works with **HSN/SAC codes**; it does not bring back paper invoices or touch Council voting or State borrowing.
xa: **E-way bill**: electronic document for moving goods worth **> ₹50,000**; valid **1 day per 200 km**.
**GSTN** does **ITC matching** and uses **AI tools**.
**Anti-profiteering (Sec 171)**: ITC benefits must reach consumers.

96.s: An e-way bill is required for movement of goods valued above:
96.x: An e-way bill is needed for goods above ₹50,000, valid one day per 200 km.
xa: **E-invoicing**: digital reporting of invoices to curb **fake invoices** and verify **ITC**; uses **HSN/SAC** codes.
**GSTN** is the IT backbone for registration, returns and ITC matching.
**GSTIN** is a **15-digit** registration number.

96.s: GST compensation to States assumed an annual revenue growth of ____ over the 2015-16 base.
96.x: Compensation was for five years at 14% annual growth over 2015-16; it ended in June 2022.
xa: Cess scrapped **22 Sep 2025** except tobacco; ended **31 March 2026**.
⚠ Compensation (ended **2022**) vs cess (ended **2026**).

96.s: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act inserted which Article relating to the GST Council?
96.x: Article 279A provides for the GST Council; the same Amendment omitted Article 268A.
xa: It also inserted **246A** (GST law-making) and **269A** (IGST).
Presidential assent: **8 September 2016**.
⚠ Bill number **122nd** vs Act number **101st** is the classic trap.

96.s: The GST constitutional amendment required ratification by at least:
96.x: Since the amendment affected the federal distribution of powers, ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures was required.
96.tq: Distinguish the constitutional ratification threshold from higher thresholds such as two-thirds or unanimity.
xs: Ratification by **at least half the State legislatures** was needed — option **(4)**.
Reason: it amended **federal provisions** of the Constitution.
xa: **Assam** ratified first (**12 Aug 2016**).
Presidential assent: **8 September 2016**.
The Act is the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016**.

96.s: The quorum of the GST Council is:
96.x: The GST Council's quorum is one-half of its total members.
xa: Centre's vote = **1/3** of votes cast; all States together = **2/3**.
Decisions need a **3/4 majority** of weighted votes of members present and voting.

96.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022)?
o: It held GST Council recommendations to be persuasive, not binding
It held that the GST Council is a statutory body
It recognised simultaneous power of Parliament and States to legislate on GST
It described India as a 'flexible federation'
96.x: The GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A and was never statutory.
xa: APPSC G1 2024 tested "statutory then constitutional" — that statement is **false**.
The Council is an institution of **cooperative federalism**.

96.s: Which of the following is outside the current GST levy?
96.x: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is outside GST, as are electricity, stamp-duty real estate transactions and ATF.
xa: Other four petroleum products: **crude, petrol, high-speed diesel, natural gas**.
⚠ Alcohol is excluded by the **Constitution**; petroleum awaits a **Council** date.

96.s: From 1 October 2024, GST anti-profiteering cases are heard by the:
96.x: Anti-profiteering functions moved from NAA to CCI in December 2022 and to the GSTAT Principal Bench from 1 October 2024.
xa: **GSTN** is the IT backbone; it uses **AI tools** for scrutiny.
**GSTIN** is a **15-digit** registration number.

96.s:
Consider the following about voting in the GST Council:
1. The Centre's vote has one-third weight and all States together two-thirds.
2. Decisions need a three-fourths majority of weighted votes of members present and voting.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
96.x: Under Article 279A the Centre has one-third and the States two-thirds of votes cast, and decisions need a three-fourths weighted majority.
xa: **Quorum = one-half** of total members.
With **1/3** weight the Centre can block a decision, but cannot pass one alone.
The **Vice-Chairperson** is chosen by State members.

96.s:
Consider the following about the GST Council:
1. It is chaired by the Union Minister of State for Finance.
2. It is a constitutional body under Article 279A.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
96.x: The GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A chaired by the Union Finance Minister; the MoS is only a member.
n: The GST Council is a constitutional body. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Article 279A provides for the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
The Union Finance Minister is the chairperson of the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
The Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance is a member of the GST Council. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
xa: Voting: Centre **1/3**, all States **2/3**; decisions need a **3/4 majority**.
**Mohit Minerals (2022):** recommendations are **persuasive, not binding**.
⚠ Council = **Article 279A**; **269A** = IGST.

96.s:
Consider the following about GST:
1. Its taxable event is manufacture.
2. It is a multi-stage, destination-based consumption tax.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
96.x: GST is a multi-stage, destination-based tax on value addition whose taxable event is supply, not manufacture.
xa: Objective: a **single destination-based tax** = "**one nation, one tax**" (APPSC 2024).
It ends **cascading** (tax on tax).
Significance: **biggest indirect tax reform since Independence**.

96.s: IGST revenue is finally settled to the:
96.x: GST is destination-based, so IGST revenue goes to the consuming State.
xa: **Destination principle**: revenue accrues to the **State of consumption**.
IGST covers inter-State supplies and **imports**; apportioned under **Art. 269A**.

96.s: Which is the largest source of Andhra Pradesh's own tax revenue (2024-25 RE)?
96.x: SGST is AP's largest own tax source at about Rs 36,296 crore (38%); State excise (22%) is second.
xa: AP HC: Centre and State tax authorities must decide **inter se** who investigates (May **2026**).
Stamp duty and **motor vehicle tax** stay **outside GST** with the States.
**SGST** is levied by the **State** on intra-State supply, in **equal halves** with CGST.

96.s: Under GST, the Centre administers and collects:
96.x: The Centre collects CGST and IGST, States collect SGST, and the GST Council recommends.
n: The GST Council makes recommendations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
The Centre administers and collects CGST and IGST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
States administer SGST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
xa: **IGST** applies to **inter-State** supply and **imports**; only **Parliament** legislates on it.
**UTGST** applies in UTs without legislature.
Act ceilings: **CGST 20%**; **IGST 40%**.

96.s: Which of the following taxes have been subsumed under GST?
96.x: Real National Income = (Nominal Income / Price Index) × 100 = (20,000 / 250) × 100 = Rs 8,000 crore.

96.s: Which State levy was NOT subsumed in GST?
96.x: Stamp duty is retained outside GST; purchase, luxury and entry taxes were subsumed.
xa: Other State taxes subsumed: **State VAT/Sales Tax**, **Central Sales Tax**, **Octroi**, taxes on **advertisements, lotteries, betting, gambling**.
Also outside GST: **electricity duty**, **motor vehicle tax**, **property tax**, **State excise on liquor**.

96.s: The number of Central and State taxes subsumed into GST, as conventionally stated, is respectively:
96.x: The conventional classification identifies eight Central taxes and nine State taxes as subsumed into GST.
96.tq: Recall the paired numerical classification rather than counting only one category.
xs: **8 Central** and **9 State** taxes were subsumed — option **(1)**.
Central: **Central Excise**, **Service Tax**, **CVD**, **SAD**, central cesses and surcharges, among others.
xa: State: **VAT/Sales Tax**, **CST**, **Purchase, Luxury, Entry Tax**, **Octroi**, **Entertainment Tax**, etc.
**Basic Customs Duty** was **not** subsumed.
The "**declared goods of special importance**" concept was dropped.

96.s: Which one of the following is constitutionally excluded from GST rather than merely awaiting a notified date for levy?
96.x: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is constitutionally excluded from GST. The listed petroleum products are constitutionally within GST but have not been brought under it for levy.
96.tq: Compare the constitutional treatment of liquor with petroleum products.
xs: **Alcoholic liquor for human consumption** is **excluded by the Constitution** itself — option **(3)**.
**ATF, natural gas, crude** are petroleum products **constitutionally within GST**, awaiting a date the **GST Council recommends**.
xa: ⚠ Petroleum = in the Constitution, waiting for Council date; alcohol = excluded and stays with **States**.
Five petroleum products: **crude, petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas**.
APPSC-G2 2025: no GST on petrol/diesel, liquor, electricity, charitable services → "**All of the above**".

96.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the five petroleum products kept outside the current levy of GST?
96.x: The five petroleum products are crude oil, petrol or motor spirit, high-speed diesel, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel. Lubricating oil is not included in that specified list.
96.tq: Recall the complete five-item list and identify the outsider.
xs: **Lubricating oil** is not among the five petroleum products — option **(1)**.
The five: **crude, petrol (motor spirit), high-speed diesel, natural gas, ATF**.
xa: These are constitutionally within GST; levy starts only from a date the **GST Council recommends**.
**Alcoholic liquor for human consumption** is excluded by the Constitution itself.
**Electricity** supply and real estate (**stamp duty**) are also outside GST.

96.s: Goods and Services Tax is regarded as the biggest indirect tax reform in India since Independence primarily because it:
o: replaced the need for all direct taxes
abolished the divisible pool of taxes
created a unified framework for a large number of indirect taxes
transferred all taxation powers to the States
96.x: GST is considered the biggest indirect tax reform since Independence because it established a unified framework for indirect taxation by subsuming several indirect taxes.
96.tq: Identify the precise significance rather than choosing extreme claims about direct taxes or complete transfer of powers.
xs: GST is the **biggest indirect tax reform since Independence** as it **created a unified framework** for many indirect taxes — option **(3)**.
It subsumed **8 Central + 9 State taxes** into a **single destination-based tax** ("one nation, one tax").
It did not replace direct taxes or move all powers to States; States in fact **gave up** indirect-tax powers.
xa: Objective: end **cascading** (tax on tax); **one nation-one market**.
GST applies at **both central and state levels** (APPSC 2023).
Record gross GST: **₹2.43 lakh crore in April 2026**.

96.s: GST aims to end 'tax on tax', known as the:
96.x: Reducing cascading (tax on tax) and creating a unified national market are major GST objectives.
n: A major objective of GST is to create a common or unified national market. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
A major objective of GST is to reduce cascading of taxes. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
xa: GST aims at "**one nation, one tax**" — a **single destination-based tax on value addition** (APPSC 2024).
GST applies at both **central and state levels** (APPSC 2023).
**GST 2.0** slabs: **5%** (merit), **18%** (standard), **40%** (demerit), from **22 Sep 2025**.

96.s: Which of the following statements regarding taxes subsumed under GST is incorrect?
o: Central Excise Duty was subsumed under GST.
State VAT was subsumed under GST.
Various other Central and State direct taxes were subsumed under GST.
Service Tax was subsumed under GST.
96.x: Option C is incorrect: GST replaced indirect taxes such as excise, service tax and State VAT, not direct taxes.
96.tq: Watch for 'direct' replacing 'indirect'.
n: Central Excise Duty was subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Service Tax was subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
State VAT was subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
Various other Central and State indirect taxes were subsumed under GST. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**Various other Central and State direct taxes were subsumed under GST**" — option **(3)**.
GST subsumed **Central Excise Duty**, **Service Tax**, **State VAT** and various other **indirect taxes**, not direct taxes.
Statements on **Central Excise**, **State VAT** and **Service Tax** are correct.
xa: Subsumed: **8 Central + 9 State taxes** (UPSC).
**Not subsumed:** **Basic Customs Duty**, stamp duty, electricity duty, alcoholic liquor, petroleum products.
⚠ **Trap:** Some notes list stamp duty as "merged" — it was not.

96.s: The Revenue Neutral Rate Committee recommended an RNR of approximately:
96.x: The Revenue Neutral Rate Committee, chaired by Arvind Subramanian, recommended an RNR of about 15–15.5% and a standard rate of 17–18%.
96.tq: Keep the RNR range distinct from the proposed standard-rate range.
xs: The RNR Committee recommended an RNR of **~15-15.5%** and a standard rate of **17-18%** — option **(4)**.
It was chaired by **Arvind Subramanian** (**2015**; some notes say **2018**).
xa: **RNR** = the rate keeping revenue equal to the **pre-GST level**.
Statutory ceilings: **CGST 20%**, **IGST 40%**.

96.s: Under the GST Acts, the ceiling for CGST is:
96.x: The CGST Act provides a ceiling of 20%. The corresponding IGST ceiling is 40%.
96.tq: Keep the CGST ceiling separate from the IGST ceiling.
xs: The CGST ceiling in the Acts is **20%** — option **(3)**.
**40%** is the **IGST** ceiling; **5%** and **18%** are GST 2.0 slabs.
xa: Rates change by **government notification on GST Council recommendation**, not by amending the Acts.
GST 2.0's top rate of **40%** (sin goods) equals the IGST ceiling.

96.s: GST rates are normally changed by:
o: An order of the Reserve Bank of India
Amending the GST Acts through Parliament in every case
Government notification issued on the recommendation of the GST Council, subject to statutory ceilings
A resolution of the Finance Commission
96.x: Rates are normally changed through government notification on the recommendation of the GST Council, rather than by amending the Acts each time.
96.tq: Ask which authority performs the operational rate change and who recommends it.
xs: GST rates are changed by **government notification on GST Council recommendation**, within statutory ceilings — option **(3)**.
The Acts need **not be amended** for each change; RBI and the Finance Commission have no role.
xa: Ceilings in the Acts: **CGST 20%**, **IGST 40%**.
GST 2.0 approved at the **56th Council (3-4 Sep 2025)**, effective **22 Sep 2025**.

96.s:
Consider the following about GST:
1. Exports and supplies to SEZs are zero-rated, with full ITC refund.
2. Nil-rated supplies allow input tax credit.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
96.x: Zero-rated supplies (exports, SEZ supplies) get full ITC refund; nil-rated supplies do not permit ITC.
xa: **Exempt** supplies are notified out of tax; **no ITC**.
ITC is not available on **exempt or non-taxable** supplies.
**Inverted duty structure**: refunds allowed.

96.s: At the 56th meeting of the GST Council, the tax slabs were identified as which of the following?
o: 5% merit, 18% standard and 40% de-merit or sin
96.x: The 56th meeting provided for slabs of 5% for merit goods, 18% as the standard rate and 40% for de-merit or sin goods.
96.tq: Match each rate with its classification instead of remembering the numbers alone.
xs: The **56th Council** set slabs of **5% (merit)**, **18% (standard)** and **40%** for sin/de-merit goods — option **(3)**.
It merged the old **5, 12, 18, 28%** slabs, so options with **12%** or **28%** are the old structure.
xa: Meeting dates: **3-4 Sep 2025**; effective **22 Sep 2025**.
Rates cut on ~**375 items**.
The **55th** meeting was held on **21 Dec 2024** at **Jaisalmer**.

96.s: Under the Reverse Charge Mechanism in GST, the liability to pay tax is shifted from the:
96.x: Under reverse charge, the recipient, rather than the supplier, pays GST on specified supplies.
96.tq: Distinguish the direction of liability by asking who actually remits the tax.
xs: Under **Reverse Charge (RCM)**, liability shifts from the **supplier to the recipient** — option **(3)**.
The **recipient**, not the supplier, pays GST on **specified supplies**.
xa: **ITC** sets off input tax against output tax.
**Composition scheme**: turnover up to **₹1.5 crore** (₹50 lakh services); flat **1%** goods, **6%** services; **no ITC**.
**E-way bill** needed for moving goods worth **> ₹50,000**.

96.s: Under the GST composition scheme, the turnover limit for goods is:
96.x: The limit is ₹1.5 crore for goods and ₹50 lakh for services, at 1% and 6%, with no ITC.
xa: ITC is not available on **exempt or non-taxable** supplies; **nil-rated/exempt** also give no ITC.
Under **RCM**, the **recipient**, not the supplier, pays GST on specified supplies.
**Budget 2026-27**: **automated registration** within **3 working days** for low-risk applicants.

96.s:
Assertion (A): Under GST, revenue ultimately accrues to the jurisdiction where goods or services are consumed.
Reason (R): GST is a destination-based tax rather than a tax based on the place where goods or services are produced.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
96.x: Both are true: GST revenue goes to the State where goods or services are consumed because GST is a destination-based tax. R explains A.
96.tq: Ask whether the principle explains the outcome.
n: GST is a multi-stage, destination-based tax. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
GST revenue ultimately accrues to the jurisdiction where goods or services are consumed. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
GST revenue does not accrue based on where goods or services are produced. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 19-22]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
GST is a **destination-based** tax, ⚠ **not** based on where goods are **produced**.
So **revenue ultimately accrues** to the **jurisdiction** where goods or services are **consumed** — R explains A.
xa: **IGST** on inter-State supply settles to the **destination (consuming) State**, under **Art. 269A**.
Manufacturing States feared loss — a reason for the **5-year compensation** guarantee.
GST nature: **multi-stage, destination-based consumption tax**.

96.s: Under the GST 2.0 changes referred to in the current tax structure, which of the following is exempted?
o: All motor vehicle insurance premiums without exception
Individual life and health insurance premiums
96.x: GST 2.0 provides exemption for individual life and health insurance premiums. The exemption is not stated as a blanket exemption for every insurance service.
96.tq: Avoid extending a specific exemption into an unsupported blanket exemption.
xs: GST 2.0 exempts **individual life and health insurance premiums** — option **(4)**.
The notes speak only of **individual** policies — no blanket exemption for all commercial or motor insurance or banking.
xa: **Rare-disease medicines** are fully exempt (Jun **2026**).
GST 2.0 slabs: **5%** merit, **18%** standard, **40%** sin/ultra-luxury.
Rates were cut on ~**375 items**.

96.s: After the general withdrawal of GST compensation cess from 22 September 2025, it continued only on:
96.x: The cess was scrapped for all goods except tobacco; its levy was extended to March 2026 to repay compensation loans.
xa: Compensation cess **ended 31 March 2026**.
From **1 Feb 2026**: higher **excise on tobacco** and **Health Security se National Security Cess** on pan masala.
Compensation itself ended in **June 2022**.

96.s: The Health Security se National Security Cess is levied on pan masala units on the basis of:
96.x: It is levied on machine production capacity, and its proceeds go to the Consolidated Fund of India without being shared with States.
xa: Tobacco faces higher excise under the **Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025**.
Criticism: **cesses** stay **outside the divisible pool**.

96.s: Which of the following replaced the compensation-cess arrangement for tobacco and pan masala from 1 February 2026?
o: A special State GST on tobacco products
A customs duty collected by the GST Council
Higher excise on tobacco and Health Security se National Security Cess on pan masala units
A surcharge under the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act
96.x: Higher excise was imposed on tobacco under the Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025, while Health Security se National Security Cess was imposed on pan masala units.
96.tq: Match the replacement measures with the correct commodities.
xs: From **1 Feb 2026**: **higher excise on tobacco** and the **Health Security se National Security Cess** on **pan masala units** — option **(3)**.
The tobacco excise comes under the **Central Excise (Amendment) Act, 2025** — a Central excise, not a State GST, customs duty or IGST surcharge.
xa: The new cess is levied on machine **production capacity**.
It is credited to the **CFI** and **not shared** with States.
Compensation cess **ended 31 March 2026**.

96.s: The ‘Goods and Services Tax’ was proposed by a task force, whose President was :
96.x: In 2004 (18th February), the Central Government formed a task force headed by Vijay L. Kelkar on Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM), which in 2004 recommended ‘Goods and Services Tax’ (GST) to replace the existing tax regime by introducing a comprehensive tax on all goods and services replacing Central level VAT and State level VATs. It recommended replacing all indirect taxes except the customs duty with value added tax on all goods and services with complete set off in all stages of the value chain.

96.s:
Which among the following is true for Central Sales Tax?
(i) It is levied on interstate trade
(ii) It is levied in the Union Territories
(iii) It is levied in the SEZ
Select the correct answer from the codes given below :
96.x: Central Sales Tax was levied on inter-state trade and trade in the Union Territories, while SEZs were exempted from it. It is subsumed by the Goods and Services Tax (GST). GST is the single comprehensive indirect tax, operational from July 1, 2017, on supply of goods and services. It has replaced various types of taxes/cesses, levied by the Central and State/ UT Governments.

96.s:
Which of the following statement (s) is / are incorrect regarding the GST Council (GSTC)?
I. The GST Council is a constitutional body established under Article 269A.
II. It makes recommendations on GST issues.
III. Every state does not have an equal vote in the GST Council.
IV. Decisions require a three-fourths majority of weighted votes of members present and voting.

Consider the following statements :
1. GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and the Minister of State-in-charge of Revenue or Finance at the centre is a member.
2. The GST Council will decide the tax rate, exempted goods and the threshold under the new taxation regime.
3. State Governments will have the option to levy VAT, if they so decide. Of these –
96.x: Goods & Services Tax Council is a constitutional body (under Article 279A) for making recommendations to the Union and State Government on issues related to Goods and Service Tax. The GST Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and other members are the Union Minister of State-in-charge of Revenue or Finance and Minister-in-charge of Finance or Taxation of all the States. The GST Council will decide about the tax rate, exempted goods and will also determine the threshold under the new tax regime. The GST Council shall recommend the date on which the goods and services tax be levied on petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel. After the imposition of GST, State Governments do not have the option to levy VAT.

96.s: Who is the Chairperson of GST Council?

Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select your answer from the codes given below.
Assertion (A): Goods and Services Tax (GST) introduced in 2017 is non-inflationary.
Reason (R): GST system avoids tax-on-tax.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation for (A),
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation for (A)
96.x: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) eliminated the cascading effect of multiple taxes by replacing indirect taxes with a unified tax system. By avoiding tax-on-tax, GST reduces production costs and helps stabilize prices in the long run.

96.s: Which of the following taxes replaced a number of indirect taxes?
96.x: The Goods and Services Tax (GST), implemented in India from 1 July 2017, subsumed a large number of indirect taxes previously levied by the Centre and States including excise duty, service tax, VAT, entry tax and several cesses — into a single unified tax regime.

96.s: What has been kept under the purview of Goods and Services Tax (GST)?
96.x: At present, Alcohol for human consumption, Electricity and Petroleum products are kept outside the purview of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India, while Ghee has been kept under the purview of GST.

96.s: What kind of tax is GST?
o: Depends on the type of goods and services
96.x: GST is known as the Goods and Services Tax. It is a single, comprehensive, indirect tax which has subsumed almost all the indirect taxes (like Service Tax, Central Excise, State Value Added Taxes - VATs etc.) except a few taxes. 96.x: One of the most important aspects of Goods and Services Tax (GST) is the Input Tax Credit (ITC) Mechanism, which ensures a seamless flow of credit, reduces the tax burden on businesses, and avoids the cascading of taxes and double taxation. Cascading of taxes, in simple language, is 'tax on tax'. Under the earlier system of taxation, credit of taxes being levied by Central Government was not available as set-off for payment of taxes levied by State Governments, and vice versa. One of the most important features of the GST system is that the entire supply chain would be subject to GST to be levied by Central and State Government concurrently. As the tax charged by the Central or the State Governments would be part of the same tax regime, credit of tax paid at every stage would be available as set-off for payment of tax at every subsequent stage. Input Tax Credit (ITC) refers to the credit that businesses receive for the GST paid on the purchase of goods or services intended for business use. ITC plays a crucial role in the GST framework by reducing the overall tax burden for businesses and ensuring that tax is levied only on the value addition. 96.x: Uninterrupted and seamless chain of input tax credit (ITC) is one of the key features of Goods and Services Tax. ITC is a mechanism to avoid cascading of taxes. Any registered person can avail credit of tax paid on the inward supply of goods or services or both, which is used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business subject to certain conditions. Thus, ITC means the credit of input tax on the supplies of goods and services or both received by a registered person. Eligibility of ITC includes taxable supply and zerorated supply, but non-taxable, exempt and nil-rated supplies are not eligible for ITC. Zero-rated supply is different from nil-rated supply (goods and services on which 0% GST is applicable). Any supplies made by a registered dealer as an export (both goods or services) or supply to an SEZ qualifies for zero-rated supplies in GST and ITC is available for them. Elected bodies, audited accounts and compliance with State Finance Commission requirements
101.x: The grants are tied to the existence of elected bodies, audited accounts and SFC compliance, so delayed elections jeopardise eligibility and release.
xa: AP **ULB** terms expired **15 March 2026**; **panchayats** **4 April 2026**.
16th FC conditions: **properly constituted (elected)** bodies, **accounts online**, **timely SFCs**.

101.s: Drone maps under which scheme can give panchayats a property-tax baseline?
101.x: SVAMITVA drone maps provide a property-tax baseline; AMRUT 2.0 incentivises property-tax reform and municipal bonds.

102.s: Which among the following is the most important item of revenue expenditure of the Union Government?
102.x: Revenue expenditure is that part of government expenditure that does not result in the creation of assets. Payment of salaries and allowances, pensions, subsidies, interest and administrative expenses fall in this category as revenue expenditure examples. Interest payment is the most important and largest item of revenue expenditure and total expenditure of the Union Government. In Union Budget 2026-27, revenue expenditure is expected to increase by 6.63%, over the revised estimates of 2025-26 to Rs. 4125494 crore. Expenditure on interest payments in 2026-27 is expected to be Rs. 1403972 crore, which is 34.03% of the government’s revenue expenditure, 39.74% of the government's revenue receipts and 26.26% of the government’s total expenditure (excluding of the States' share of taxes and duties). Budget estimate of interest payments in 2026-27 is 10.17% higher than the revised estimate of 2025-26.

102.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the revenue-capital classification?
o: Maintenance of existing assets — Capital expenditure
Loans and advances to States — Capital expenditure
102.x: Loans and advances to States are capital expenditure because they affect the Government's financial assets. Maintenance of existing assets and interest payments are revenue expenditure, while repayment of loans reduces liabilities and is capital expenditure.
102.tq: Use the effect on assets or liabilities to identify the correct classification.
xs: **Loans and advances to States — Capital expenditure** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Repayment of loans** is **capital** (it reduces a liability), not revenue.
**Maintenance of existing assets** and **interest payments** are **revenue** expenditure.
xa: **Test:** an expense that changes Govt's **assets or liabilities** = capital; all else = revenue.
⚠ **Grants to States** = **revenue** even if they create assets; **loans to States** = **capital**.
Loans and advances to **PSUs** and **foreign governments** are also capital.

102.s: Government expenditure that creates an asset or reduces a liability is classified as:
102.x: Capital expenditure either creates assets or reduces liabilities; revenue expenditure generally does neither.
xa: Thumb rule: **Revenue = running the government; Capital = creating assets**.
Revenue spending is **recurring**; capital spending is mostly **non-recurring**.
Purchase of **defence equipment** is **capital outlay**.

102.s: Subsidies are ordinarily classified as:
102.x: Subsidies are revenue expenditure; grants to States are also revenue expenditure, while defence equipment purchase can be capital outlay.
xa: Exam angle: food and fertiliser subsidies are revenue expenditure (**APPSC-G2 2008**).
**Loans and advances to States** = capital.
**Interest payments**, salaries and pensions = revenue.

102.s: Which of the following correctly defines effective capital expenditure?
o: Capital expenditure plus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Revenue expenditure plus loans to State Governments
Capital expenditure minus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Capital outlay plus interest payments on public debt
102.x: Effective capital expenditure is calculated as capital expenditure plus grants-in-aid for the creation of capital assets.
102.tq: Test the exact formula by distinguishing additions from deductions.
xs: **Effective capex** = **capital expenditure + grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option **(3)** subtracts the grants instead of adding them.
Revenue expenditure and interest payments are not part of it.
xa: BE 2026-27 effective capex: **₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP)**.
Of this, grants: **₹4.93 lakh crore**.
Effective capex / fiscal deficit = **101.1%**.

102.s: The Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) provides States with:
102.x: SASCI provides 50-year interest-free loans to States for capital expenditure.
102.tq: Use the application-purpose and loan-terms pair to distinguish the scheme from ordinary grants.
xs: **SASCI** gives States **50-year interest-free loans** for **capex** — option **(1)** is correct.
They are **loans**, not grants, and for **capital** not revenue spending.
Allocation **₹1.85 lakh crore** in **2026-27**.
xa: Effective capex includes **grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets**.
**Golden Rule**: borrowing only for assets.

102.s: The Union capital expenditure of ₹12,21,821 crore in Budget 2026-27 is made up of:
o: Capital outlay plus loans and advances
Capital outlay plus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Revenue expenditure plus loans and advances
102.x: Capex 2026-27 (₹12,21,821 crore, +11.5%) = capital outlay ₹9,43,042 crore + loans ₹2,78,780 crore. Adding grants-in-aid for capital assets gives effective capex, not capex. Revenue expenditure and interest payments are not part of capital expenditure.
102.tq: Capex = outlay + loans; effective capex adds capital grants.
xs: Capex **₹12,21,821 crore** = **capital outlay + loans and advances** — option **(1)** is correct.
Capital outlay **₹9,43,042 crore** + loans **₹2,78,780 crore**.
Adding grants for capital assets gives **effective capex**, not capex (option 2).
xa: Effective capex **₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP)**.
⚠ Loans and advances to States are **capital**; grants to States are **revenue**.

102.s: The 'Golden Rule' of public finance says government borrowing should ordinarily be used for:
o: Creation of assets through capital expenditure
102.x: The Golden Rule allows borrowing only for asset creation, so the quality and composition of spending matter more than its size.
xa: Effective capex / fiscal deficit = **101.1%** in BE 2026-27.
Revenue expenditure share fell **88% → about 77%**.
**9 of 18** large States budget revenue deficits for 2026-27.

102.s:
Assertion (A): Capital expenditure strengthens long-term productive capacity.
Reason (R): It is directed toward acquiring, creating, upgrading or extending the life of assets.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
102.x: Both are true: capital spending builds long-term capacity because it buys, creates, upgrades or extends the life of assets. R explains A.
102.tq: Ask whether the nature explains the effect.
n: Capital expenditure is directed toward acquiring assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Capital expenditure is directed toward creating assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Capital expenditure is directed toward upgrading assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Capital expenditure is directed toward extending the life of assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Capital expenditure strengthens long-term productive capacity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Infrastructure or asset creation is an example of capital expenditure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Capital expenditure** is directed toward **acquiring, creating, upgrading** and **extending the life of assets**.
Because it builds assets, it **strengthens long-term productive capacity** — R explains A.
xa: Examples: **land and buildings**, **equipment**, **computers**, **software**, **infrastructure**.
**Revenue expenditure** does **not create assets** — salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest.
⚠ Grants to States = **revenue** even if they create assets; **loans to States** = **capital**.

102.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Capital expenditure – directed toward creation or acquisition of assets
Non-plan expenditure – included subsidies, interest payments and defence
Revenue expenditure – involves no creation of assets
Revenue deficit – revenue receipts minus revenue expenditure
102.x: Revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, not the reverse.
n: Capital expenditure strengthens long-term productive capacity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Revenue expenditure does not create assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Capital expenditure involves asset creation or acquisition. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Non-plan expenditure includes subsidies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Non-plan expenditure includes interest payments. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Non-plan expenditure includes defence services. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Infrastructure or asset creation is an example of capital expenditure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
xa: Thumb rule: **Revenue = running the government; Capital = creating assets**.
**Repayment of loans** is capital expenditure — it **reduces liability**.
Food and fertiliser **subsidies** are **revenue expenditure** (APPSC-G2 2008).

102.s: The Oil Pool Account under the Administered Price Mechanism was dismantled in:
102.x: It was dismantled in April 2002; later OMC under-recoveries were compensated through oil bonds.
xa: NBS (**1 April 2010**) covers **22 grades** of P&K fertilisers.
Major subsidies up **37.4%** in Q1 2026-27 on crude prices (**West Asia** crisis).
LPG subsidy 2026-27: **₹12,085 crore**.

102.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission's approach to subsidies favoured:
o: Well-targeted subsidies with exclusion criteria and sunset clauses
102.x: It supported well-targeted subsidies with exclusion criteria and sunset clauses, not unrestricted off-budget financing.
xa: Major subsidies: **₹4.11 lakh crore = 1.0% of GDP**.
Likely overshoot ≈ **₹50,000 crore** on crude prices.

102.s: Wagner’s law states that, as an economy industrialises:
o: Public expenditure rises faster than national income
Public expenditure falls faster than national income
Public expenditure rises only during wars and crises
Public expenditure remains constant irrespective of national income
102.x: Wagner’s law, also called the law of increasing state activity, holds that public expenditure rises faster than national income as an economy industrialises.
102.tq: Match the law with its distinctive continuous income-related trend.
xs: **Wagner's law**: public expenditure rises **faster than national income** as the economy industrialises — option **(1)** is correct.
It is also called the **law of increasing state activity**.
Rises only during **wars and crises** describes **Peacock-Wiseman**, not Wagner.
xa: Peacock-Wiseman (**1961**, UK data): spending rises in **steps** — the **displacement effect**.
After a crisis spending **does not fall back**.
Exam angle: "continuous rise with income" = **Wagner**.

102.s: The displacement effect in public expenditure theory is associated with:
o: The fiscal multiplier of capital expenditure
102.x: The displacement effect is associated with the Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis. Wars and crises raise the tolerable tax burden and displace public spending to a higher level.
102.tq: Discriminate between the two theories using their signature concepts.
xs: The **displacement effect** belongs to the **Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis** — option **(3)** is correct.
Wars/crises raise the **tolerable tax burden**; spending rises in **steps** and **does not fall back**.
**Wagner's law** is about a **continuous** rise with income.
xa: Peacock-Wiseman used **UK data** (**1961**).
Wagner's law = **law of increasing state activity**.
The **Golden Rule** concerns borrowing only for **assets**.

102.s: Stepwise increases in public expenditure caused by wars and crises (the displacement effect) are explained by:
102.x: Peacock-Wiseman explains discontinuous rises through crises; Wagner's law links continuous growth of spending to industrialisation.
xa: Wagner: spending rises **faster than national income**.
Peacock-Wiseman: crises raise the **tolerable tax burden** — **displacement effect**.
Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis: **1961**, UK data.

102.s:
Arrange the following components of Union Budget 2026-27 expenditure in descending order of their stated shares:
A. Defence
B. Central Sector Schemes
C. Interest
D. States' share of taxes
102.x: The shares were States' share of taxes 22 per cent, interest 20 per cent, Central Sector Schemes 17 per cent and defence 11 per cent.
102.tq: Rank the options by the numerical shares, starting with the largest component.
xs: Order: **States' share of taxes 22% > interest 20% > central sector schemes 17% > defence 11%** (**D, C, B, A**) — option **(1)**.
This is the "rupee goes to" breakup for **2026-27**.
States' share of taxes is the single largest item, ahead of **interest**.
xa: After defence: **CSS 8%**, FC and other transfers **7%** = other **7%**.
Major subsidies **6%**; pensions **2%**.

102.x: Interest payments of ₹14,03,972 crore represented 26 per cent of total expenditure and 40 per cent of revenue receipts.

xs: Interest payments were **26%** of total expenditure and **40%** of revenue receipts — option **(3)** is correct.
Option **(1)** reverses the two figures.
Interest = **₹14,03,972 crore** in BE 2026-27.
xa: Interest/revenue receipts: **37%** in **2013-14**; **42%** in **2020-21**.

**Committed expenditure** = **65.3%** of revenue receipts.

102.s: Committed expenditure consisting of salaries, pensions and interest payments accounted for what proportion of revenue receipts?

xs: **Committed expenditure** (salaries, pensions, interest) = **65.3%** of revenue receipts — option **(3)** is correct.
It leaves **little room** for discretionary spending.
Interest alone is **40%** of revenue receipts.
xa: States: committed expenditure + subsidies = **51.76%** of revenue expenditure in **FY24**.

102.s: For Indian States during 2014-24, revenue expenditure formed approximately what share of their total expenditure?
102.x: States' revenue expenditure was 80-87% of their total expenditure, while total State spending was 16.15-17.49% of GSDP in 2014-24. 50-55% and 60-65% understate the share; 92-97% overstates it.
102.tq: States spend mostly on revenue account: 80-87%.
xs: States' revenue expenditure was **80-87%** of total — option **(3)** is correct.
State spending was **16.15-17.49%** of GSDP over **2014-24**.
The other ranges understate or overstate the share.

**9 of 18** large States budget revenue deficits for 2026-27.

102.s: Closure of Oil-Pool account effected from :
102.x: Administered price mechanism (APM) in oil sector in India was abolished on 1.4.2002 during the finance ministership of Yashwant Sinha. Consequently Oil-Pool-Account was abolished. Petrol (decontrolled w.e.f. 26.06.2010), Diesel (decontrolled w.e.f. 19.10.2014), PDS Kerosene and Domestic LPG were being insulated from the impact of unprecedented high international oil prices by the Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) namely IOCL, HPCL & BPCL.

Grants to States are revenue expenditure even when used to create assets
It excludes grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets

102.s: Which of the following is an example of an implicit or hidden subsidy?
o: A fertiliser subsidy shown in the Budget
An export incentive shown as a Budget provision
A food subsidy shown as a separate Budget line item
Under-pricing of higher education in a public university

102.tq: Distinguish a visible Budget line item from under-pricing of a publicly provided service.
xs: **Under-pricing of higher education in a public university** is a hidden subsidy — option **(4)** is correct (**APPSC 2018**).
Food and fertiliser subsidies and **export incentives** shown in the Budget are **explicit** subsidies.

xa: Other hidden subsidies: **public health**, **irrigation water**, **power**.
Other explicit subsidies: **LPG**, **interest subvention**.
Budget 2026-27 subsidy bill: **₹4,54,773 crore**.

102.x: Revenue expenditure constituted approximately 83% of Andhra Pradesh’s total expenditure in the 2026-27 Budget Estimates.

xs: AP's revenue expenditure was about **83 percent** of the **2026-27 BE** total — option **(3)** is correct.
It is AP's largest component: **Revenue Expenditure > Capital Outlay > Loans and Advances**.
For comparison, States generally spend **80-87%** on revenue.

103.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the classification of the Union Government's liabilities?
o: Loans from foreign governments — Internal debt
103.x: Small savings and post-office deposits are other liabilities recorded in the Public Account. Market loans are internal debt, while loans from foreign governments are external debt.
103.tq: Distinguish internal debt, other liabilities and external debt by identifying the correct category.
xs: **Post-office deposits — Other liabilities** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Small savings** are also **other liabilities** (Public Account), not internal debt.
**Market loans** are **internal debt**; **loans from foreign governments** are **external debt**.

103.s: Internal debt constitutes what share of India's public debt?
103.x: Internal debt is 96.7% of public debt; G-Secs are over 90% of Central Government debt.

103.s: Public debt is classified into internal and external debt on the basis of the:
103.x: Internal and external debt are distinguished by where the government borrows from.
n: Internal debt is government debt raised within the domestic economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
External debt is government debt raised from external or foreign sources. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
Public debt is classified into internal debt and external debt. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
xa: **Public Debt (Art. 292)** = borrowings against the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
**Internal debt** = **96.7%** of public debt.

103.s: Short-term government debt instruments are called:
103.x: Treasury Bills are short-term; G-Secs are long-term and SDLs are issued by States.
n: Government dated securities, or G-Secs, are long-term government securities. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
Treasury bills are short-term government debt instruments. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
Market-based securities are issued through auctions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
The major conceptual instruments of external debt are external assistance and foreign borrowings. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
xa: T-Bills are of **91, 182, 364-day** tenors.
**Small savings**, **provident funds** and **reserve funds** are "**other liabilities**" in the Public Account.
⚠ Not all external debt is in **US dollars** (UPSC 2019).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about Internal Debt:
I. Its source is the domestic economy.
II. Its key idea is domestic borrowing.
III. It may involve foreign-denominated obligations.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: I and II are correct: internal debt is borrowed within the country. III is false because foreign-currency obligations belong to external debt.
n: The source of internal debt is the domestic economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
External debt may involve foreign currency or foreign-denominated obligations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
The key idea of internal debt is domestic borrowing. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
xs: Statements **I and II only** are correct — option **(4)**.
I: correct — internal debt is **raised within the domestic economy**.
II: correct — its key idea is **domestic borrowing**, generally in **domestic currency**.
III: incorrect — **foreign-denominated obligations** belong to **external debt**.
xa: Internal debt creditors: **domestic lenders, institutions or investors**.
Instruments: **G-Secs**, **T-Bills** and others; G-Secs are over **90%** of Central debt.
**Market loans** are a component of internal debt (APPSC-G2 2017).

103.s:
Assertion (A): External Debt may involve foreign currency or foreign-denominated obligations.
Reason (R): External Debt is government borrowing from external or foreign sources.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
